text: Duff Pringle is driving across the country to begin a new job in Silicon Valley. His used Ford Escort fails after only a hundred miles, forcing him to call a towing service. The car requires three to four days of repairs, but Duff has only two weeks to reach California. He checks into a motel near the repair center, intending to wait out the delay. While there, he finds a note offering a ride to St. Louis, and replies to it. The sender, a man named Stu, confirms they will deliver the car to the motel. Duff meets Stu in the parking lot. Stu is a hitchhiker heading west, and despite his worn clothes and restless manner, he asks to join Duff on the trip. Duff agrees. They drive the 1957 Chevrolet Bel Air to St. Louis, delivering it to a woman named Rosalie Hopgood. Along the way, they encounter several others: Bonnie, an aspiring singer whose mother is a fugitive con artist who stole money from many people; two thugs searching for a trunk full of cash; and Moony, a terrier dog who becomes ill in moving vehicles. The journey continues with no pause, as Duff and Stu travel toward California, carrying not only the car but the weight of unknown risks.

text: Birds, Beasts, and Relatives, like My Family and Other Animals, presents a series of autobiographical anecdotes from the Durrell family’s five-year stay on the Greek island of Corfu between 1935 and 1939. Gerald was ten when his mother, sister, and two brothers left England for Corfu. The stories are not arranged chronologically and, in places, are semi-fictionalised. For instance, Gerald’s eldest brother Larry—later known as the novelist Lawrence Durrell—did not live with the family as the book suggests; he was separated, residing with his wife Nancy, who does not appear in the narrative. The family includes their widowed mother, the gun-loving brother Leslie, sister Margo, and Roger the dog. They are sheltered by their close friend Spiro, a local taxi-driver known as Spyros "Americano" Chalikiopoulos, and guided by Dr Theodore Stephanides, a physician and polymath who becomes Gerald’s mentor in natural history.

text: In a study assessing the utility of optical spectral transmission (OST) for detecting synovitis in hand and wrist joints of patients with primary hand osteoarthritis (OA), 47 individuals with at least one clinically inflamed joint were evaluated using both OST and ultrasound (US) as the reference standard. The analysis focused on associations between standardized OST scores and US-confirmed synovitis across all joint types combined, as well as individually for wrist, proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. Linear mixed effects models were adjusted for OA features previously linked to US synovitis, including osteophytes and dorsal vascularity. Synovitis was detected in 6.7% of joints via US. Statistically significant associations between OST scores and US synovitis were observed for all joints combined (Δ0.37SD, p<0.001) and specifically for PIP joints (Δ0.81SD, p<0.001), though no significant associations were found for DIP joints (Δ0.14SD, p=0.484) or wrist joints (Δ0.37SD, p=0.178). These relationships remained significant after adjusting for osteophytes and dorsal vascularity, indicating independence from structural OA features. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. The area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC) was 0.74 for all joints together (p<0.001), 0.69 for PIP joints (p<0.001), 0.54 for DIP joints (p=0.486), and 0.61 for wrist joints (p=0.234). These findings confirm a significant, independent association between OST and US-verified synovitis, with OST demonstrating fair diagnostic accuracy specifically for PIP joints in hand OA patients.

To determine whether optical spectral transmission (OST) can be used to assess synovitis in hand and wrist joints of patients with hand osteoarthritis (OA).

Hand and wrist joints of 47 primary hand OA patients with at least one clinically inflamed hand or wrist joint were assessed for synovitis by OST and ultrasound (US). Associations between standardized OST and US synovitis were studied in linear mixed effects models, across all joint types together and individually for wrist, proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, and were adjusted for OA features that showed associations with US synovitis. Diagnostic performance was determined using receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curves analysis, with US as reference standard.

Altogether, 6.7% of joints showed US synovitis. Statistically significant associations between OST scores and US synovitis were found for all joints combined (Δ0.37SD, p<0.001) and PIP joints (Δ0.81SD, p<0.001), but not for DIP (Δ0.14SD, p = 0.484) or wrist joints (Δ0.37SD, p = 0.178). All associations were independent of other OA features, i.e. osteophytes and dorsal vascularity. Analysis of diagnostic performance of OST, revealed an area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.74 for all joints together (p<0.001), 0.69 for PIP joints (p<0.001), 0.54 for DIP joints (p = 0.486), and 0.61 for wrist joints (p = 0.234).

OST scores and US synovitis are statistically significantly associated, independent of osteophytes and dorsal vascularity. At this stage, OST performs fair in the assessment of synovitis in PIP joints of hand OA patients.
</source>

text: In Haa province, Bhutan, where rabies is not endemic, a study compared intramuscular (IM) and intradermal (ID) vaccination with inactivated rabies vaccine (Raksharab, Indian Immunologicals) in cattle. One hundred animals from 27 farms were assigned to receive either 1 mL IM or 0.2 mL ID. Virus neutralising antibody (VNA) titres were measured on day 0 and days 14, 30, 60, and 90 post-vaccination using the fluorescent antibody virus neutralisation test. An adequate response was defined as VNA ≥0.5 IU/mL. At day 0, no animals had detectable antibody levels. By day 14, 36% of ID-vaccinated cattle achieved adequate titres, compared to 78% in the IM group (p<0.02). At day 30, 58% of ID-vaccinated cattle met the threshold, versus 77% in the IM group (p<0.02). The overall proportion with adequate titres was 71% in the ID group and 89% in the IM group. Mean VNA titres were significantly lower in the ID group across all time points (p<0.001), with a mean difference exceeding 0.6 IU/mL. Although the ID route elicited a detectable immune response, it was consistently lower than that achieved by IM vaccination. The 0.2 mL ID dose did not produce equivalent or superior antibody titres compared to the 1 mL IM dose. These findings indicate that a single 0.2 mL ID dose of Raksharab vaccine is inferior to 1 mL IM in cattle. While intradermal vaccination offers potential for cost reduction through dose sparing, this study demonstrates that a single 0.2 mL ID dose is not sufficient to achieve equivalent immunogenicity. Further research is required to determine optimal dosing and regimens for intradermal rabies vaccination in cattle before it can be considered a viable alternative.

In developing countries, the cost of vaccination limits the use of prophylactic rabies vaccination, especially in cattle. Intradermal vaccination delivers antigen directly to an area with higher number of antigen-presenting cells. Therefore, it could produce equivalent or higher antibody titres than conventional intramuscular vaccination even when a lower dose is given. This study aimed to compare the antibody response in cattle vaccinated intramuscularly with 1mL of inactivated rabies vaccine (Raksharab, Indian Immunologicals) against intradermally vaccinated cattle with 0.2mL of the same vaccine. The study was conducted in Haa province of Bhutan where rabies is not endemic. One hundred cattle from 27 farms were selected for the study. Virus neutralising antibody (VNA) response was measured using the fluorescent antibody virus neutralisation test on the day of vaccination (day 0) and 14, 30, 60 and 90 days later. Overall, 71% of intradermally vaccinated cattle and 89% of the intramuscularly vaccinated cattle produced an adequate response (≥0.5IU/mL). On days 14 and 30 post vaccination fewer cattle (P<0.02) in the intradermal group had adequate titres with 36% and 58%, respectively, having titres ≥0.5 IU/mL compared to the equivalent figures of 78% and 77% in the intramuscular group. The mean VNA titres were lower for the intradermal group than intramuscular group (p<0.001) with the mean difference being > 0.6 IU/mL. Although low dose intradermal vaccination did produce a detectable antibody response, it was inferior to intramuscular vaccination. Thus, although intradermal vaccination has the potential to reduce the cost of vaccination by reducing the dose required, this study showed that a single dose of 0.2 mL intradermally was inferior to an intramuscular dose of 1 mL. Further research evaluating dose and dose regimen is needed before intradermal vaccination using the Raksharab rabies vaccine can be recommended in cattle.
</source>

text: Indonesia’s state-owned carrier Garuda Indonesia, along with private airlines Mandala Airlines and Airfast, had undertaken efforts to meet European Union aviation safety standards. The progress received support in May when Garuda passed a safety audit conducted by the International Air Transport Association. Despite this, a review committee noted that inspectors lacked authority to ground aircraft found to be substandard and recommended that Indonesia expand its own inspection capacity. Data from the Indonesian director-general of civil aviation showed that between January and April, Garuda completed only nine of 56 required surveys, while Mandala conducted just two of 27. The committee acknowledged partial improvement but unanimously rejected the airlines’ request to lift the EU ban. The restriction dates to 2007, following deregulation in the 1990s that preceded a series of aviation accidents. On New Year’s Day 2007, 102 people died when an Adam Air Boeing 737 crashed into the sea near Sulawesi. In March, a Garuda 737 overshot the runway at Yogyakarta International Airport, killing 21. Adam Air has since been grounded. Egypt has invited Israeli and Palestinian representatives to return to negotiations in Cairo next week, aiming to solidify the ceasefire reached two months ago after 50 days of intense fighting that left significant destruction and many casualties. The previous talks, which led to the truce, were brokered by Egypt and concluded with a plan to reconvene by the end of October to address outstanding issues.  

According to Hamas deputy leader Mousa Abu Marzook, the new round of talks will begin next Monday and will focus on several key items not fully settled in the initial agreement. These include plans for a marine port in the Gaza Strip, the long-stalled proposal to reopen the Gaza airport, efforts to reconstruct the territory, and the status of Palestinian prisoners held by Israel.  

The Palestinian delegation will be led by Fatah’s Azzam el-Ahmad, with participation from the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), Hamas, and the Palestinian Islamic Jihad. There has been no confirmation from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on whether Israel will attend the talks.  

The August 26 ceasefire, which ended the most recent major conflict between Israel and Gaza-based armed factions, was the result of backchannel discussions facilitated by Egypt. Now, with the truce still in effect but several major issues unresolved, Egypt’s renewed push seeks to stabilize the situation on the ground and prevent a return to violence.

text:
On Wednesday, an Emirates Boeing 777, flight EK52, crash-landed at Dubai International Airport with 282 passengers and 18 crew members on board. The aircraft landed with smoke visible shortly after touchdown and quickly caught fire. A firefighter, Jasim Issa Mohammed Hassan, died while responding to the blaze. The UAE's General Civil Aviation Authority Director-General, Saif Al Suwaidi, acknowledged the man’s sacrifice in saving numerous lives.

Passenger accounts described the pilot announcing an emergency landing minutes before impact. Survivors reported intense fear during the descent and immediate aftermath. The airport closed for four hours following the incident. All passengers and crew were accounted for and confirmed safe. Fourteen individuals were hospitalized with minor injuries.

The cause of the crash remains under investigation. Preliminary reports suggest the landing gear may not have deployed properly. An aviation safety consultant speaking to Australia’s ABC News said the successful evacuation of all on board, given the aircraft’s size, was a notable accomplishment.

Emirates confirmed the flight carried two Australians, eleven from the UAE, 24 from the UK, and 226 from India. The co-pilot, an Australian with about 7,000 hours of flight experience, was identified by Emirates chairman Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum. He stated the crash was not linked to any security failure.

text:
Chelsea’s parents don’t want her to have a birthday party because they think it would be too expensive. This makes Chelsea jealous of her siblings Geneva and Warwick, who receive more financial support from their parents. She finds comfort in a new friendship with Bex at the Stomping Ground nightclub. Their bond strengthens a few weeks later when Fee’s friend Eddie tries to assault Chelsea, and Bex rushes in to help her. 

Barry Gee opens his own restaurant, which he plans to name Gee Zone. Meanwhile, Jemma wants to become an actress, but her parents are upset when she skips school to attend acting and dancing lessons. She ignores their concerns and trusts Ms. Olivia Ockley, the head of the acting school, who tells her she has real talent. Still, Jemma feels frustrated when Alexa Browning is given a lead role instead of her. She also begins dating Rob, which causes tension with Chelsea—though they make peace after Chelsea’s encounter with Eddie.

Jon had hoped to date Sumitha, but she’s no longer interested. He’s frustrated by his parents’ lack of attention, but his feelings change after Laura is injured in front of him during one of his mother’s animal rights demonstrations. He realizes he likes her and asks her out. Laura’s mother is pregnant, and her boyfriend Melvyn disapproves of Laura spending time at the demonstrations with her neighbour Daniel. When Laura’s brother is born prematurely, she suggests naming him Charlie.

Sumitha becomes more focused on her studies after developing a crush on her new science teacher, Paul Sharpe. At the end of the term, she tells him how she feels—but learns he is engaged to Mrs. McConnell. When Sandeep asks her to return home, she refuses, and later feels guilty after hearing he’s being bullied by Kevin and Matthew.

text:
In the winter of 1864, in a small Dutch village near the canals of Holland, fifteen-year-old Hans Brinker and his younger sister Gretel dream of competing in the year’s most celebrated event: the great ice-skating race on the frozen canal. Their skates are homemade, cobbled together from wood, and far too frail for the demands of the course, but the promise of the Silver Skates—the coveted prize—keeps their hopes alive. Hans is no stranger to hardship. His father, Raff Brinker, lies ill and confused, his mind fractured by a fall from the dike years before, leaving him unable to work and prone to violent outbursts. With their mother laboring long hours and Hans and Gretel scraping for scraps, the family lives on the margins of village life, treated with quiet disdain for their poverty.

Hans chances upon Dr. Boekman, a renowned surgeon still raw from the grief of losing his wife and son. The doctor is stern, withdrawn, and dismissive—too expensive for the Brinkers to afford. Yet when Hans, trembling with resolve, offers every coin he’s saved, not for new skates but for his father’s life, the surgeon is moved. He agrees to examine Raff Brinker and finds that pressure on the brain requires an operation so delicate and dangerous it carries great risk. Still, he performs the trephining at no cost, swayed by Hans’s sacrifice.

With the surgery successful, Raff Brinker wakes not only healed but restored—his memory intact, his mind clear. The family’s fortunes begin to shift. The boy who once begged for help now stands on the ice, wearing steel skates he could only have dreamed of, racing in the boys’ event. Though he finishes first, he lets his friend claim the Silver Skates, knowing the boy’s need outweighs his own. Gretel wins the girls’ race, her joy as pure as the ice beneath her blades.

The miracle does not end there. Mr. Brinker’s long-lost savings, thought stolen or vanished a decade prior, are found intact in a forgotten trunk. The family, once on the edge of ruin, now has a future. Dr. Boekman, softened by the reunion with his long-missing son—guided by Raff’s recollections—becomes a quiet pillar in their lives. He sees to Hans’s education, and the boy becomes a doctor. Gretel, too, finds lasting peace and contentment. The Brinkers, once forgotten, rise—not by luck, but by the quiet dignity of a boy who gave everything for his father, and a doctor who learned kindness again.

text: It is increasingly recognized that cognitive and audiological factors are linked to self-perceived hearing handicap in older adults. This study compared self-perceived hearing handicap across subgroups of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and a cognitively normal elderly (CNE) group, and examined which factors—demographic, audiometric, or neuropsychological—are associated with hearing handicap in each group. A total of 46 MCI patients and 39 hearing threshold-matched CNE participants, aged 55 to 80, took part. MCI patients were reclassified into two subgroups: 16 with frontal-executive dysfunction (FED) and 30 without FED. All participants completed audiometric testing, neuropsychological assessments, and self-reported hearing handicap evaluations using the Korean version of the Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly (K-HHIE). After adjusting for age, years of education, and depression levels, no significant difference in K-HHIE scores was observed between the MCI and CNE groups as a whole. However, when MCI patients were divided into subgroups, those with FED reported significantly higher hearing handicap scores than both MCI patients without FED and the CNE group. After controlling for depression, significant partial correlations were found between hearing handicap scores and performance on frontal-executive function tasks and speech-in-noise perception within the MCI groups. In contrast, in the CNE group, hearing handicap scores were associated with peripheral hearing sensitivity and years of education. These findings indicate that MCI patients with FED report greater everyday hearing difficulties than those without FED or cognitively normal peers. While education and peripheral hearing function contribute to self-perceived hearing handicap in cognitively normal older adults, speech-in-noise perception and frontal-executive function appear to play a more central role in shaping hearing handicap among individuals with MCI.

text:
This study aimed to assess the incidence and risk factors for glucose intolerance one year postpartum within a sub-cohort of the Riyadh Mother and Baby Cohort Study (RAHMA), conducted at King Khalid University Hospital (KKUH). A follow-up survey was performed by telephone with women from the RAHMA database who had completed one year since delivery. Demographic, clinical, and biochemical data previously collected in the RAHMA registry were linked to this study. Anthropometric measurements included current weight, height, and waist circumference, used to calculate BMI. Fasting blood glucose (FPG) and HbA1c were measured to classify participants into three categories: normal glucose tolerance, prediabetes, or diabetes. Incidence rates of diabetes and prediabetes were determined across the cohort. Univariate comparisons of clinical, biochemical, and sociodemographic factors were performed between groups, and variables with p-values < 0.05 were included in multivariate regression models using bootstrapping to estimate relative risk (RR) and 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals (C.I.).

Of the 407 women who met inclusion criteria and participated, 250 (61.4%) had normal glucose tolerance, 142 (35.0%) were classified as pre-diabetic, and 15 (3.6%) were diabetic. After multivariable analysis, three factors independently predicted postpartum glucose intolerance: history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) (RR 1.74, 95% C.I. 1.06–2.84, p = 0.01), obesity (RR 1.69, 95% C.I. 1.01–3.11, p = 0.04), and diastolic blood pressure (RR 1.04, 95% C.I. 1.01–1.09, p = 0.03). The high incidence of postpartum glucose intolerance in this cohort underscores the critical role of GDM and obesity as key risk factors, highlighting the need for targeted screening and early intervention in postpartum Saudi women.

text:
The health economic evidence on the value and optimal targeting of genetic testing for preventing coronary heart disease (CHD) events remains limited and uncertain. This study aims to optimize the population-level use and targeting of genetic testing in conjunction with traditional risk factors to assess its cost-benefit in CHD prevention.

We evaluate multiple strategies for integrating traditional risk factors and genetic testing in guiding statin therapy. The targeting of genetic testing across patient subgroups within these strategies is optimized using a decision-analytic model that updates individual CHD risk estimates based on test results via Bayesian methods. The analysis adopts the healthcare sector’s perspective, drawing on an exceptionally broad dataset combining national healthcare registers, the Finnish Institute for Molecular Medicine, and published literature. Our findings indicate that the highest expected net benefit arises when genetic testing is directed toward patients for whom traditional risk factors alone provide insufficiently precise risk assessment. Specifically, compared to relying solely on traditional risk factors, optimally targeted genetic testing reduces the expected costs of an average patient aged 45 or older by 2.54€ over a 10-year period—without compromising the expected health outcome. This demonstrates that genetic testing, when used strategically alongside traditional risk factors, forms a cost-beneficial component of CHD prevention. The conclusion holds under reasonable variations in model inputs, indicating robustness. Thus, if applied with optimal targeting, genetic testing alongside traditional risk factors constitutes a cost-beneficial approach to preventing CHD.

text:
European Union leaders, during the second day of their summit in Brussels, reached agreement on a set of binding targets aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions and expanding the use of biological fuels. The 27 member states endorsed three core objectives, designed to support the broader international goal of keeping global temperature rise below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. National emission reduction plans will be developed according to each country’s existing energy infrastructure and potential for change, though no formal enforcement mechanism has yet been established. The E.U. has indicated it may raise its targets if other developed nations commit to comparable actions, and has urged non-E.U. countries to submit their own environmental strategies ahead of the 2012 expiration of the Kyoto Protocol. German Chancellor Angela Merkel plans to present the E.U.’s framework to the Group of Eight in June.

The agreement respects national sovereignty over energy choices, including the option to adopt or reject nuclear power. This flexibility acknowledges divergent national policies: Germany is actively phasing out nuclear energy, while France generates 70% of its electricity through nuclear reactors—accounting for 13% of the country’s total energy consumption. The discussion emphasized that nuclear safety remains a critical factor in any assessment of nuclear energy’s role.

The summit also directed the European Commission to draft proposals for reducing energy use in lighting and office equipment by 2008 and 2009, with a focus on phasing out conventional incandescent bulbs in favor of energy-efficient alternatives. Additionally, the E.U. reaffirmed its commitment to enhancing energy security, particularly for eastern member states, through greater market integration, cross-border infrastructure, and solidarity among members in the event of supply disruptions, including potential cuts from Russia.

Beyond energy policy, the two-day meeting addressed economic growth, employment, regulatory reform, and external relations.

text:
A multi-institutional retrospective study evaluated outcomes in 152 patients with stage II–IV bladder cancer treated with curative-intent radiotherapy between 2000 and 2010. Patients were stratified by stage: 72 with stage II, 49 with stage III, and 31 with stage IV. Treatment consisted of either concurrent chemoradiotherapy (n = 97) or radiotherapy alone (n = 55). Pelvic radiation was delivered with a median dose of 63 Gy, primarily using cisplatin-based regimens. Median follow-up duration was 35.5 months.

A complete response to radiotherapy was observed in 69 patients (45.4%). The 5-year overall survival rate was 45.8%, the 5-year cause-specific survival rate was 48.9%, and the 5-year disease-free survival rate was 20.8%. Univariate analysis identified significant associations between survival outcomes and patient age, initial hemoglobin level, clinical T stage, clinical N stage, clinical stage group, tumor response to radiotherapy, presence of hydronephrosis, and use of concurrent chemotherapy. Multivariate analysis confirmed patient age as a significant predictor of both overall survival (p = 0.003) and cause-specific survival (p < 0.017). Tumor response to radiotherapy remained a significant factor for improved overall survival (p = 0.002) and cause-specific survival (p < 0.001). Concurrent chemotherapy was independently associated with better disease-free survival (p = 0.046). The survival rates observed are consistent with those reported in similar cohorts. Tumor response to radiotherapy and concurrent chemoradiotherapy emerged as key prognostic factors. Further randomized trials are required to determine the definitive role of radiotherapy in muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

<source>
Although radical cystectomy is a standard treatment in muscle-invasive bladder cancer, bladder preservation therapy including transurethral resection of bladder tumor, radiotherapy, and concurrent chemotherapy has been widely adopted, recently. This retrospective analysis was performed to evaluate the survival rates and prognostic factors related to treatment outcomes following bladder-preserving therapy including radiotherapy (RT) in bladder cancer with a curative intent.

We conducted a multi-institutional retrospective study of 152 patients with stage II-IV bladder cancer treated with curative RT between 2000 and 2010. There were 72 patients in stage II, 49 in stage III, and 31 in stage IV. Ninety-seven patients were treated with concurrent chemoradiotherapy and fifty-five with RT alone. Radiation was delivered to the pelvis (median 63 Gy), mainly with cisplatin. The median follow-up time was 35.5 months.

Sixty-nine patients (45.4%) showed a complete response to RT. The 5-year overall survival (OS) rate was 45.8%, the 5-year cause-specific survival (CSS) rate was 48.9%, and the 5-year disease-free survival (DFS) rate was 20.8%. Univariate analysis revealed significant differences in the following factors according to the survival rates: patient age, initial hemoglobin level, clinical T stage, clinical N stage, clinical stage group, tumor response to RT, hydronephrosis, and concurrent chemotherapy. Multivariate analysis also revealed a significant difference in patient age (p = 0.003 in OS, p<0.017 in CSS) and tumor response to RT (p = 0.002 in OS, p<0.001 in CSS). Concurrent chemotherapy was significantly different in the DFS rates (p = 0.046).

The survival rates reported herein are comparable to those from other studies, and tumor response and concurrent chemoradiotherapy were significant prognostic factors for better survival rates. Further randomized studies are needed to elucidate the impact of RT in bladder cancer.
</source>

Indonesia has implemented a program to bring state-owned Garuda Indonesia up to European Union aviation standards, as well as upgrading private carriers Mandala Airlines and Airfast. The effort received a boost in May when Garuda passed a safety audit conducted by the International Air Transport Association. On New Year’s Day 2007, 102 people died when an Adam Air Boeing 737 crashed into the sea near Sulawesi. In March, a Garuda 737 overshot the runway at Yogyakarta International Airport, killing 21. Adam Air has since been grounded. On Thursday, Captain Marwoto Komar, the pilot of the Garuda aircraft involved in the Yogyakarta incident, began trial on multiple charges, including one that could result in life imprisonment.

text:
Forty families have been evacuated from the Guardia Civil barracks in Calahorra, La Rioja, after a car bomb exploded there this afternoon, due to structural damage to the building. The blast, which occurred around 2 p.m., caused only minor injuries: some cuts and bruises among those nearby. Among the injured was a Civil Guard who sustained a neck injury after diving to the ground to avoid the explosion. National Radio reported that eight people were treated at the local hospital; all have since been released.

The device was planted by the Basque terrorist group ETA. Half an hour before detonation, a phone call was made to the DYA road assistance association in Vizcaya, claiming responsibility in ETA’s name. The bomb was placed in a blue Honda Civic, which was hurled across the street by the blast’s force. The car’s owners were found later today, bound and gagged in a remote mountain area about 100 kilometers away. They told police their vehicle had been stolen at gunpoint earlier that morning.

The site of the explosion is a heavily trafficked area, not least because a major Holy Week procession had just concluded. The barracks had previously been targeted by ETA in 1983, also without loss of life. Authorities remain concerned that a second device may still be active in the vicinity.

A public demonstration against the attack is scheduled for 8 p.m. tonight outside Calahorra Town Hall. La Rioja regional president Pedro Sanz plans to visit the scene and join the protest. He stated that a massacre had been avoided only because the area was evacuated in time. The incident follows, just two weeks after, the killing of Isaías Carrasco, a former Socialist councillor, who was shot dead in his home in Mondragón.

text:
In 19th century Georgia, under Russian imperial rule, a peasant boy named Iago falls in love with Nunu, a young woman whose mother died early. Her father, a soldier in the Shamil rebellion, lacks the means to support her, so she lives with her uncle’s family. They disapprove of her relationship with Iago, whom they see as a mere plebeian. Instead, they favor Grigola, the Russian-appointed village governor, a man who is married yet obsessed with Nunu. Grigola pretends his brother wishes to marry her, but intends to keep her as his mistress. To eliminate Iago, Grigola accuses him of stealing state property and has him imprisoned in the Ananuri fortress. He then kidnaps and rapes Nunu.

Koba, Iago’s closest friend, witnesses the abduction. He fights through Grigola’s guards to reach her but arrives too late. He vows revenge. With help from another friend, Koba breaks Iago out of jail. The three decide to flee to the Northern Caucasus and seek refuge in Chechnya, where Russian police and Cossacks are actively hunting them across Georgia. Though many Georgians fought for the Russian side, Shamil receives them and offers sanctuary. The narrative contrasts the Chechens—portrayed as free men fighting for their independence—with the Georgians, who, under rulers like Grigola, are denied basic freedoms, even the right to hold town meetings, a tradition that once endured since the Middle Ages.

Meanwhile, Nunu escapes from Grigola. Koba contacts her and instructs her to meet the group in Vladikavkaz, in North Ossetia, along with her father. The night before their reunion, Koba’s host, who has been sheltering them, betrays them. Hoping to gain their horses, he informs Grigola of their whereabouts. After midnight, Grigola arrives with armed men. He kills Iago, the host, and Nunu’s father, intending to frame Nunu and have her sent to Siberia. Koba escapes the massacre. Upon learning of his lover’s death and the murder of his friend and Nunu’s father, Nunu dies from grief.

In the story’s final act, Koba tracks down Grigola and his superior. He waits for them in a forest and shoots both in a cab. Koba becomes the story’s hero—not only for his courage and loyalty, but for upholding friendship, defending truth, honoring women, and carrying out justice. His actions complete the arc of retribution, leaving no ambiguity about who bears responsibility for the tragedy that unfolded in the shadow of empire.

text:
This study aimed to determine the incidence and risk factors for glucose intolerance one year postpartum within a sub-cohort of the Riyadh Mother and Baby Cohort Study (RAHMA). The analysis was conducted using data from a follow-up of women enrolled in RAHMA at King Khalid University Hospital (KKUH). All women in the RAHMA database who had completed one year since delivery were contacted by telephone to assess eligibility and participation. Previously collected data from the RAHMA registry were linked to this study’s dataset. Clinical measurements included current weight and height for body mass index (BMI) calculation, waist circumference, fasting blood glucose (FPG), and HbA1c. Based on these results, participants were classified into three categories: normal glucose tolerance, prediabetes, or diabetes. The overall incidence of diabetes and prediabetes was calculated. Clinical, biochemical, and sociodemographic factors were compared across groups. Variables with univariate P-values less than 0.05 were further evaluated in multivariable regression models using bootstrapping to estimate relative risk (RR) and 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals (C.I.).

Of the 407 women who met inclusion criteria and participated, 250 (61.4%) had normal glucose tolerance, 142 (35.0%) were classified as pre-diabetic, and 15 (3.6%) were diabetic. After multivariable adjustment, three factors independently predicted postpartum glucose intolerance: a history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.06–2.84, P = 0.01), obesity (RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.01–3.11, P = 0.04), and diastolic blood pressure (RR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01–1.09, P = 0.03). The high prevalence of postpartum glucose intolerance in Saudi women underscores GDM and obesity as key modifiable risk factors requiring targeted screening and intervention.

The novel is set in 19th-century Georgia, under Russian imperial rule. It centers on Iago, a peasant boy, and Nunu, a young woman of striking beauty. Nunu’s mother died when she was young; her father, a soldier in the coalition army fighting the Shamil rebellion, could not support her. She lives with her uncle’s family, who disapprove of her relationship with Iago, viewing him as a mere plebeian. Instead, they favor Grigola, the Russian-appointed village governor, who is married but obsessed with Nunu. Grigola, driven by desire, convinces her family that his brother wishes to marry her—though he intends to keep her as his mistress. To secure her, he must first eliminate Iago.

Grigola accuses Iago of stealing state property and orders him imprisoned in the Ananuri fortress. Shortly after, he kidnaps and rapes Nunu. Koba, Iago’s closest friend, witnesses the abduction. He fights through Grigola’s guards to reach her, but arrives too late. Consumed by rage, Koba swears revenge. With the help of another friend, he helps Iago escape from prison. Together, they decide to flee to the Northern Caucasus and seek refuge in Chechnya, as Russian police and Cossacks are hunting them throughout Georgia. Though many Georgians fought for Russia, Shamil welcomes them and offers shelter.

The author presents the Chechens as free people who resist oppression, contrasting them with Georgians, who, under rulers like Grigola, have lost the right to hold town meetings—once a longstanding tradition. Meanwhile, Nunu escapes from Grigola. Koba contacts her and instructs her to meet them in Vladikavkaz, in North Ossetia, along with her father. The night before their reunion, Iago and Koba’s host betray them, informing Grigola of their location in exchange for horses. After midnight, Grigola arrives. He kills Iago, the host, and Nunu’s father, hoping to frame Nunu and have her exiled to Siberia. Koba escapes the massacre, but when he learns of his friend’s and father-in-law’s deaths, Nunu dies from sorrow.

At the story’s end, Koba avenges both Iago and Nunu. He tracks down Grigola and his superior, killing them both in a forest cabin, after they are trapped in a cab. Koba emerges as the story’s hero—loyal to friendship, committed to truth, protective of women, and determined to uphold justice.

text:
Forty families have been evacuated from the Guardia Civil barracks in Calahorra, La Rioja, following a car bomb explosion at approximately 2 p.m. The blast caused structural damage to the building, prompting the emergency evacuation. Among the injured was a Civil Guard officer who sustained a neck injury after diving to the ground to avoid the explosion; he was treated for minor trauma. National Radio reported that eight individuals received medical attention at the local hospital, all of whom were released after treatment. No fatalities occurred.

The device was placed in a blue Honda Civic, which was hurled across the street by the force of the explosion. The vehicle had been stolen at gunpoint earlier that morning, and its owners were found later in the afternoon, bound and unconscious in a remote mountainous area about 100 kilometers away. Police have confirmed the vehicle’s disappearance and the circumstances of its theft.

The attack was carried out by the Basque separatist group ETA. A phone call to the DYA road assistance association in Vizcaya, made 30 minutes before the explosion, claimed responsibility in ETA’s name. The location of the blast is a high-traffic area, coinciding with the conclusion of one of Spain’s major Holy Week processions. The barracks had previously been targeted by ETA in 1983, when an attack occurred without casualties.

Security forces remained alert for a secondary device, as the area was considered vulnerable. The regional government of La Rioja, led by President Pedro Sanz, condemned the attack. Sanz planned to visit the scene and participate in a demonstration scheduled for 8 p.m. at Calahorra Town Hall. He stated that a large-scale loss of life would have occurred had the evacuation not been carried out in time. The incident follows the assassination of Isaías Carrasco, a former Socialist councillor, in Mondragón two weeks prior—an attack also attributed to ETA.

text:
Von Willebrand factor (VWF) plays a central role in primary hemostasis and wound sealing through its multimeric structure and functional interactions. The release of arginine vasopressin (AVP) triggers the secretion of VWF, particularly high molecular weight multimers, into circulation. In a prior study, we observed markedly elevated serum copeptin levels—reflecting AVP activity—in children experiencing febrile seizures (FS) compared to those with fever alone. Whether this neuroendocrine activation confers a physiological effect remains unclear. We hypothesized that increased AVP release during FS would be accompanied by enhanced VWF activity, supporting a functional link between neurohormonal stress and hemostatic activation.

A prospective, cross-sectional design was employed to evaluate children aged 6 months to 5 years presenting to the emergency department with fever or within four hours of a febrile seizure. Serum copeptin, VWF:antigen (VWF:Ag), VWF:collagen binding activity (VWF:CB), and multimeric profiles were measured in three groups: 30 with FS, 10 with febrile infection but no seizure, and 14 without fever. Median copeptin concentrations were significantly higher in the FS group (24.73 pmol/L, IQR 13.65–68.65) versus both febrile controls (5.66 pmol/L, IQR 4.15–8.07; p = 0.002) and non-febrile controls (4.78 pmol/L, IQR 3.33–5.30; p < 0.001). VWF:CB was also significantly elevated in FS patients (2.29 U/mL, IQR 1.88–2.97) compared to febrile (1.41 U/mL, IQR 1.27–1.93; p = 0.048) and non-febrile (1.15 U/mL, IQR 0.98–1.21; p < 0.001) controls. VWF:Ag showed a nonsignificant trend toward higher values in FS. Multivariate regression identified FS status and copeptin as independent predictors of VWF:CB. These findings indicate that neuroendocrine activation during febrile seizures is associated with measurable increases in VWF functional activity, particularly collagen binding capacity. This supports a biological role for AVP in modulating hemostatic pathways during febrile seizures and suggests VWF:CB as a potential biomarker in the context of FS.

Primary blood coagulation and wound sealing are orchestrated by von Willebrand factor (VWF), a large multimeric glycoprotein. Upon release of arginine vasopressin (AVP), VWF containing high molecular weight multimers is secreted. By measuring copeptin, the C-terminal part of the AVP prohormone, we recently found strongly increased AVP levels in children with febrile seizures (FS) as compared to children with fever but without seizures. It is unknown if increased AVP levels in FS are of any biological function. Therefore, our a priori hypothesis was that children with FS have increased VWF parameters in parallel with higher AVP levels.

We conducted a prospective, cross-sectional study of children aged between 6 months and 5 years. Children that presented at our emergency department with fever or a recent FS (within four hours) were evaluated to be included to the study. We measured serum copeptin and VWF parameters, including analyses of VWF:Antigen (WVF:Ag), VWF:collagen binding activity (VWF:CB) and VWF multimers in children with FS, febrile infections without seizures and additionally, in a non-febrile control group.

We included 54 children in our study, 30 with FS, 10 in the febrile control group, and 14 in the non-febrile control group. Serum copeptin levels were significantly higher in children with FS (median [IQR] 24.73 pmol/l [13.65–68.65]) compared to the febrile control group (5.66 pmol/l [4.15–8.07], p = 0.002) and the non-febrile control group (4.78 pmol/l [3.33–5.3], p<0.001). VWF:CB levels were also significantly higher in children with FS (VWF:CB 2.29 U/ml [1.88–2.97]) as compared to the febrile (VWF:CB 1.41 U/ml [1.27–1.93], p = 0.048) and the non-febrile control group (VWF:CB 1.15 U/ml [0.98–1.21], p<0.001). VWF:Ag tended to be higher in children with FS compared to both control groups. Multivariate regression analysis revealed FS and copeptin as major determinants of VWF:CB.

Our results suggest that increased secretion of AVP in children with FS is associated with higher plasma levels of VWF parameters. Especially VWF:CB may serve as additional biomarker in the diagnosis of FS.
</source>

An effort by British Petroleum to contain the large oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico encountered another setback, according to company officials. The operation involved deploying a tube via robotic submarines to connect with the ruptured pipe, but the attempt on Friday failed. The company has already spent several hundred million U.S. dollars on response efforts. Additionally, BP received authorization from the U.S. Coast Guard and the Environmental Protection Agency to apply chemical oil dispersants to mitigate the spill’s spread.

text:
Although radical cystectomy remains a standard treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, bladder preservation strategies—including transurethral resection of bladder tumor, radiotherapy (RT), and concurrent chemotherapy—have been widely adopted in recent years. This retrospective analysis evaluates survival outcomes and identifies prognostic factors associated with curative-intent bladder-preserving RT in patients with locally advanced bladder cancer.

We conducted a multi-institutional retrospective study of 152 patients with clinical stage II–IV bladder cancer treated with curative RT between 2000 and 2010. Of these, 72 were stage II, 49 were stage III, and 31 were stage IV. Ninety-seven received concurrent chemoradiotherapy; 55 received RT alone. Pelvic radiation was delivered at a median dose of 63 Gy, primarily with cisplatin. Median follow-up was 35.5 months.

Sixty-nine patients (45.4%) achieved a complete response to RT. The 5-year overall survival (OS) rate was 45.8%, the 5-year cause-specific survival (CSS) rate was 48.9%, and the 5-year disease-free survival (DFS) rate was 20.8%. Univariate analysis identified significant associations with survival for patient age, initial hemoglobin level, clinical T stage, clinical N stage, clinical stage group, tumor response to RT, presence of hydronephrosis, and use of concurrent chemotherapy. Multivariate analysis confirmed that patient age (p = 0.003 for OS, p < 0.017 for CSS) and tumor response to RT (p = 0.002 for OS, p < 0.001 for CSS) were independently significant predictors of survival. Concurrent chemotherapy was significantly associated with improved DFS (p = 0.046).

Survival outcomes in this cohort are consistent with those reported in other series. Tumor response to RT and concurrent chemoradiotherapy emerged as key prognostic factors for improved survival. Future randomized trials are needed to clarify the long-term role of RT in bladder cancer management.

text: Student-centered pedagogies improve learning and retention. To assess curricular transformation in an introductory biology course at a small liberal arts college, we implemented the Integrating Biology and Inquiry Skills (IBIS) curriculum and measured learning gains and student perceptions over time. Quantitative assessments confirmed significant learning gains in core biological concepts, aligning with student-reported improvements. Students across successive cohorts consistently reported higher perceived learning, with increasing confidence in the curriculum’s effectiveness. Over time, student buy-in strengthened, as evidenced by longitudinal data from multiple assessment instruments. This pattern suggests that as more students successfully complete the course, shared experience fosters a sense of community and enhances trust in the pedagogical approach. Students increasingly identified specific IBIS components—such as inquiry-based laboratories and structured peer discussions—as central to their academic progress. These findings support the hypothesis that cumulative success within a cohort enhances student engagement and perceived value of active learning. The results indicate that sustained implementation of student-centered curricula like IBIS contributes to both measurable learning outcomes and a self-reinforcing culture of academic investment.

text: The book follows Catherine McKenna, a Northern Irish music teacher and composer living in Scotland, as she grapples with postpartum depression. Amid preparations for her father’s funeral, she confronts disturbing visions of her newborn daughter, Anna, and navigates restrictions imposed by the Catholic Church on her family and her childhood. In response, she channels her anguish into music—drawing on intuition and catharsis to compose. Later in the narrative, she begins work on a master symphony. The novel concludes with a powerful live radio broadcast of her completed work. The title evokes grace notes—“the notes between the notes,” as one character puts it—symbolizing both the elusive beauty of music and the quiet, unspoken moments that shape experience. The redemptive power of art emerges as a central theme. Critics have noted that the novel’s delicate, precise style mirrors the fleeting quality of these minute musical notes (Donath).

text:
We aimed to evaluate whether optical spectral transmission (OST) can assess synovitis in hand and wrist joints of patients with primary hand osteoarthritis (OA). In a cohort of 47 patients with at least one clinically inflamed hand or wrist joint, synovitis was assessed using both OST and ultrasound (US), with US serving as the reference standard. We analyzed associations between standardized OST scores and US-defined synovitis using linear mixed effects models, examining all joint types collectively and separately for wrist, proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. Analyses were adjusted for OA features—specifically osteophytes and dorsal vascularity—that were independently associated with US synovitis. Diagnostic performance was assessed via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

Overall, 6.7% of joints showed US-defined synovitis. Significant associations between OST scores and US synovitis were observed for all joints combined (Δ0.37SD, p < 0.001) and PIP joints (Δ0.81SD, p < 0.001), but not for DIP joints (Δ0.14SD, p = 0.484) or wrist joints (Δ0.37SD, p = 0.178). These associations remained significant after adjusting for osteophytes and dorsal vascularity. ROC analysis revealed an area under the curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.74 for all joints (p < 0.001), 0.69 for PIP joints (p < 0.001), 0.54 for DIP joints (p = 0.486), and 0.61 for wrist joints (p = 0.234). 

OST scores are significantly associated with US-defined synovitis, independent of osteophytes and dorsal vascularity. At present, OST shows fair diagnostic performance for detecting synovitis in PIP joints of hand OA patients.

Hand and wrist joints of 47 primary hand OA patients with at least one clinically inflamed hand or wrist joint were assessed for synovitis by OST and ultrasound (US). Diagnostic performance was determined using receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curves analysis, with US as reference standard.

Altogether, 6.7% of joints showed US synovitis. Statistically significant associations between OST scores and US synovitis were found for all joints combined (Δ0.37SD, p<0.001) and PIP joints (Δ0.81SD, p<0.001), but not for DIP (Δ0.14SD, p = 0.484) or wrist joints (Δ0.37SD, p = 0.178). All associations were independent of other OA features, i.e. osteophytes and dorsal vascularity. Analysis of diagnostic performance of OST, revealed an area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.74 for all joints together (p<0.001), 0.69 for PIP joints (p<0.001), 0.54 for DIP joints (p = 0.486), and 0.61 for wrist joints (p = 0.234).

OST scores and US synovitis are statistically significantly associated, independent of osteophytes and dorsal vascularity. At this stage, OST performs fair in the assessment of synovitis in PIP joints of hand OA patients.

text: Youth with chronic illnesses are increasingly common worldwide, and they report alcohol and marijuana use at levels comparable to or exceeding those of their healthy peers. When they use substances, they face heightened risks of regular or problematic use, as well as adverse outcomes related to their medical conditions. Despite this, little is known about whether established behavioral theories of adolescent substance use apply to this population, which limits the development of effective, tailored prevention strategies. To address this gap, we conducted in-depth interviews with youth aged 16 to 19 who were receiving care for a chronic illness. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using thematic coding. Three core themes emerged. First, a chronic illness shapes how youth understand and prioritize health-protecting behaviors, often motivating them to avoid substance use due to concerns about disease flares or complications. Second, typical adolescent developmental impulses—such as increased sensation-seeking and risk-taking—can override this medical awareness, leading some youth to make maladaptive decisions in an attempt to manage perceived risks. Third, many youth lack accurate knowledge about how substance use affects specific aspects of their illness, which distorts their perception of risk and undermines protective behaviors. In response, youth employ various strategies: some abstain entirely or temporarily, others continue use while minimizing perceived risks, and some adjust their treatment regimens without medical input. These patterns reflect a complex interplay between illness-related concerns, developmental factors, and knowledge limitations. The findings suggest that integrating targeted, patient-centered guidance into clinical care could help youth align personal goals with health-protecting behaviors, supporting better long-term outcomes.

Increasing numbers of youth globally live with a chronic illness. These youth use alcohol and marijuana at levels equal to or greater than their healthy peers and, when using, are at elevated risk for regular or problem use and adverse consequences to their condition. Little is known about whether behavioral theories commonly invoked to explain adolescent substance use apply to this group, limiting our ability to develop, tailor and target preventive interventions. We interviewed youth ages 16–19 years in care for a chronic disease to gain knowledge of this group’s perspectives on substance use risk, decision-making, and preferences for clinical guidance. Interviews were transcribed and thematically analyzed. Three principal themes emerged: first, having a chronic disease frames understanding of and commitment to health protecting behaviors and impacts decisions to avoid behaviors that carry risks for disease complications and flares; second, developmental impulses typical of adolescence can amplify an adolescent’s propensity to take risks despite medical vulnerability and direct youth toward maladaptive choices to mitigate risk; and third, poor knowledge about effects of substance use on specific features of a disease shapes perceived risk and undermines health protecting decisions. Youth navigate these issues variously including by avoiding substance use at a specific time or entirely, using while cognitively discounting risks and/or adjusting treatment outside of medical advice. Their perceptions about substance use are complex and reveal tension among choices reflecting a chronic illness frame, developmental impulses, and knowledge gaps. Delivery of targeted guidance in healthcare settings may help youth navigate this complexity and connect patient-centered goals to optimize health with health protecting behavioral decisions.
</source>

text:
Euskadi Ta Askatasuna (ETA), the Basque separatist group active in northern Spain and parts of south-western France, declared a permanent ceasefire effective at 00:00 AM on 24 March 2006. The organization, which has sought independence for the seven regions in northern Spain and south-western France historically claimed by Basque separatists, stated that the ceasefire was intended to enable a democratic process through dialogue, negotiation, and agreement. ETA, whose name means Basque Homeland and Freedom, originated in the 1960s as a student resistance movement opposing General Franco’s military dictatorship. The group has been designated a terrorist organization by Spain, France, the European Union, and the United States, with more than eight hundred killings linked to its activities.

The ceasefire followed a prior pattern of broken ceasefires in the 1990s. A permanent end to hostilities had been a condition set by Spain’s Socialist government under Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero for initiating negotiations with ETA. The group asserted that the democratic framework necessary for the Basque Country must recognize the rights of the Basque people and allow for the full development of all political options. It emphasized that citizens of the Basque region must have the right to decide their future through democratic means. ETA maintained that the process must reflect the plurality and totality of Basque society and that the Spanish and French states must recognize its outcome without interference or limitation. The group asserted that any decision made by Basque citizens must be respected.

ETA called on Spain and France to respond positively to the ceasefire, urging them not to obstruct the democratic process by resorting to repression. It also addressed the citizens of the Basque region and members of the Abertzale Left, urging their participation in the new phase. The organization reaffirmed its commitment to achieving the rights of Euskal Herria—Basque Country—through agreed steps and stated that peace based on justice was now possible. It described the ceasefire as a step toward ending a long-standing conflict, emphasizing that the time had come for open dialogue and that responsible, negotiated action was necessary to build a lasting democratic solution.

text: Antisense molecules designed as antibiotics hold promise for overcoming acquired resistance, as their sequences can be rapidly redesigned in response to bacterial mutations in the target gene. Once resistance emerges through target sequence alteration, a new antisense can be synthesized using updated genetic information. However, these molecules require engineered delivery vehicles to traverse bacterial membranes and avoid degradation. While developing new delivery systems poses greater challenges than redesigning antisense cargo, the effort appears less formidable than discovering entirely new conventional small molecule antibiotics. Here, we present a protocol that optimizes the synergy between tailored delivery vehicles and antisense payloads by minimizing the selective advantage conferred to pathogens by mutations in entry mechanisms, while simultaneously enhancing the fitness cost of mutations in the antisense target. Computer simulations demonstrate that, when properly designed, antisense therapies could remain effective for significantly longer durations than conventional antibiotics before resistance compromises their efficacy. Although the simulations model an in-vitro environment, comparisons with established in-vitro resistance studies suggest this strategy offers a substantially higher potential for sustained therapeutic success in vivo.

An effort to contain the massive oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico has struck another setback, according to officials at British Petroleum (BP). The latest attempt to insert a containment tube into the ruptured pipe failed Friday when robotic submarines tried to deploy it. BP plans a new attempt Saturday night (local time), using a reconfigured version of the tube in hopes of slowing the leak. If that fails, the company will deploy the smaller dome previously used in earlier efforts. Meanwhile, the company is already drilling relief wells—expected to take several more months—to permanently stop the flow.

The volume of oil escaping remains disputed, but BP confirmed it has spent several hundred million U.S. dollars on containment and cleanup operations. In addition, BP was granted authorization Friday by the U.S. Coast Guard and the Environmental Protection Agency to apply chemical dispersants, aiming to break up surface oil and reduce environmental impact.

text: Cognitive and audiological factors are increasingly recognized as contributors to self-perceived hearing handicap in older adults. This study compared self-perceived hearing handicap across mild cognitive impairment (MCI) subgroups and a cognitively normal elderly (CNE) group, and examined which demographic, audiometric, or neuropsychological factors correlate with hearing handicap in each group. Forty-six MCI patients and 39 hearing threshold-matched CNE subjects, aged 55 to 80 years, participated. MCI patients were reclassified into two subgroups: 16 with frontal-executive dysfunction (FED) and 30 without FED. All participants completed audiometric testing, neuropsychological assessments, and the Korean version of the Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly (K-HHIE) to measure self-perceived hearing handicap. After adjusting for age, years of education, and depression levels, no significant difference in K-HHIE scores was observed between the overall MCI group and the CNE group. However, when MCI patients were divided by FED status, those with FED reported significantly higher hearing handicap scores than both MCI patients without FED and the CNE group. In MCI patients, after controlling for depression, significant partial correlations emerged between K-HHIE scores and performance on frontal-executive function tasks and speech-in-noise perception. In the CNE group, hearing handicap scores were significantly associated with peripheral hearing sensitivity and years of education. These findings indicate that MCI patients with FED experience greater everyday hearing difficulty than those without FED or cognitively normal older adults. While peripheral hearing function and educational attainment predict self-perceived hearing handicap in cognitively normal individuals, speech-in-noise perception and frontal-executive function are primary correlates in MCI patients, suggesting distinct pathways linking cognition and hearing handicap in older adults with MCI.

<source>
It is increasingly agreed upon that cognitive and audiological factors are associated with self-perceived hearing handicap in old adults. This study aimed to compare self-perceived hearing handicap among mild cognitive impairment (MCI) subgroups and a cognitively normal elderly (CNE) group and determine which factors (i.e., demographic, audiometric, or neuropsychological factors) are correlated with self-perceived hearing handicap in each group. A total of 46 MCI patients and 39 hearing threshold-matched CNE subjects participated in this study, and their age ranged from 55 to 80 years. The MCI patients were reclassified into two groups: 16 with frontal-executive dysfunction (FED) and 30 without FED. All subjects underwent audiometric, neuropsychological, and self-perceived hearing handicap assessments. The Korean version of the Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly (K-HHIE) was administered to obtain the hearing handicap scores for each subject. After controlling for age, years of education, and depression levels, we found no significant differences in the K-HHIE scores between the MCI and the CNE groups. However, after we classified the MCI patients into the MCI with FED and MCI without FED groups, the MCI with FED group scored significantly higher than did both the MCI without FED and the CNE groups. In addition, after controlling for depression levels, significant partial correlations of hearing handicap scores with frontal-executive function scores and speech-in-noise perception performance were found in the MCI groups. In the CNE group, the hearing handicap scores were related to peripheral hearing sensitivity and years of education. In summary, MCI patients with FED are more likely to experience everyday hearing handicap than those without FED and cognitively normal old adults. Although educational level and peripheral hearing function are related to self-perceived hearing handicap in cognitively normal old adults, speech-in-noise perception and frontal-executive function are mainly associated with hearing handicap in patients with MCI.
</source>

text: In 1935, ten-year-old Gerald Durrell and his family relocated from England to the Greek island of Corfu, where they lived for five years. The family included his mother, sister Margo, brother Leslie, and brother Larry, who was not actually present in Corfu as the book portrays, but instead lived separately with his wife Nancy, a figure omitted from the narrative. The family resided in a house near the sea, where Gerald began his lifelong fascination with animals. Their lives were shaped by the island’s natural world and by two key figures: Dr. Theodore Stephanides, a physician and naturalist who became Gerald’s mentor in biology and natural history, and Spiro, a local taxi-driver who served as a trusted protector and guide. The family’s experiences, as told in Birds, Beasts, and Relatives, are not arranged chronologically and contain elements of creative reinterpretation. The book reflects the closeness of family bonds, the intensity of childhood observation, and the deep influence of place, particularly through the lens of Gerald’s early curiosity and the presence of animals, including his dog Roger.

<source>
 Birds, Beasts, and Relatives, like My Family and Other Animals, offers a series of autobiographical anecdotes from the Durrell family's five year sojourn on the Greek island of Corfu between 1935 and 1939. Gerald was aged ten when his mother, sister and two brothers moved from England to Corfu. The stories related in the book do not occur in chronological order, and are in some cases semi-fictionalised. For example, Gerald's eldest brother Larry - the novelist Lawrence Durrell - was not living with the rest of his family as is depicted in the stories, but was living separately with his wife Nancy, who is not mentioned in the books. Characters in the book also include their widowed mother, the gun-mad brother Leslie, his sister Margo, and Roger the dog. The family are protected by their local friend, taxi-driver Spiro (Spyros "Americano" Chalikiopoulos) and mentored by the physician and polymath Dr Theodore Stephanides, who provides Gerald with his education in natural history.
</source>

Near the book’s end, Mulch learns that Artemis has cleared his criminal record and assigned him to restore Artemis’s memory. At the conclusion, Artemis’s memory is erased. In an epilogue, it is revealed the LEP questioned him about any plans to retain his memory, but he successfully concealed his intentions.

text: Eight people have died and two others are missing and presumed dead after an explosion and fire tore through the cargo ship MV Yenisey while it was undergoing repairs at a naval dockyard in Kaliningrad, Russia. The incident happened around 3:00 p.m. Moscow time (11:00 GMT) in drydock at the facility in Baltiysk, a closed military town near Kaliningrad. Initially, ten people were unaccounted for; today, the eighth body has been recovered, and authorities now believe the two still missing are also dead. Three others were injured in the blast. The ship, owned by a private company based in St. Petersburg, was being repaired under a lease agreement with the naval dockyard. The investigation into the cause is being led by the Russian navy, under Admiral Vladimir Vysotsky, who has pointed to serious violations of welding safety regulations by both the vessel’s owner and dockyard management. text: Antisense molecules as antibiotics present a dynamic approach to circumventing acquired resistance, enabling rapid re-design in response to target sequence mutations in bacterial pathogens. Unlike conventional small-molecule antibiotics, where new compound discovery is often arduous and time-consuming, antisense sequences can be redesigned efficiently using genomic information from target genes. However, effective delivery into bacterial cells remains a critical challenge, requiring engineered vehicles to overcome membrane barriers and prevent nuclease degradation. Though developing novel delivery systems is more complex than modifying antisense cargo, evidence suggests this barrier is less formidable than the hurdles in discovering entirely new small-molecule antibiotics. In this study, we implement a protocol that optimizes the synergy between engineered delivery vehicles and antisense cargo by minimizing the fitness advantage conferred to pathogens by mutations in entry mechanisms, while simultaneously increasing the selective cost of mutations in the antisense target site. Through in-vitro computer simulations, we demonstrate that a rationally designed antisense therapy can maintain efficacy over substantially longer durations than conventional antibiotics, with resistance emergence significantly delayed. Although these results are derived from in-vitro modeling, comparative analysis with similar in-vitro resistance studies supports the inference that this dual-strategy approach offers greater long-term therapeutic sustainability in vivo.

text: Carnelian, son and heir to Lord Suth, and prince Osidian have been abducted, drugged and smuggled out of the capital of the three lands, Osrakum, in funeral urns. Carnelian is awakened by a would-be grave robber seeking spoils in the urns. The robber is immediately placed in the dilemma of having looked upon the face of one of the exalted chosen lords, for which the penalty is death, of killing them and risking eventual discovery and death, of being caught in the inevitable hunt for such exalted missing persons and being executed, or fleeing far from the capital with his captives in the hope of selling them as valuable slaves. He chooses the latter as his only chance of survival and thus Carnelian and Osidian are set upon a very different course than Osidians anticipated coronation. Osidian having failed to appear at the coronation, his brother Molochite would automatically be made emperor instead. As mortal brother to the new divine emperor, Osidian would take Molochite's place as blood sacrifice. Carnelian and Osidian are bound and disguised and marched away from the capital. Osidian is in worse shape than Carnelian, so that Carnelian must make the difficult choices of attempting their escape. Carnelian has a possibility of escape and return to the capital, but either abandoning Osidian or bringing him back would mean his inevitable death. Instead he seizes the opportunity of an attack by nomad tribesmen to transfer them to captivity with the tribesmen, instead of the slavers. As the party returns to the plains which are home to the ochre tribe, Osidian recovers somewhat and his reckless determination defending the party from wild animals, plus his navigational skills and knowledge of the plains drawn from his unconventional and privileged education, impresses the tribesmen. Some of them start to defer to Osidian both as a clearly recognisable member of the ruling race which they have been taught to fear, and as a natural replacement for the dead leaders of their party. The tribesmen return to their village, where a combination of fast talking by Carnelian (whose family had a number of plainsmen as slaves), and growing respect for Osidian mean they are allowed to live as part of the village. Carnelian is accepting of their new life, but Osidian is at first suicidal, but then vengeful. He embarks on a plan to recover his position and sets about manipulating the tribesmen to his ends. By a number of staged encounters, he sets tribesmen from different villages against each other, until he controls a steadily growing warband. This he intends to use as the start of an army to wage war against his brother.

text: The novel represents Maupin's return to the Tales of the City characters some eighteen years after the sixth book in the series was published. As well as further developing familiar characters, it explores the differences between the San Francisco of the 1980s, bearing the brunt of the developing AIDS crisis, and the city in the first decade of the new millennium. The realities of aging, both distressing and graceful, is a major theme of the book – as well as the generation gap between gays from the 1970s and 80s and gays from the 2000s. In a departure from the third-person style of the original Tales sequence, Michael Tolliver Lives is narrated in the first person by the title character. In the book's opening pages, Michael encounters a half-remembered old flame, prompting him to reflect on his status as a survivor of both the HIV epidemic (which killed many of his peers in the 1980s and 1990s but is now a more treatable chronic illness thanks in part to better medication) and of a San Francisco that has transformed due in large part to the dot com boom. Characters from the original series include Anna Madrigal, the one-time landlady of 28 Barbary Lane; Brian Hawkins and his now-adult daughter Shawna, a pansexual aspiring writer; and Brian's ex-wife Mary Ann Singleton. New characters include Michael's much younger partner Ben and his transgendered co-worker Jake Greenleaf. Much of the plot's tension derives from the impending death of Michael's elderly mother in Florida, a test case of changes in attitude since she refused to accept Michael's homosexuality in the second Tales book. Several chapters involve a secondary plot thread concerning Michael's relationship with his brother Irwin. Eventually Michael finds himself forced to choose between being present for his mother's last days and attending to an aging Anna, described in the book as part of his "logical" (as opposed to "biological") family.

text: A homeless man calling himself "Mister" enters the offices of the Washington DC law firm Drake & Sweeney and takes many of the lawyers hostage. Although he is eventually shot by a police sniper and the hostages freed, one of the hostages, an antitrust lawyer named Michael Brock, is concerned by what he has learned and feels compelled to investigate further. He finds his way to the 14th Street Legal Clinic, where he meets Mordecai Green, an advocate for the homeless, who asks him to help one night at a homeless shelter. As Brock's investigation deepens, he finds that his own employer was complicit in an illegal eviction, which eventually resulted in the death of a young homeless family. He takes a confidential file, intending to copy it, but is quickly suspected of its theft. Shocked by what he has found, Brock leaves his firm to take a poorly-paid position with the 14th Street Legal Clinic, which works to protect the rights of the homeless. This leads to his wife divorcing him. He admits one of his clients, Ruby, to a therapy class for drug-addicted women, and in the process meets Megan, the Brock's love interest. As Drake & Sweeney comes after Brock with theft and malpractice allegations, the Clinic launches a lawsuit against the law firm and its business partners. Terrified of the certain bad publicity, the matter is settled by mediation and the clinic receives a large payout to be shared with the victims of the eviction. Drake & Sweeney's head partner, deeply troubled by the events, offers to make pro bono staff available to assist the work of the Clinic in fighting for the rights of homeless people. The book ends with Brock taking a short vacation with Megan and Ruby, and them reflecting on their lives.

text: The nuclear war between Nazi Germany and the Race ends with a German surrender after Ernst Kaltenbrunner, the Führer, is killed and replaced by Walter Dornberger. Dornberger agrees to disband the Axis Forces, withdraw German troops from occupied France, and disband the German rocket and nuclear forces. The German withdrawal results in instability in the governments of its allies, such as the British Union of Fascists in Britain, as well as clashes between the Free French Forces and the new government of liberated France, and radioactive drift into the Soviet Union. However, Dornberger secretly begins stockpiling weapons and missile parts, allowing Germany the option to rearm itself in the future. Meanwhile, the nuclear attack on the Race's colony fleet from Second Contact is finally revealed: it was an American attack, ordered by Earl Warren. When it is revealed, Fleetlord Atvar gives Warren a choice: dismantle the American space program, or allow the Race to nuke Indianapolis for revenge. To the surprise of all, Warren allows the Race to destroy Indianapolis, and then commits suicide, with Vice President Harold Stassen taking over. It is eventually stated that the reason Warren allowed the city to be destroyed over the space program was that the Americans were working on a starship that would allow them to journey to the Race's homeworld and repay their visit to Earth. During this time, the Race itself undergoes large social unrest, due to the effects of ginger on their females. Drug addiction, the black market, and prostitution all arise from it, along with a reproductive system that is unregulated, much like that of humans.

text: In the beginning, Freddy had the idea to establish a tourism company called Barnyard Tours Inc. The animals agreed, and the company was formed. Animals could pay for a tour with food, or by doing work for Mr. Bean. Soon, however, Freddy and Jinx, the cat, were sick and tired of conducting the tours. Freddy suggested a trip to the North Pole. So they and four other animals set off. A year passed, and the animals left began to worry. A mob formed in the barnyard triggered by a speech by Charles, the rooster. Then, Ferdinand, a crow from the expedition, came back and organized a rescue party. He said they had gone on a ship and crew were planning to eat Freddy. The sailors had said that they might try going to Santa Claus’ house. Later, in the woods of Canada, two children and a bear joined the rescue party. However, it soon was discovered that Ferdinand forgot to bring food and clothing for the animals. Everything looked grim for Ferdinand for a minute, but he suddenly came up with the idea for a lecture tour. The animals of the woods brought in food and clothing they found in the woods. Also, a few weeks later Charles and Jack, a dog, wandered away and were captured by some wolves. The animals, Charles and Jack, managed to drive the wolves away with the help of some ants. They finally arrived at Santa Claus’ house. The animals found Freddy there and also found a problem: The sailors were trying to turn Santa Claus’s irregular workshop into an ordinary, assembly line factory. The animals tried to make the sailors leave. They played ghosts, but one sailor wasn’t scared. Then, Freddy sent the captain, Mr. Hooker, a treasure map. He thought all the sailors would go with him, but instead, he tried to get all of it for himself. Freddy and Jinx chased after him and took it back. Later, the whole crew of the ship was shown the map. The sailors left and Santa Claus’s workshop went back to normal. Santa Claus took the animals and the two children to the Bean Farm.
