text: The title of the book refers to the Old Tolbooth Prison in Edinburgh, Scotland, at the time in the heart of the Scottish county of Midlothian. The historical backdrop was the event known as the Porteous Riots. In 1736, a riot broke out in Edinburgh over the execution of two smugglers. The Captain of the City Guards, Captain John Porteous, ordered the soldiers to fire into the crowd, killing several people. Porteous was later killed by a lynch mob who stormed the Old Tolbooth. The second, and main element of the novel was based on a story Scott claimed to have received in an unsigned letter. It was about a certain Helen Walker who had travelled all the way to London by foot, in order to receive a royal pardon for her sister, who was unjustly charged with infanticide. Scott put Jeanie Deans in the place of Walker, a young woman from a family of highly devout Presbyterians. Jeanie goes to London, partly by foot, hoping to achieve an audience with the Queen through the influence of the Duke of Argyll. Jeanie Deans' role in the novel is described in more detail in Jeanie Deans (fictional character). Jeanie Deans is the first woman among Scott's protagonists, and also the first to come from the lower classes. While the heroine is idealized for her religious devotion and her moral rectitude, Scott nevertheless ridicules the moral certitude represented by the branch of Presbyterianism known as Cameronians, represented in the novel by Jeanie’s father David. Also central to the novel is the early-18th century Jacobitism, a theme found in so many of Scott’s novels. Scott’s sympathies can be seen in the ideal figure of the Duke of Argyll, a moderate on these issues. The Heart of Midlothian has been adapted for the screen once, in 1914, and for television once, in 1966. Two operas have also been based upon the novel - La Prigione di Edimburgo (Imprisoned in Edinburgh) by the Italian composer Federico Ricci (1809–1877) and Jeanie Deans by the Scottish classical composer, Hamish MacCunn (1868–1916).

text: Basal autophagy is as a compressive catabolic mechanism engaged in the breakdown of damaged macromolecules and organelles leading to the recycling of elementary nutrients. Thought essential to cellular refreshing, little is known about the origin of a constitutional rate of basal autophagy. Here, we found that loss of Drosophila vacuolar peduncle (vap), a presumed GAP enzyme, is associated with enhanced basal autophagy rate and physiological alterations resulting in a wasteful cell energy balance, a hallmark of overactive autophagy. By contrast, starvation-induced autophagy was disrupted in vap mutant conditions, leading to a block of maturation into autolysosomes. This phenotype stem for exacerbated biogenesis of PI(3)P-dependent endomembranes, including autophagosome membranes and ectopic fusions of vesicles. These findings shed new light on the neurodegenerative phenotype found associated to mutant vap adult brains in a former study. A partner of Vap, Sprint (Spri), acting as an endocytic GEF for Rab5, had the converse effect of leading to a reduction in PI(3)P-dependent endomembrane formation in mutants. Spri was conditional to normal basal autophagy and instrumental to the starvation-sensitivity phenotype specific of vap. Rab5 activity itself was essential for PI(3)P and for pre-autophagosome structures formation. We propose that Vap/Spri complexes promote a cell surface-derived flow of endocytic Rab5-containing vesicles, the traffic of which is crucial for the implementation of a basal autophagy rate.

text:
Active tuberculosis (TB) and latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) are a public health threat in prisons around the world. The objectives of the study were to estimate the prevalence of LTBI and TB as well as to investigate TB transmission inside one prison, in Colombia.

A Cross-sectional study was conducted in inmates who agreed to participate. Inmates with respiratory symptoms (RS) of any duration underwent to medical evaluation and three sputum samples were taken for smear microscopy and culture for TB diagnosis. Drug susceptibility was analyzed using BACTEC MGIT 960 and GenoType MTBDRplus. Molecular genotyping of Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates was performed by 24-Locus MIRU-VNTR and spoligotyping. LTBI was evaluated according to the result of the tuberculin skin test (TST). Close contact investigation was conducted inside the prison for inmates that shared the cell with the index TB case.

Among 301/2,020 (15%) inmates with RS of any duration, 8% were diagnosed with active TB. The prevalence of active TB was 1,026 cases/100,000 inmates. We isolated M. tuberculosis in 19/24 (79%) TB cases, 94.7% were susceptible to first line drugs and only one was monoresistant to isoniazid. The most prevalent sub-lineage was Haarlem (68.4%), followed by LAM (26.3%) and T superfamily (5.3%). 24-Locus MIRU-VNTR typing results alone or in combination with spoligotyping identified three clusters containing two isolates each. Two clusters corresponded to inmates that shared the same cell, but each one was located in different blocks of the prison. Inmates from the last cluster were in the same block in nearby cells. TST reading was performed in 95.6% inmates, and 67.6% had a positive reaction.

The prevalence of LTBI and TB was higher in prison than in the general population. Molecular genotyping suggests that TB in this prison is mainly caused by strains imported by inmates or endogenous reactivation.

text: Seabirds and pinnipeds play an important role in biogeochemical cycling by transferring nutrients from aquatic to terrestrial environments. Indeed, soils rich in animal depositions have generally high organic carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus contents. Several studies have assessed bacterial diversity in Antarctic soils influenced by marine animals; however most have been conducted in areas with significant human impact. Thus, we chose Cape Shirreff, Livingston Island, an Antarctic Specially Protected Area designated mainly to protect the diversity of marine vertebrate fauna, and selected sampling sites with different types of animals coexisting in a relatively small space, and where human presence and impact are negligible. Using 16S rRNA gene analyses through massive sequencing, we assessed the influence of animal concentrations, via their modification of edaphic characteristics, on soil bacterial diversity and composition. The nutrient composition of soils impacted by Antarctic fur seals and kelp gulls was more similar to that of control soils (i.e. soils without visible presence of plants or animals), which may be due to the more active behaviour of these marine animals compared to other species. Conversely, the soils from concentrations of southern elephant seals and penguins showed greater differences in soil nutrients compared to the control. In agreement with this, the bacterial communities of the soils associated with these animals were most different from those of the control soils, with the soils of penguin colonies also possessing the lowest bacterial diversity. However, all the soils influenced by the presence of marine animals were dominated by bacteria belonging to Gammaproteobacteria, particularly those of the genus Rhodanobacter. Therefore, we conclude that the modification of soil nutrient composition by marine vertebrates promotes specific groups of bacteria, which could play an important role in the recycling of nutrients in terrestrial Antarctic ecosystems.

text: Stress profoundly impacts the brain and increases the risk of developing a psychiatric disorder. The brain’s response to stress is mediated by a number of pathways that affect gene expression and protein function throughout the cell. Understanding how stress achieves such dramatic effects on the brain requires an understanding of the brain’s stress response pathways. The majority of studies focused on molecular changes have employed repeated or chronic stress paradigms to assess the long-term consequences of stress and have not taken an integrative genomic and/or proteomic approach. Here, we determined the lasting impact of a single stressful event (restraint) on the broad molecular profile of the basolateral amygdala complex (BLC), a key brain region mediating emotion, memory and stress. Molecular profiling performed thirty days post-restraint consisted of small RNA sequencing, RNA sequencing and quantitative mass spectrometry and identified long-lasting changes in microRNA (miRNA), messenger RNA (mRNA) and proteins. Alignment of the three datasets further delineated the regulation of stress-specific pathways which were validated by qPCR and Western Blot analysis. From this analysis, mir-29a-5p was identified as a putative regulator of stress-induced adaptations in the BLC. Further, a number of predicted mir-29a-5p targets are regulated at the mRNA and protein level. The concerted and long-lasting disruption of multiple molecular pathways in the amygdala by a single stress event is expected to be sufficient to alter behavioral responses to a wide array of future experiences, including exposure to additional stressors.

In many sub-Saharan African countries, confronting the dual epidemic of HIV and NCDs is a public health priority especially in high HIV burden countries such as South Africa. Evidence shows that poor health as a consequence of NCDs and HIV among the workforce increases absenteeism and leads to decrease in productivity. However, the prevalence of these co-occurring chronic conditions and associated factors is unknown in the educator workforce. Improved understanding has implications for their management and wellbeing of educators. This paper reports the prevalence of selected NCDs and associated factors among HIV positive educators in South Africa using the 2015/6 survey of Educators in Public Schools in South Africa.

This was a second-generation surveillance undertaken among educators in selected public schools in all nine provinces in South Africa. A multi-stage stratified cluster design with probability proportional to size sampling was used to draw a random sample of schools. Factors associated with presence of NCDs were determined using a multivariate backward stepwise logistic regression analysis.

A total of 1 365 schools were sampled within which 21 495 (85.5%) educators were interviewed. Out of 2691, HIV Positive educators that responded to the questions on NCDs, 36.9% reported having NCDs. The most commonly reported NCDs were high blood pressure (17.4%), and stomach ulcers (13.5%). The increased odds of reporting the presence of NCDs was significantly associated with being female than male [aOR = 1.5: 95% CI (1.1–1.9), p<0.002], age 45 to 54 years [aOR = 1.8: 95% CI (1.4–2.2), p = p<0.001], and age 55 years and older than those 18 to 24 years [aOR = 2.7: 95% CI (1.8–3.9), p<0.001). The decreased odds of reporting the presence of NCDs was significantly associated with not being absent from school for health reasons [aOR = 0.7: 95% CI (0.6–0.9), p = 0.003].

NCDs care and active screening should be an integral part of HIV programmes including interventions such as prevention, treatment, care and support amongst public school educators in SA. The education department will need to invest in health promotion intervention programmes to prevent and mitigate the negative impact of NCDs and HIV on the sector.

text:
A disturbed self-image is central to the characteristic symptoms of borderline personality disorder (BPD). Evaluations of self-relevance (SR) are highly important in cognitive and emotional processing of information and adaptive behavior.

In the current study, we used affective statements to investigate if SR is altered in patients with higher scores on Borderline Symptom List (BSL-95). Forthyfemale adults with BPD and 20 healthy participants assessed a set of stimuli consisting of sentences in third-person for relevance to self.

BPD patients exhibited a higher SR for negative contents as compared to healthy controls (p < .001). Furthermore, a significant positive correlation coefficient was found between the increased bias in evaluating the SR of stimuli and borderline symptom severity scores, as measured by BSL-95 questionnaire (r = 0.67, p < .001). This effect persisted after controlling for depressive symptoms by a partial correlation analysis.

Our results revealed an enhanced SR for negative statements, which was related to the severity of individuals’ BPD symptoms. These findings add to the diagnostic information regarding the disturbed organization of self in this clinical population. We suggest the maladaptive evaluation of SR offers an important treatment target for therapeutic approaches to BPD.

text: Representations of the body and peripersonal space can be distorted for people with some chronic pain conditions. Experimental pain induction can give rise to similar, but transient distortions in healthy individuals. However, spatial and bodily representations are dynamic, and constantly update as we interact with objects in our environment. It is unclear whether induced pain disrupts the mechanisms involved in updating these representations. In the present study, we sought to investigate the effect of induced pain on the updating of peripersonal space and body representations during and following tool-use. We compared performance under three conditions (pain, active placebo, neutral) on a visuotactile crossmodal congruency task and a tactile distance judgement task to measure updating of peripersonal space and body representations, respectively. Consistent with previous findings, the difference in crossmodal interference from visual distractors in the same compared to opposite visual field to the tactile target was less when tools were crossed than uncrossed. This suggests an extension of peripersonal space to incorporate the tips of the tools. Also consistent with previous findings, estimates of the felt tactile distance judgements decreased after active tool-use. In contrast to our predictions, however, we found no evidence that pain interfered with performance on either task when compared to the control conditions. Our findings suggest that the updating of peripersonal space and body representations is not disrupted by induced pain. That is, experiencing acute pain does not give rise to distorted representations of the body and peripersonal space that can be present in people with chronic pain conditions.

text:
Epidural catheters are state of the art for postoperative analgesic in abdominal surgery. Due to neurolysis it can lead to postoperative urinary tract retention (POUR), which leads to prolonged bladder catheterization, which has an increased risk for urinary tract infections (UTI). Our aim was to identify the current perioperative management of urinary catheters and, second, to identify the optimal time of suprapubic bladder catheter removal in regard to the removal of the epidural catheter.

We sent a questionnaire to 102 German hospitals and analyzed the 83 received answers to evaluate the current handling of bladder drainage and epidural catheters. Then, we conducted a retrospective study including 501 patients, who received an epidural and suprapubic catheter after abdominal surgery at the University Hospital Würzburg. We divided the patients into three groups according to the point in time of suprapubic bladder drainage removal in regard to the removal of the epidural catheter and analyzed the onset of a UTI.

Our survey showed that in almost all hospitals (98.8%), patients received an epidural catheter and a bladder drainage after abdominal surgery. The point in time of urinary catheter removal was equally distributed between before, simultaneously and after the removal of the epidural catheter (respectively: ~28–29%). The retrospective study showed a catheter-associated UTI in 6.7%. Women were affected significantly more often than men (10,7% versus 2,5%, p<0.001). There was a non-significant trend to more UTIs when the suprapubic catheter was removed after the epidural catheter (before: 5.7%, after: 8.4%).

The point in time of suprapubic bladder drainage removal in relation to the removal of the epidural catheter does not seem to correlate with the rate of UTIs. The current handling in Germany is inhomogeneous, so further studies to standardize treatment are recommended.

text: Yellow seed is a desirable trait in Brassica oilseed crops. The B. rapa var. Yellow Sarson carry unique yellow seed color genes which are not only important for the development of yellow-seeded oilseed B. rapa cultivars but this variant can also be used to develop yellow-seeded B. napus. In this study, we developed near-isogenic lines (NILs) of Yellow Sarson for the major seed coat color QTL SCA9-2 of the chromosome A9 and used the NILs to fine map this QTL region and to identify the candidate genes through linkage mapping and transcriptome sequencing of the developing seeds. From the 18.4 to 22.79 Mb region of SCA9-2, six SSR markers showing 0.63 to 5.65% recombination were developed through linkage analysis and physical mapping. A total of 55 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in the SCA9-2 region through transcriptome analysis; these included three transcription factors, Bra028039 (NAC), Bra023223 (C2H2 type zinc finger), Bra032362 (TIFY), and several other genes which encode unknown or nucleic acid binding protein; these genes might be the candidates and involved in the regulation of seed coat color in the materials used in this study. Several biosynthetic pathways, including the flavonoid, phenylpropanoid and suberin biosynthetic pathways were significantly enriched through GO and KEGG enrichment analysis of the DEGs. This is the first comprehensive study to understand the yellow seed trait of Yellow Sarson through employing linkage mapping and global transcriptome analysis approaches.

The European Union (EU) competitions commission has announced its decision to fine the Microsoft Corporation €899 million (US$1.35 billion), approximately 1/10th of the company's gross yearly earnings, for failing to comply with the 2004 antitrust order. It is the highest ever fine charged by the EU (also being the largest fine of its kind ever imposed upon a company), and the first time that the EU has fined a company because of non-compliance with an antitrust decision.

The first decision in this antitrust case was given in 2004 citing that Microsoft withheld needed interoperability information from rival software companies which prevented them from making software compatible with Windows. The commission ordered Microsoft to provide this information. Microsoft agreed to this, providing the information for royalty fees of 6.5% of the licensee's revenues for the product on grounds of innovation (specifically, 3.87% for the patent license and of 2.98% for the information license). The EU found these royalty fees unreasonable and Microsoft was ordered to lower them. Microsoft complied with this, adjusting the royalty rates to 1.2% (changing the rates for the licenses to 0.7% and 0.5%, respectively) in the European Union, while keeping the rate the same for the rest of the world. The EU still saw this as an unreasonable rate, and Microsoft, two month after lowering the rates, reduced the rates yet again to a flat rate of €10000 or a royalty of 0.4% applicable worldwide. Microsoft's royalty rates, which were deemed unreasonable for the period of 15 months between June 21, 2006 and October 21, 2007 are the cause for the fine. So far, the EU has fined Microsoft €1.68 billion in 3 separate fines in this case. This fine will go towards the European Union annual budget.

This may not be the end of Microsoft's troubles with the European Union yet, as the commission is currently investigating two other complaints about the company's anti-competition practices.

A new explosive detonated on Sunday near the Pyramids of Giza in Egypt police said. It was reportedly carried by a man from a tourist bazaar. The man allegedly was carrying the bomb in a sack. It might accidentally have exploded in the area of Kufr Tuhurmus. No other injuries were reported except to the bomber himself, Sami Gamal Ahmad, who was too badly injured to be questioned. The man may have been taking the explosive to the tourist area of Kerdassa, where souvenir shops are located in a bazaar near the pyramids, said an official.

Egyptian security forces have detained 70 suspects in a sweep to find the perpetrators in Saturday's early morning bombings that killed 88 and left hundreds injured.

The police investigation of the bombings has targeted a smaller number of people than the October 2004 roundup that followed attacks in the Sinai resorts of Tabas and Ras Shitan. 3,000 people were detained for questioning in those bombings. According to Canadian CTV, 200 of those people are believed to still be in custody.

Among the dead, officials said victims included British, Russian, Dutch, Kuwaitis, Saudis, Qataris, Czech Republic, U.S., and native Egyptians. Sixty were identified as Egyptians, and at least eight were foreigners.

Resort hotels are being abandoned by tourists. At the nearest international airport, hundreds are reported trying to get flights out.

Three bombs erupted in the Red Sea resort of Sharm el-Sheikh just after 1am. At the Ghazala Gardens hotel, work is underway to clear the destroyed reception lobby where emergency teams have gavin up the search for survivors. A car with 660 pounds of explosives drove into the hotel's driveway and detonated in an apparent suicide attack.

The day of the bombings is marked as an Egyptian national holiday that commemorates the bloodless coup by a group of army officers that brought them to power after deposing King Farouk in 1952. Egypt has been the victim of 15 tourist attacks since October 1992.

Anti-government protestors in Egypt rallying against the rule of president Hosni Mubarak took to the streets for a fourth straight day, demanding the long-time leader step down and complaining of poverty, corruption, and oppression. The demonstrations were supposedly inspired by a popular uprising that saw Tunisian president Zine al-Abidine Ben Ali ousted from office. A national curfew is in effect, but is being ignored by many.

Police responded to protestors by deploying rubber bullets, tear gas, and water cannons. In addition, Mubarak ordered the army out onto the streets to help quell the conflict. He was earlier supposed to make a statement, but hasn't yet done so.

In Cairo, demonstrators targeted the heavily-guarded state broadcasting building, as well as the building of the ruling National Democratic Party, which was set on fire, according to a BBC reporter. In Sinai, armed men took several policemen hostage after seizing a road leading into a nearby town.

Former International Atomic Energy Agency head Mohamed ElBaradei, a prominent opposition figure, was taken into custody by authorities and now under house arrest, The Telegraph reports.

Meanwhile, according to media reports and statistics, Egypt has shut down practically all Internet traffic both out of and into the nation, as well as disrupting cellphone usage. A graph by Arbor Networks available on the New York Times website shows an almost vertical drop in overall Egypt internet traffic, starting shortly before four o'clock in the afternoon with over 2.5 million megabits per second down to almost zero in the space of an hour.

Indonesian officials have said an underwater earthquake measuring 6.6 on the Richter scale has erupted off the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. At first, officials told residents to flee coastal areas as a safety measure, but they later said there had been no tsunami. According to reports, no damage has been caused.

Last week, an underwater quake with a magnitude of 7.7 produced a tsunami that ravaged a 200km stretch of Java's southern coast. Six hundred and fifty people perished after the deadly two-metre high tidal wave struck, and it is estimated that over three hundred people are still missing.

Navy boats and marine police have been searching for dead bodies off Java's coast, but according to the Associated Press, rough seas today have forced teams to abort their operations.

Regions hardest hit, like the small town of Pangandaran, are starting to return to normality. However, people who have taken refuge in camps are refusing to return home due to fears of another tsunami.

Indonesia's President has said efforts to build an early warning system planned after the 2004 Asian tsunami are to be accelerated. His government has been criticised as to why local people weren't informed that a tsunami was imminent last week.

Some minutes before midnight local time on Thursday, Eduardo Rodriguez Veltzé, then President of the Supreme Court of Justice, took oath as the new president of Bolivia, a country that has found itself plunged in a serious crisis for several months.

Earlier on Thursday, the Legislature had suspended the session that had predicted, in the House of the Liberty of Sucre, to decide the name of the new president of the Bolivians, due to the intensified protests after it become known that a minor was killed by the Army. The demonstrations also brought along a strong resistance of various social sectors to possible appointment of Hormando Vaca Diez, president of the Senate, or Mario Cossío, president of the House of Representatives, who constitutionally would have to succeed departing president Carlos Mesa, who resigned on Monday night.

The coca leader Evo Morales, main opponent of Mesa and Vaca Diez, has previously endorsed the appointment of Rodriguez Veltzé and, although he wants a constitutional assembly, probably desists as the temporary president fulfills his promise to call anticipated polls, possibly next December. By aside, the Congress would have that to call to parliamentary elections, since the Constitution only obliges the temporary president to call assemblies for president and vice president.

Zahi Hawass, Egypt's pre-eminent archaeologist, revealed the first ancient artifacts which may lead to the discovery of Cleopatra and Marc Antony's resting place.

Recently, outside the temple colourful mummies of nobles were excavated at a neighbouring necropolis. These discoveries have lead the archaeologists to believe that a ruler or person of royalty is interred within the temple itself. It was the practice of the Greco-Roman era to assemble the tombs of persons of status and other high ranking officials near their rulers.

Dr. Roger Vickers team used radar to locate three chambers within the rocky hill atop of which is the Temple of Taposiris Magna dedicated to the goddess Isis. The temple was constructed about 300 BC by Ptolemy II.

The Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA) expedition led by Hawass has yet to excavate the burial chambers 40 feet (12 meters) underground where they hope to find a crown or Egyptian hieroglyph {{w|cartouche]]s revealing the names of royalty. The team will employ radar again on April 22.

The Supreme Council of Antiquities expedition consists of Zahi Hawass, Secretary General of the SCA, and Martinez who has extensively researched the life of Cleopatra.

According to Plutarch who studied Roman history, Caesar allowed Marc Antony and Cleopatra to be buried in the same tomb.

Alexandria is located about 30 miles (48 km) from the Temple of Taposiris Magna. The archaeological site is on a hill along the Mediterranean Sea overlooking the summer home of Hosni Mubarak, president of Egypt. The archaeologists fear they may have to postpone work for security reasons over the summer months.

An elderly man's body has been found floating in the water near Owhiro Bay quarry car park, by a man walking alone. The man who found the body immediately called the police. The body of the man, determined to be in his 60s, was found at 8:30 a.m. NZST.

His body was found partially dressed and with both hands cut off at the wrists. The New Zealand Police report that there are signs that someone had tried to decapitate him.

Detectives, Wellington Police Maritime and the Police National Dive Squad, totalling more than 40 officers, are working on the case. They are searching for items and the two missing hands.

The victim is European, in his 60s, grey hair, moderately built, between 175 and 180-centimetres tall and, when found, was wearing dark trousers and black leather shoes.

The police have yet to determine the man's identity, or how long the body had been in the water.

Police are seeking any information on this death. If you have any information, you can call the hot line: 0508 Redrocks (0508 733 762).

An earthquake of magnitude 7.2 struck Japan at 2:46 UTC (11:46 am local time), off the eastern coast of northern Honshu, 95 km (60 miles) from Sendai. Buildings in Tokyo, 350 km (220 miles) from the epicenter, were swayed by the trembler and trains were shut down. A tsunami bulletin was issued by the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center and small tsunamis were observed thereafter. (1) (2).

As a precaution, the Tohoku Electric nuclear power plants have been shut down.

Electric supply ceased due to the earthquake in the Miyagi Prefecture and in its southern neighbor, Fukushima Prefecture, and 17,000 households in total have been affected and lost power.

Railway transports including Tōhoku Shinkansen have been stopped. Sendai Airport has been temporally closed.

No casualties have been reported. So far over 69 people have been injured in Miyagi, Iwate, Fukushima, Saitama and Tokyo Prefectures including 26 people who have been injured due to falling roof in an indoor swimming pool in Sendai. 687 houses in Tohoku region were destroyed to some extent. In addition, a house by wood in Saitama Prefecture. A female resident was trapped by this broken house and rescued after 50 minutes.

text:
Australia —The whole of the east coast of Australia has been lashed by severe storms in the last 24 hours, with at least one reported death. Wind gusts in some areas reached 110 kilometers per hour, and flash flooding and power cuts were reported from Far North Queensland to Tasmania in the South.

State Emergency Services (SES) crews are stretched to the limit, working into the night to cope with the effects of the freak weather.

Sixty millimetres of rain fell in an hour on the region around Herberton, in Far North Queensland. A man and woman were rescued from nearby Sandy Creek after their car was swept off the road while trying to cross the Creek during heavy storms last night.

The man had escaped to cling to a tree, but lost sight of his wife as the car was washed away. Rescuers later found the woman on the bank. Neither was seriously injured.

About 150 kilometres to the south-west, a search continues for missing stockman, a 38-year-old from Carpentaria Downs Station near Einasleigh who failed to return after checking fences yesterday.

The NSW State Emergency Service reported receiving more than 2,300 requests for assistance, mostly in Western Sydney and Gosford.

In the southern Sydney suburb of Bexley North three people were rescued from vehicles when they attempted to drive along a flooded road, and a girl was killed near Mittagong when a tree fell on the tent in which she was sleeping.

Melbourne has been hit by severe flooding as wild storms and heavy rain strike the east coast of Australia. With triple the city's average February rainfall in just 24 hours, major roads and train lines have been cut and travel is extremely difficult.

A search involving police and State Emergency Service volunteers is currently underway for a schoolboy, believed to have been swept into floodwaters north of Werribee, and a 10 year old girl narrowly escaped being killed when a tree fell through the house in which she was sleeping. The tree missed her by centimeters. She was trapped for an hour before being freed by emergency services and taken to the Royal Childrens Hospital in a serious condition.

The Spirit of Tasmania I was also forced to return to Station Pier, in Port Melbourne, after windows were broken when the Bass Strait ferry encountered 20 metre waves caused by the gale force winds.

The city received 120mm of rain in the 24 hours to 9am, while the average monthly rainfall for February is 45mm. Making this the largest measured rainfall in a 24 hour period for Melbourne since records began in 1856. The rainfall stopped sometime this afternoon local time. Authorities urged people to stay away from Melbourne city centre.

South Australia has, for the first time in 27 years, experienced hail in February.

For the last few days, Egypt has sporadically opened and closed the Rafah Border Crossing with the Gaza Strip.

On Thursday, Egypt opened the Rafah Border Crossing for a limited time to transfer only 11 wounded, out of dozens of Gaza residents injured during the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which has intensified significantly lately. The 11 wounded were to be sent for medical treatment in several hospitals, North Sinai's Governor Abdel Fatah Harhor told MENA news agency. On Friday, the crossing closed again, and then opened Saturday for food and medical supplies to be transported into Gaza. Monday, pilgrims were allowed to cross into Egypt, so they will be able to travel to Mecca to fulfil Islamic traditions.

Mohamed Morsi during his tenure as President of Egypt strengthened the connection between Egypt and the Gaza Strip. At the end of 2012, his government aided the coordination between the two sides and advanced a peace. Since the removal of president Morsi by the military and election of the current president, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, the Egyptian army has destroyed tunnels that had been dug between Gaza and Sinai, through which resources had been smuggled.

The day started strangely for the Dalmatians. They woke to find humans and other animals in an unusual, deep sleep. Then, they heard Cadpig's bark, echoing from London. She was now the Prime Minister's pet and had summoned them. Reports from across the country confirmed the same peculiar phenomenon.

Pongo and Missus decided to check on Cruella de Vil. They gathered a few dogs, plus Tommy and a white Persian cat (both honorary dogs), and set off. They "swooshed" to her house—the doors magically opened, but inside, she was asleep like everyone else.

Next, they went to Trafalgar Square. Sirius, the Dog Star's extraterrestrial lord, stood atop Nelson's Column. Every dog saw him as their own breed. He invited them to his home, promising safety from Earth's nuclear threats and human cruelty. The dogs debated. Pongo, known for his intelligence and bravery, was asked to decide.

During the discussion, three thin, mixed-breed strays arrived. Pongo assumed they'd want to leave Earth, but they didn't. They wanted to stay, hoping to find owners. Pongo told Sirius the dogs wouldn't abandon their humans. Sirius accepted this and granted them a final gift: the power to reach his home before the humans awoke. The strays seized the chance to go to the Battersea Dogs and Cats Home.

text:
Stress has a significant impact on the brain, increasing the risk of psychiatric disorders. This impact is mediated through various pathways that influence gene expression and protein function within cells. To understand how stress brings about such extensive changes in the brain, it is crucial to study the brain's stress response pathways. Most studies investigating molecular changes have used repeated or chronic stress models to assess long-term effects, but these studies have not integrated genomic and proteomic approaches.

In our study, we examined the long-term molecular effects of a single stressful event (restraint) on the basolateral amygdala complex (BLC), a brain region critical for emotion, memory, and stress. Thirty days after the restraint, we performed molecular profiling using small RNA sequencing, RNA sequencing, and quantitative mass spectrometry. This comprehensive approach identified lasting changes in microRNA (miRNA), messenger RNA (mRNA), and proteins.

By aligning these three datasets, we pinpointed specific stress-related pathways, which were confirmed through qPCR and Western Blot analysis. Our analysis identified mir-29a-5p as a potential regulator of stress-induced changes in the BLC. Additionally, several predicted targets of mir-29a-5p were found to be regulated at both the mRNA and protein levels.

The sustained disruption of multiple molecular pathways in the amygdala by a single stress event is likely to alter behavioral responses to future experiences, including exposure to additional stressors.

text:
In 2288, Jared Ramirez, imprisoned on the moon for his part in a failed attempt to cull the human population, receives an alien transmission through his telescopic array. John Shillinglaw, Associate Director of the European Space Agency, includes Ramirez on the science team aboard the Galileo, tasked with investigating the transmission's source: an object named "Spindrift."

The Galileo's first officer, Ted Harker, is both efficient and respected. He serves under Captain Ian Lawrence, a politically savvy but arrogant leader. Harker uncovers Lawrence's covert actions that could jeopardize potential first contact with an alien species. Despite this tension, the crew survives the journey to Spindrift. Lawrence appears eager for Harker to lead a team of four to explore Spindrift while the rest of the crew investigates a nearby hyperspace gate.

Harker's team makes remarkable discoveries, witnesses the Galileo's destruction, and encounters an alien. The alien proposes an unexpected idea for human space trade.

Fifteen-year-old Bobby, an African American boy living in the South Bronx with his mother and siblings, possesses an intellect that outshines most of his peers. He and his Hispanic girlfriend, Maria, often spend time together, looking forward to plans for the upcoming summer. Their lives take a devastating turn when a brutal Hispanic street gang attacks them as they walk to school. Bobby and Maria are severely beaten, with Maria suffering near-fatal wounds and being rushed to the hospital.

After the attack, Bobby is found and taken in by Moishe, an elderly Holocaust survivor. An unlikely friendship blossoms between the two. Tragically, Maria, unable to cope with the disfigurement caused by lye, takes her own life. As Bobby and Moishe share their stories—Moishe recounting his harrowing experiences in a concentration camp and Bobby detailing the attack and its aftermath—they form a bond. Despite everything, Bobby confesses that he still harbors a desperate desire for revenge.

text: Basal autophagy is a key process that cells use to break down damaged parts and recycle them into useful nutrients. It's like the cell's way of cleaning up and refreshing itself. However, we're not entirely sure how this process is regulated under normal conditions. In our study, we found that when a gene called Drosophila vacuolar peduncle (vap), which is thought to be a type of enzyme, is lost, it leads to an increase in basal autophagy. This might sound good, but it actually causes problems. The cells start wasting energy, which is a sign that autophagy is working too hard. Interestingly, when the cells were starved, this overactive autophagy didn't happen. Instead, the starvation-induced autophagy was disrupted, and the cells couldn't form structures called autolysosomes. We think this might be because there's too much of a certain type of membrane involved in autophagy. This finding helps explain why mutant vap adult brains showed signs of neurodegeneration in a previous study. We also found that a partner of Vap, called Sprint (Spri), has the opposite effect. It reduces the formation of these membranes and is important for both normal basal autophagy and the starvation-sensitivity seen in vap mutants. Rab5 activity, which is involved in forming these membranes and pre-autophagosome structures, is also crucial. We propose that Vap and Spri work together to control the flow of vesicles from the cell surface, which is important for regulating basal autophagy.

Basal autophagy is as a compressive catabolic mechanism engaged in the breakdown of damaged macromolecules and organelles leading to the recycling of elementary nutrients. Thought essential to cellular refreshing, little is known about the origin of a constitutional rate of basal autophagy. Here, we found that loss of Drosophila vacuolar peduncle (vap), a presumed GAP enzyme, is associated with enhanced basal autophagy rate and physiological alterations resulting in a wasteful cell energy balance, a hallmark of overactive autophagy. Spri was conditional to normal basal autophagy and instrumental to the starvation-sensitivity phenotype specific of vap. Rab5 activity itself was essential for PI(3)P and for pre-autophagosome structures formation. We propose that Vap/Spri complexes promote a cell surface-derived flow of endocytic Rab5-containing vesicles, the traffic of which is crucial for the implementation of a basal autophagy rate.
</source>

text: This study focused on the yellow seed trait in Brassica oilseed crops, specifically utilizing the unique yellow seed color genes found in B. rapa var. Yellow Sarson. The objective was to develop yellow-seeded cultivars of both B. rapa and B. napus. Researchers developed near-isogenic lines (NILs) of Yellow Sarson for the major seed coat color quantitative trait locus (QTL) SCA9-2 on chromosome A9. These NILs facilitated fine mapping of the QTL region and identification of candidate genes through linkage mapping and transcriptome sequencing of developing seeds. Linkage analysis and physical mapping identified six SSR markers within the 18.4 to 22.79 Mb region of SCA9-2, displaying recombination rates ranging from 0.63 to 5.65%. Transcriptome analysis revealed 55 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the SCA9-2 region, including three transcription factors: Bra028039 (NAC), Bra023223 (C2H2 type zinc finger), and Bra032362 (TIFY). Additionally, several genes encoding unknown or nucleic acid binding proteins were identified as potential candidates for regulating seed coat color. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses of the DEGs highlighted significant enrichment in biosynthetic pathways, including flavonoid, phenylpropanoid, and suberin pathways. This research represents the first comprehensive investigation into the yellow seed trait of Yellow Sarson, employing both linkage mapping and global transcriptome analysis approaches.

On Sunday, a new explosive device detonated near the Pyramids of Giza in Egypt, police reported. Initial accounts suggest that a man, possibly a tourist, was carrying the bomb in a sack from a bazaar. The explosion reportedly occurred accidentally in the area of Kufr Tuhurmus. Apart from the bomber, Sami Gamal Ahmad, who sustained severe injuries and is unable to be questioned, no other casualties were reported. The man may have been transporting the explosive to the tourist area of Kerdassa, home to souvenir shops and a bazaar near the pyramids, according to an official.

text:
A magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck Japan at 2:46 UTC (11:46 am local time), roughly 95 km (60 miles) off the eastern coast of northern Honshu, near Sendai. The quake swayed buildings in Tokyo, 350 km (220 miles) away, and led to the shutdown of trains. The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center issued a bulletin, and small tsunamis were subsequently observed.

As a safety measure, Tohoku Electric's nuclear power plants were shut down. The earthquake caused power outages in Miyagi and Fukushima Prefectures, leaving about 17,000 households without electricity.

Transport services, including the Tōhoku Shinkansen, were halted, and Sendai Airport was temporarily closed.

There have been no reported fatalities. However, over 69 people across Miyagi, Iwate, Fukushima, Saitama, and Tokyo Prefectures have been injured. Notably, 26 individuals were hurt by a collapsing roof in an indoor swimming pool in Sendai. The disaster damaged 687 houses in the Tohoku region and one wooden house in Saitama Prefecture. A woman trapped in the collapsed Saitama house was rescued after 50 minutes.

Egypt has intermittently opened and closed the Rafah Border Crossing with the Gaza Strip over the past few days. text:
So, you've got this book, right? "The Heart of Midlothian." It's all about this old prison in Edinburgh, Scotland, during a time when something pretty wild called the Porteous Riots happened. Back in 1736, there was a riot over the execution of two smugglers. The guy in charge, Captain John Porteous, told his soldiers to shoot into the crowd, killing a few people. Later, a mob got so mad they lynched Porteous and stormed the Old Tolbooth.

But that's just the backdrop. The main story is about this girl, Jeanie Deans. She's based on a real person, Helen Walker, who walked all the way to London to get a pardon for her sister, who was wrongly accused of infanticide. Scott, the author, took that story and made it his own. Jeanie's from a family of really devout Presbyterians, and she's on a mission to London, partly on foot, to try and meet the Queen with the help of the Duke of Argyll.

Jeanie's a big deal in this book. She's the first female protagonist Scott wrote, and she's from the lower classes. She's all about her faith and doing the right thing, but Scott also pokes a little fun at her family's extreme Presbyterian beliefs. There's also this big theme of Jacobitism, which is something Scott often wrote about. You can tell where his sympathies lie with the Duke of Argyll, who's more moderate about all that.

Oh, and if you're into adaptations, the book's been turned into a movie, a TV show, and even two operas. Pretty neat, huh?

<source>
 The title of the book refers to the Old Tolbooth Prison in Edinburgh, Scotland, at the time in the heart of the Scottish county of Midlothian. The historical backdrop was the event known as the Porteous Riots. In 1736, a riot broke out in Edinburgh over the execution of two smugglers. The Captain of the City Guards, Captain John Porteous, ordered the soldiers to fire into the crowd, killing several people. Porteous was later killed by a lynch mob who stormed the Old Tolbooth. The second, and main element of the novel was based on a story Scott claimed to have received in an unsigned letter. It was about a certain Helen Walker who had travelled all the way to London by foot, in order to receive a royal pardon for her sister, who was unjustly charged with infanticide. Scott put Jeanie Deans in the place of Walker, a young woman from a family of highly devout Presbyterians. Jeanie goes to London, partly by foot, hoping to achieve an audience with the Queen through the influence of the Duke of Argyll. Jeanie Deans' role in the novel is described in more detail in Jeanie Deans (fictional character). Jeanie Deans is the first woman among Scott's protagonists, and also the first to come from the lower classes. While the heroine is idealized for her religious devotion and her moral rectitude, Scott nevertheless ridicules the moral certitude represented by the branch of Presbyterianism known as Cameronians, represented in the novel by Jeanie’s father David. Also central to the novel is the early-18th century Jacobitism, a theme found in so many of Scott’s novels. Scott’s sympathies can be seen in the ideal figure of the Duke of Argyll, a moderate on these issues. The Heart of Midlothian has been adapted for the screen once, in 1914, and for television once, in 1966. Two operas have also been based upon the novel - La Prigione di Edimburgo (Imprisoned in Edinburgh) by the Italian composer Federico Ricci (1809–1877) and Jeanie Deans by the Scottish classical composer, Hamish MacCunn (1868–1916).
</source>

text:
In May 1844, Miranda Wells, the daughter of a farmer in Greenwich, Connecticut, receives an invitation from her wealthy relative, Nicholas Van Ryn. As Patroon of Dragonwyck Manor near Hudson, New York, Van Ryn invites one of the Wells sisters to live with his family. Despite initial hesitation, Miranda's parents agree to the arrangement, and she travels to Dragonwyck. Miranda is drawn to her enigmatic cousin, but not everyone is pleased by her arrival. Nicholas's wife, the corpulent and indolent Johanna, views Miranda as a threat and seeks to keep her away from Nicholas.

Shortly after Miranda's arrival, she meets Dr. Jeff Turner, a skilled physician and ardent anti-renter. He believes that wealthy Patroons like the Van Ryns should relinquish their vast estates. Miranda and Dr. Turner take an immediate dislike to each other, so she is surprised when Nicholas asks the doctor to tend to Johanna, who has a cold. However, Johanna's condition suddenly worsens, and she dies. As Dr. Turner departs, puzzled by the abrupt turn of events, Nicholas proposes to Miranda, and she accepts.

Married life with Nicholas proves far different from Miranda's expectations. As the story progresses, Nicholas's mental instability and lust for power become apparent. Following the death of their only child, Miranda's relationship with Nicholas deteriorates, while her bond with Dr. Turner grows stronger. They eventually uncover that Nicholas poisoned his first wife, Johanna, with oleander. Upon confronting him, they attempt to escape but are pursued by Nicholas. He catches up with Miranda on a steamboat traveling down the Hudson River. The steamboat becomes engulfed in a race, catches fire, and crashes. Nicholas saves Miranda but perishes while trying to rescue other passengers.

In the aftermath, Miranda and Dr. Turner marry and leave the Hudson Valley for a new life in California.

text:
Basal autophagy is a catabolic process that break down damaged macromolecules and organelles, recycling them into essential nutrients. While it's crucial for cellular maintenance, the origin of its constitutive rate isn't well understood. Our study found that loss of Drosophila vacuolar peduncle (vap), a putative GTPase-activating protein (GAP) enzyme, increased basal autophagy rates. This led to physiological changes, including an imbalanced, wasteful cell energy state, a sign of overactive autophagy. Interestingly, starvation-induced autophagy was disrupted in vap mutants, blocking autolysosome maturation.

This issue stemmed from excessive PI(3)P-dependent endomembrane biogenesis, affecting autophagosome membranes and causing aberrant vesicle fusions. These findings help explain the neurodegenerative phenotype observed in vap mutant adult brains in previous research. Conversely, Sprint (Spri), a Vap partner and endocytic guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for Rab5, reduced PI(3)P-dependent endomembrane formation in mutants. One year after the passing of Archbishop Iakovos of America, Professor Athanasios Angelopoulos from Aristotle University of Thessaloniki and his colleague Nicolas Mottas, a politics graduate from Westminster University in London, attended the first annual memorial service held in Boston on April 9, 2006. They represented the Ecumenical Hellenism program and the Institute for National and Religious Studies of Thessalonika at this event.

While in Boston, Angelopoulos and Mottas took the opportunity to meet with Nikie Calles, the director of Archbishop Iakovos' archives and his personal secretary for many years, at the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America. They also met with Paulette Poulos, the director of development at Leadership 100 and a former secretary of Iakovos at the Onassis Cultural Centre in New York City. These meetings discussed the unpublished correspondence of the late Archbishop on human rights and national issues, which is set to be published in both Greek and English later this year.

The representatives of Ecumenical Hellenism, a program initiated in 1996 under the patronage of former Hellenic Republic President Constantinos Stephanopoulos and now under the patronage of the Ecumenical Patriarchate and the Church of Greece, also had the chance to meet with the current Archbishop of America, Demetrios.

text:
In 1987, an elderly woman named Katy Thatcher recounts a pivotal time in her life that took place between 1908 and 1911. Katy, whose father was the community doctor, aspired to follow in his footsteps and become a doctor herself. She took a particular interest in Jacob, a boy known as "touched" who lived on a neighboring farm. Jacob couldn't speak, but he hummed softly to himself and seemed to have a unique connection with animals. He would often visit the Thatcher home to be with the animals in the barn. Katy shared Jacob's love for animals and felt that she could communicate with him in a simple, empathetic way.

Trouble brewed when Jacob's sister, Nell, had a baby out of wedlock with Paul Bishop. Jacob, aware of the situation, took matters into his own hands. One stormy night, he abducted the baby and brought it to the Thatcher's house, hoping to save it as he had saved orphaned lambs by finding them a substitute mother. However, his plan didn't go as intended.

Years later, Katy married Austin Bishop and eventually became a doctor. Fifty years after these events, the local asylum closed down. Jacob was never seen again, and there were no records of him ever being there.

text:
Marine animals, particularly seabirds and pinnipeds, significantly contribute to biogeochemical cycling by facilitating the transfer of nutrients from aquatic to terrestrial ecosystems. Soils enriched by animal excreta typically exhibit high levels of organic carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus. While numerous studies have explored bacterial diversity in Antarctic soils influenced by marine fauna, the majority have focused on areas with substantial human impact. Consequently, we selected Cape Shirreff, Livingston Island, an Antarctic Specially Protected Area established primarily to preserve marine vertebrate diversity, as our study site. We chose sampling locations with varying types of animal assemblages in close proximity and minimal human disturbance.

Employing 16S rRNA gene analysis through high-throughput sequencing, we evaluated the impact of animal concentrations—via their alteration of edaphic characteristics—on soil bacterial diversity and composition. The nutrient profiles of soils influenced by Antarctic fur seals and kelp gulls were more akin to those of control soils (i.e., soils devoid of visible plant or animal presence). This similarity may stem from the more active behavioral patterns of these marine species compared to others. In contrast, soils from southern elephant seal and penguin colonies exhibited greater nutrient compositional disparities compared to control soils. Correspondingly, the bacterial communities associated with these animals diverged most significantly from those of the control soils, with penguin colony soils displaying the lowest bacterial diversity.

Despite these differences, all soils impacted by marine animals were predominantly populated by bacteria from the Gammaproteobacteria class, notably the genus Rhodanobacter. Thus, we posit that the alteration of soil nutrient composition by marine vertebrates fosters specific bacterial groups, potentially playing a crucial role in nutrient recycling within terrestrial Antarctic ecosystems.

Seabirds and pinnipeds play an important role in biogeochemical cycling by transferring nutrients from aquatic to terrestrial environments. Indeed, soils rich in animal depositions have generally high organic carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus contents. Several studies have assessed bacterial diversity in Antarctic soils influenced by marine animals; however most have been conducted in areas with significant human impact. Thus, we chose Cape Shirreff, Livingston Island, an Antarctic Specially Protected Area designated mainly to protect the diversity of marine vertebrate fauna, and selected sampling sites with different types of animals coexisting in a relatively small space, and where human presence and impact are negligible. Using 16S rRNA gene analyses through massive sequencing, we assessed the influence of animal concentrations, via their modification of edaphic characteristics, on soil bacterial diversity and composition. The nutrient composition of soils impacted by Antarctic fur seals and kelp gulls was more similar to that of control soils (i.e. soils without visible presence of plants or animals), which may be due to the more active behaviour of these marine animals compared to other species. Conversely, the soils from concentrations of southern elephant seals and penguins showed greater differences in soil nutrients compared to the control. In agreement with this, the bacterial communities of the soils associated with these animals were most different from those of the control soils, with the soils of penguin colonies also possessing the lowest bacterial diversity. However, all the soils influenced by the presence of marine animals were dominated by bacteria belonging to Gammaproteobacteria, particularly those of the genus Rhodanobacter. Therefore, we conclude that the modification of soil nutrient composition by marine vertebrates promotes specific groups of bacteria, which could play an important role in the recycling of nutrients in terrestrial Antarctic ecosystems.
</source>

text:
Addressing the concurrent epidemics of HIV and non-communicable diseases (NCDs) is a critical public health concern in many sub-Saharan African nations, particularly in those with high HIV prevalence such as South Africa. Research indicates that the coexistence of HIV and NCDs within the workforce exacerbates absenteeism and diminishes productivity. However, the prevalence and contributing factors of these chronic conditions among educators remain undocumented. Enhancing our comprehension of this issue is vital for the effective management and well-being of educators. This study presents findings on the prevalence of selected NCDs and associated factors among HIV-positive educators in South Africa, utilizing data from the 2015/6 survey of Educators in Public Schools in South Africa.

This study was conducted as a second-generation surveillance initiative involving educators from randomly selected public schools across all nine provinces in South Africa. A multi-stage stratified cluster design with probability proportional to size sampling was employed to select the schools. Factors linked to the presence of NCDs were identified through multivariate backward stepwise logistic regression analysis.

A total of 1,365 schools were sampled, with 21,495 educators (85.5%) participating in interviews. Of the 2,691 HIV-positive educators who responded to NCD-related questions, 36.9% reported having at least one NCD. The most frequently reported NCDs were high blood pressure (17.4%) and stomach ulcers (13.5%). The likelihood of reporting NCDs was significantly higher among females compared to males [adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 1.5; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.1–1.9; p<0.002] and among educators aged 45–54 years (aOR = 1.8; 95% CI, 1.4–2.2; p<0.001) and those aged 55 years and older compared to those aged 18–24 years (aOR = 2.7; 95% CI, 1.8–3.9; p<0.001). Conversely, the likelihood of reporting NCDs was significantly lower among educators who had not been absent from school for health reasons (aOR = 0.7; 95% CI, 0.6–0.9; p=0.003).

Incorporating NCD care and proactive screening into HIV programs is essential, encompassing prevention, treatment, care, and support strategies for public school educators. The education department must prioritize health promotion intervention programs to prevent and mitigate the adverse impacts of NCDs and HIV on the educational sector.

text:
The Dalmatians' day of enchantments begins when they wake up to find all humans and other animals in an unusually deep sleep. They hear Cadpig's bark, echoing from London, where she serves as the Prime Minister's pet. She reports that this phenomenon is occurring nationwide and calls delegate dogs to London. The dogs journey there by "swooshing," a gliding motion just above the ground.

Pongo and Missus decide to investigate Cruella de Vil, suspecting her involvement. They are joined by Tommy, the white Persian cat (an "honorary dog"), and a few other dogs. Upon arriving at Cruella's house, the doors magically open. However, they find her asleep like the other humans. The dogs then gather at Trafalgar Square, where Sirius, Lord of the Dog Star, an extraterrestrial dog, addresses them from Nelson's Column. Each dog sees Sirius as a member of their own breed.

Sirius invites the dogs to his home for safety from Earth's nuclear threats and human mistreatment. Opinions vary, but ultimately, the dogs agree that Pongo, known for his intelligence and bravery, should decide. Pongo confers with Cadpig and her "cabinet" about whether to join Sirius. Then, three thin, mixed-breed strays arrive, requesting to speak. Pongo assumes they will want to leave with Sirius, but they wish to stay, hoping to find owners. Pongo tells Sirius the dogs won't abandon their humans. Sirius accepts this decision but grants each dog the power to reach his home before the humans awaken. All stray dogs seize this opportunity to go to the Battersea Dogs and Cats Home.

text: In May 1844, Miranda Wells, the daughter of a modest farmer in Greenwich, Connecticut, received an invitation from her wealthy relative, Nicholas Van Ryn. Nicholas, the Patroon of the grand manor Dragonwyck near Hudson, New York, asked one of the Wells girls to stay at Dragonwyck and keep his daughter Katrine company. Despite initial hesitations, Miranda's parents allowed her to go. Miranda was immediately drawn to her enigmatic and affluent relative, Nicholas. However, not everyone at Dragonwyck welcomed Miranda. Nicholas's wife, the corpulent and indolent Johanna, viewed Miranda as a threat and sought to keep her away from Nicholas. Shortly after Miranda's arrival, she met Dr. Jeff Turner, a skilled physician and ardent anti-renter who believed that wealthy Patroons like the Van Ryns should relinquish their vast estates. Miranda and Dr. Turner initially disliked each other, so she was surprised when Nicholas asked Dr. Turner to tend to his wife, who had a cold. While Dr. Turner was at Dragonwyck, Johanna's condition suddenly worsened, and she died. As Dr. Turner left, pondering the cause of Johanna's abrupt death, Nicholas proposed to Miranda, and she accepted. Miranda's married life with Nicholas, however, was not what she had envisioned. As the story progressed, Nicholas's true mental state and his hunger for power became apparent. After their only child died, Miranda's relationship with Nicholas deteriorated, while her bond with Dr. Turner grew stronger. Miranda and Dr. Turner eventually uncovered that Nicholas had poisoned his first wife, Johanna, with oleander. They confronted him and attempted to escape, but Nicholas caught up with Miranda on a steamboat traveling down the Hudson River. The steamboat became engulfed in a race, caught fire, and crashed. Miranda was rescued by Nicholas, who perished trying to save other passengers. Following this ordeal, Miranda and Dr. Turner married and left the Hudson Valley for a new life in California.

text:
In the late hours of Thursday night, Eduardo Rodriguez Veltzé, who previously served as President of the Supreme Court of Justice, was sworn in as Bolivia's new interim president. This transition comes amidst a profound political crisis that has gripped the nation for months.

Earlier that day, the Bolivian Legislature halted its planned session in Sucre's House of Liberty, which was intended to elect a new president following Carlos Mesa's resignation on Monday night. This decision followed heightened protests sparked by the tragic killing of a minor by the military. The demonstrations also reflected widespread opposition to the potential appointment of Hormando Vaca Diez, president of the Senate, or Mario Cossío, president of the House of Representatives, who were next in line for the presidency according to the constitution.

Evo Morales, the influential coca leader and a prominent opponent of both Mesa and Vaca Diez, had previously supported Rodriguez Veltzé's appointment. While Morales advocates for a constitutional assembly, he may now withdraw this demand as the interim president has pledged to hold early elections, potentially as soon as December. Additionally, the Congress is expected to call for parliamentary elections, although the constitution only mandates that the temporary president must call elections for the presidency and vice presidency.

text:
This research delved into how induced pain affects our sense of body and the space around us during and after tool use. We know that chronic pain can mess with these perceptions, but it's not clear if acute, experimental pain does the same. Our bodies and the space right around us are always updating based on what we're doing, like when we use tools. So, we wanted to see if pain gets in the way of this updating process.

We set up three scenarios: one with induced pain, one with a placebo, and a neutral one. Participants did two tasks: one to measure how their perception of space around their body changed with tool use, and another to see how their sense of body size shifted after using a tool.

As expected, using tools changed how people perceived the space around them, extending to the tool's tip. And after actively using a tool, their sense of body size shrank a bit. But here's the surprising part: pain didn't seem to interfere with any of this. Unlike what we predicted, induced pain didn't disrupt the updating of these spatial and bodily perceptions. So, it seems that acute pain doesn't distort our body and space representations like chronic pain can.

<source>
Representations of the body and peripersonal space can be distorted for people with some chronic pain conditions. Experimental pain induction can give rise to similar, but transient distortions in healthy individuals. However, spatial and bodily representations are dynamic, and constantly update as we interact with objects in our environment. It is unclear whether induced pain disrupts the mechanisms involved in updating these representations. In the present study, we sought to investigate the effect of induced pain on the updating of peripersonal space and body representations during and following tool-use. We compared performance under three conditions (pain, active placebo, neutral) on a visuotactile crossmodal congruency task and a tactile distance judgement task to measure updating of peripersonal space and body representations, respectively. Consistent with previous findings, the difference in crossmodal interference from visual distractors in the same compared to opposite visual field to the tactile target was less when tools were crossed than uncrossed. This suggests an extension of peripersonal space to incorporate the tips of the tools. Also consistent with previous findings, estimates of the felt tactile distance judgements decreased after active tool-use. In contrast to our predictions, however, we found no evidence that pain interfered with performance on either task when compared to the control conditions. Our findings suggest that the updating of peripersonal space and body representations is not disrupted by induced pain. That is, experiencing acute pain does not give rise to distorted representations of the body and peripersonal space that can be present in people with chronic pain conditions.
</source>

text:
Epidural catheters represent the current standard for postoperative analgesia in abdominal surgery. However, they can induce neurolysis, potentially leading to postoperative urinary tract retention (POUR), which may necessitate prolonged bladder catheterization. This extended catheterization carries an elevated risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs).

This study sought to examine two primary objectives: first, to assess the contemporary perioperative management of urinary catheters; and second, to determine the optimal timing for suprapubic bladder catheter removal in relation to epidural catheter removal.

An initial questionnaire was dispatched to 102 German hospitals, with 83 responses analyzed to evaluate the existing protocols for bladder drainage and epidural catheter management. Subsequently, a retrospective study was conducted on 501 patients who had received both an epidural and suprapubic catheter following abdominal surgery at the University Hospital Würzburg. Patients were stratified into three groups based on the timing of suprapubic catheter removal relative to epidural catheter removal, and the incidence of UTIs was scrutinized.

The survey results indicated that in nearly all participating hospitals (98.8%), patients received both an epidural catheter and bladder drainage post-abdominal surgery. The timing of urinary catheter removal was evenly distributed among the three categories: before, simultaneous with, or after the removal of the epidural catheter (approximately 28-29% for each). The retrospective study revealed a 6.7% incidence of catheter-associated UTIs, with women experiencing significantly higher rates than men (10.7% versus 2.5%, p<0.001). Notably, there was a non-significant trend suggesting a higher UTI incidence when the suprapubic catheter was removed after the epidural catheter (5.7% before, 8.4% after).

The timing of suprapubic bladder drainage removal relative to epidural catheter removal appears not to correlate with UTI rates. Given the observed heterogeneity in current practices across Germany, further research to establish standardized treatment protocols is recommended.

text:
Krish and Ananya, a Punjabi guy from Delhi and a Tamilian girl from Chennai, respectively, meet at IIM Ahmedabad's mess. Krish is struck by Ananya's beauty and her fiery argument with the mess staff about the food. She's known as the "Best girl of the fresher batch." They become friends quickly and start studying together every night, which eventually turns into a romantic relationship. Both secure jobs and start planning their wedding. Krish takes the initiative to win over Ananya's family. He helps her father with his first PowerPoint presentation, tutors her brother Manju, and arranges a concert at his workplace, Citibank, where Ananya's mother gets to sing with T.S Subramanium and Hariharan, fulfilling her lifelong dream. She's won over. The real challenge is Krish's mother and her relatives, who oppose the marriage because Ananya is a Madrasi. But Ananya wins them over by helping Krish's cousin find a match.

With both families convinced, Krish and Ananya plan to introduce their parents in Goa. However, their dream takes a hit when Ananya's parents suspect something fishy between Krish's mom and him, leading them to call off the wedding. Just when all seems lost, Krish's father, who had been distant, steps in and convinces Ananya's family. After much effort, the couple's wedding becomes a reality. The story is narrated in the first person with a humorous tone, poking fun at both Tamil and Punjabi cultures. It wraps up with Ananya giving birth to twin boys, symbolizing unity as they say the babies belong to a state called 'India.' Interestingly, a character from the author's previous work, Five Point Someone, makes an appearance here as well.

<source>
 Partly autobiographical, the story is about Krish and Ananya who hail from two different states of India, are deeply in love and want to get married. The story begins in the IIM Ahmedabad mess, where Krish, a Punjabi boy from Delhi sights a beautiful girl, Ananya, a Tamilian from Chennai, quarreling with the mess staff about the food. Ananya was tagged as the "Best girl of the fresher batch". They become friends within a few days and decide to study together every night. In mean time, they become romantically involved. They both get jobs, and have serious plans for their wedding. At first Krish tries to convince his girlfriend Ananya's parents and at last and convinces them by helping Ananya's father to do his first PowerPoint Presentation, her brother, Manju, by giving him tuition and later convinces her mom by asking her sing in a concert organised by Krish's office, i.e Citibank. She was convinced as she had her biggest dream of singing in a big concert comes to be true. She sang along with T.S Subramanium and Hariharan. Then they tried to convince Krish's mom the problem was Krish's mother's relatives who doesn't quite like this, they say that Krish should not marry a Madrasi but ends up agreeing with them when Ananya tries to help one of Krish's cousin to get married and succeeds to do so. Now as they have convinced both their parents they now try to make their parents meet each other to know each. They go to GOA. But this dream of theirs ends as Ananya's parents finds something fishy between Krish's mom and him. Ananya's family end up deciding that Krish and Ananya will not marry each other But at last Krish's father who was like an enemy for Krish helps Krish and Ananya to get married as he convinces Ananya's family well. They really do very hard to convince each other parents and finally make it. It is narrated in a first person point of view in a humorous tone, often taking digs at both Tamil and Punjabi cultures . The novel ends with Ananya giving birth to twin boys. They say that the babies belong to a state called 'India'; with a thought to end inequality. What is even more interesting is the continuation of character Hari of Five Point Someone in Krish.
</source>

text: A homeless man, self-named "Mister," storms into the Washington DC law firm of Drake & Sweeney, taking numerous lawyers hostage. The standoff ends when police shoot and kill the intruder, freeing the captives. Among them, antitrust lawyer Michael Brock is haunted by what he's uncovered and embarks on a personal investigation. His path leads him to the 14th Street Legal Clinic, where he meets Mordecai Green, an advocate for the homeless. Green enlists Brock to volunteer at a homeless shelter. As Brock digs deeper, he uncovers his own firm's involvement in an illegal eviction that led to the tragic death of a young homeless family. He secretly takes a confidential file, intending to make copies, but is swiftly suspected of theft. Horrified by his discovery, Brock quits his high-paying job to join the 14th Street Legal Clinic, advocating for the homeless. This decision drives a wedge between him and his wife, leading to divorce. At the clinic, Brock helps a client, Ruby, enroll in a therapy program for women battling drug addiction, where he meets Megan, who will become his love interest. As Drake & Sweeney retaliates with theft and malpractice accusations, the clinic counters by suing the firm and its associates. Fearing the negative publicity, both sides agree to mediation, resulting in a substantial settlement for the clinic to distribute among the eviction's victims. Moved by these events, Drake & Sweeney's head partner offers pro bono assistance to support the clinic's mission. The story concludes with Brock, Megan, and Ruby enjoying a brief vacation, reflecting on their lives and the journey that brought them together.

text:
Distortions in body and peripersonal space representations can occur in those with certain chronic pain conditions. Similarly, experimental pain induction in healthy individuals can lead to temporary distortions. Yet, spatial and bodily representations are dynamic, continually updating as we engage with our surroundings. It's unclear whether induced pain disrupts the mechanisms that update these representations. Our study aimed to examine how induced pain affects the updating of peripersonal space and body representations during and after tool-use.

We compared performance under three conditions—pain, active placebo, and neutral—on two tasks: a visuotactile crossmodal congruency task and a tactile distance judgment task. These tasks measure the updating of peripersonal space and body representations, respectively. As expected, based on prior findings, the difference in crossmodal interference from visual distractors in the same compared to the opposite visual field to the tactile target was less when tools were crossed than uncrossed. This suggests an extension of peripersonal space to the tool tips. Also as expected, estimates of felt tactile distance decreased after active tool-use. However, contrary to our predictions, pain did not interfere with performance on either task compared to the control conditions.

Our findings indicate that induced pain doesn't disrupt the updating of peripersonal space and body representations. In other words, acute pain doesn't cause the distorted representations of the body and peripersonal space seen in some chronic pain conditions.

<source>
Representations of the body and peripersonal space can be distorted for people with some chronic pain conditions. Experimental pain induction can give rise to similar, but transient distortions in healthy individuals. However, spatial and bodily representations are dynamic, and constantly update as we interact with objects in our environment. It is unclear whether induced pain disrupts the mechanisms involved in updating these representations. In the present study, we sought to investigate the effect of induced pain on the updating of peripersonal space and body representations during and following tool-use. We compared performance under three conditions (pain, active placebo, neutral) on a visuotactile crossmodal congruency task and a tactile distance judgement task to measure updating of peripersonal space and body representations, respectively. Consistent with previous findings, the difference in crossmodal interference from visual distractors in the same compared to opposite visual field to the tactile target was less when tools were crossed than uncrossed. This suggests an extension of peripersonal space to incorporate the tips of the tools. Also consistent with previous findings, estimates of the felt tactile distance judgements decreased after active tool-use. In contrast to our predictions, however, we found no evidence that pain interfered with performance on either task when compared to the control conditions. Our findings suggest that the updating of peripersonal space and body representations is not disrupted by induced pain. That is, experiencing acute pain does not give rise to distorted representations of the body and peripersonal space that can be present in people with chronic pain conditions.
</source>
