text: In the Southeast USA, major contributors to estuarine soundscapes are the courtship calls produced by fish species belonging to the family Sciaenidae. Long-term monitoring of sciaenid courtship sounds may be valuable in understanding reproductive phenology, but this approach produces massive acoustic datasets. With this in mind, we designed a feature-based, signal detector for sciaenid fish calls and tested the efficacy of this detector against manually reviewed data. Acoustic recorders were deployed to collect sound samples for 2 min every 20 min at four stations in the May River estuary, South Carolina, USA from February to November, 2014. Manual analysis of acoustic files revealed that four fish species, belonging to the family Sciaenidae, were the major sound producers in this estuarine soundscape, and included black drum (Pogonias cromis), silver perch (Bairdiella chrysoura), spotted seatrout (Cynoscion nebulosus), and red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus). Recorded calls served as an acoustic library of signature features that were used to create a signal detector to automatically detect, classify, and quantify the number of calls in each acoustic file. Correlation between manual and automatic detection was significant and precision varied from 61% to 100%. Automatic detection provided quantitative data on calling rates for this long-term data set. Positive temperature anomalies increased calling rates of black drum, silver perch, and spotted seatrout, while negative anomalies increased calling rates of red drum. Acoustic monitoring combined with automatic detection could be an additional or alternative method for monitoring sciaenid spawning and changes in phenology associated with climate change.

text: Epidermal ceramides are indispensable lipids that maintain the functions of the stratum corneum. Esterified omega-hydroxyacyl-sphingosine (EOS) ceramide with a linoleate moiety is one of the most important ceramide species for forming cornified lipid envelopes. This linoleate moiety is eventually metabolized to trihydroxy-linoleic acid (triol, 9,10,13-trihydroxy-11E-octadecenoic acid). Thus, we assumed that a decrease of triols might reflect skin barrier dysfunction. Against this background, the purposes of this study were to measure the triols by a simple tape-stripping method and to determine the correlation between the amount of triols and transepidermal water loss (TEWL) as an indicator of barrier dysfunction in atopic dermatitis patients. Twenty Japanese subjects with normal skin and 20 atopic dermatitis patients were enrolled in this study. TEWL was measured and triols of the stratum corneum were analyzed by tape-stripping. The results showed for the first time that triols in the stratum corneum could be simply measured using the tape-stripping method. The triol levels in atopic dermatitis patients were much higher than those in healthy subjects. Moreover, the triol levels correlated with TEWL of non-lesional forearm skin in patients with atopic dermatitis. The results suggest that the assaying of triol levels via non-invasive tape-stripping could be beneficial for monitoring barrier function in atopic dermatitis.

text: The carabid subfamily Paussinae contains many species known to be obligately associated with ants during at least one stage of their life history. Myrmecophilous larvae have been documented for members of the tribe Paussini as well as several genera in the tribes Ozaenini, including Physea and Eustra. Here we describe the first instar larva of Ozaena lemoulti, and find it to be the most highly modified ozaenine larva that we have examined to date. Many structures of the larva suggest that it is a myrmecophile. Unlike all other described ozaenine larvae, which live in burrows that they construct and seal with their terminal disk, the completely unique larval morphology suggests Ozaena has adapted to living without the protection of a burrow and therefore must have a completely different feeding strategy than the typical ambush strategy of burrow dwelling larvae. We hypothesize that Ozaena larvae live in association with ants and use their long legs for running within the nest, and modifications of the mouthparts suggest the larva feeds on soft lightly sclerotized prey, such as ant brood. Our findings support an earlier hypothesis that Ozaena is mymecophilous during the adult stage. Comparisons of the functional anatomy of the eggs, larvae and adult between Ozaena lemoulti and the closely related, non-myrmecophilous general arthropod predator, Goniotropis kuntzeni, provide complementary, yet independent, evidence suggestive of this shift in lifestyle. We also examine and molecularly identify gut contents, providing direct evidence that adult Ozaena exclusively eat Camponotus ants. We conclude that Ozaena represents an independent shift to adopting a life of myrmecophily among beetles classified within the carabid subfamily Paussinae and document the morphological changes at each life history stage associated with the shift to a nest parasite lifestyle.

text: Mycoplasma hyorhinis and M. hyosynoviae are agents associated with arthritis in pigs. This study investigated the tonsillar detection patterns of M. hyorhinis and M. hyosynoviae in a swine population with a history of lameness. The plausibility of dual PCR detection of these agents in dams at one and three weeks post-farrowing and their offspring at the same time was determined. The association between M. hyorhinis and M. hyosynoviae detection in piglets and potential development of lameness in wean-to-finish stages was evaluated by correlating individual piglet lameness scores and PCR detection in tonsils. Approximately 40% of dams were detected positive for M. hyorhinis and M. hyosynoviae at both one and three weeks post-farrowing. In first parity dams, M. hyorhinis was detected in higher proportions (57.1% and 73.7%) at both weeks of sampling compared to multi-parity dams. A lower proportion of first parity dams (37.5%) were detected positive at week one with M. hyosynoviae and an increase in this proportion to 50% was identified in week three. Only 8.3% of piglets were detected positive for M. hyorhinis in week one compared to week three (50%; p<0.05). The detection of M. hyosynoviae was minimal in piglets at both weeks of sampling (0% and 0.9%). Lameness was scored in pigs 5–22 weeks of age, with the highest score observed at week 5. The correlation between PCR detection and lameness scores revealed that the relative risk of developing lameness post-weaning was significantly associated with detection of M. hyorhinis in piglets at three weeks of age (r = 0.44; p<0.05).The detection pattern of M. hyorhinis and M. hyosynoviae in dams did not reflect the detection pattern in piglets. Results of this study suggest that positive detection of M. hyorhinis in piglets pre-weaning could act as a predictor for lameness development at later production stages.

text: This paper evaluates the development impacts of migration and remittances in migrant source communities by applying insights from the New Economics of Labor Migration (NELM) theory to Ethiopia’s migration. Using household survey data, we empirically evaluate how household participation in migration arises and so that the subsequent labor losses and the influx of remittances affect income sources and asset accumulation of smallholder farm households. To account several econometric issues and consistently estimate the impacts of migration and remittances, we adopted three-stage least-squares method complemented with endogeneity and multicollinearity test. Besides, using logistic and multinomial logistic regressions respectively, we estimate the determinants of the household migration decision to have migrants, as well as the probability of the household to send out temporary or permanent migrants. Findings suggest that larger and wealthier households are less likely to have migrant family members, while households living below the poverty line, as well as villages with the highest unemployment rate, are the most likely to have both temporary and permanent migrants. However, a rise in months spent out of agriculture has a significant negative effect on crop income and asset accumulation, but only for permanent migration. By contrast, the influx of remitted income from migrants has led to increased crop income and asset values in the form of land and livestock holdings. Finally, this manuscript provides more comprehensive evidence by showing the net-returns of migration in terms of initial lost-labor effects and the positive developmental impacts that it produces varied for households with different types of migration and production conditions.

text: The incidence of stillbirth in Sweden has essentially remained constant since the 1980’s, and despite thorough investigation, many cases remain unexplained. It has been suggested that a proportion of stillbirth cases is caused by heart disease, mainly channelopathies. The aim of this study was to analyze DNA from 290 stillbirth cases without chromosomal abnormalities for pathogenic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in 70 genes associated with cardiac channelopathies and cardiomyopathies. The HaloPlex Target Enrichment System (Agilent Technologies) was utilized to prepare sequencing libraries which were sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq platform. We found that 12.1% of the 290 investigated stillbirth cases had one (n = 31) or two (n = 4) variants with evidence supporting pathogenicity, i.e. loss-of-function variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice site substitutions), evidence from functional studies, or previous identification of the variants in affected individuals. Regarding identified putative pathogenic variants in genes associated with channelopathies, the prevalence was significantly higher in the stillbirth cohort (n = 23, 7.93%) than the corresponding prevalence of the same variants in the non-Finnish European population of the Exome Aggregation Consortium (2.70%, p<0.001) and SweGen, (2.30%, p<0.001). Our results give further support to the hypothesis that cardiac channelopathies might contribute to stillbirth. Screening for pathogenic SNVs in genes associated with heart disease might be a valuable complement for stillbirth cases where today’s conventional investigation does not reveal the underlying cause of fetal demise.

text: Dementia is a neurological and cognitive condition that affects millions of people around the world. At any given time in the United Kingdom, 1 in 4 hospital beds are occupied by a person with dementia, while about 22% of these hospital admissions are due to preventable causes. In this paper we discuss using Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and in-home sensory devices in combination with machine learning techniques to monitor health and well-being of people with dementia. This will allow us to provide more effective and preventative care and reduce preventable hospital admissions. One of the unique aspects of this work is combining environmental data with physiological data collected via low cost in-home sensory devices to extract actionable information regarding the health and well-being of people with dementia in their own home environment. We have worked with clinicians to design our machine learning algorithms where we focused on developing solutions for real-world settings. In our solutions, we avoid generating too many alerts/alarms to prevent increasing the monitoring and support workload. We have designed an algorithm to detect Urinary Tract Infections (UTI) which is one of the top five reasons of hospital admissions for people with dementia (around 9% of hospital admissions for people with dementia in the UK). To develop the UTI detection algorithm, we have used a Non-negative Matrix Factorisation (NMF) technique to extract latent factors from raw observation and use them for clustering and identifying the possible UTI cases. In addition, we have designed an algorithm for detecting changes in activity patterns to identify early symptoms of cognitive decline or health decline in order to provide personalised and preventative care services. For this purpose, we have used an Isolation Forest (iForest) technique to create a holistic view of the daily activity patterns. This paper describes the algorithms and discusses the evaluation of the work using a large set of real-world data collected from a trial with people with dementia and their caregivers.

text: Living fungal mycelium with abolished ability to form fruiting bodies is a self-healing substance, which is particularly valuable for further engineering and development as materials sensing environmental changes and secreting signals. Suppression of fruiting body formation is also a useful tool for maintaining the stability of a mycelium-based material with ease and lower cost. The objective of this study was to provide a biochemical solution to regulate the fruiting body formation, which may replace heat killing of mycelium in practice. The concentrations of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) inhibitors, such as lithium chloride or CHIR99021 trihydrochloride, were found to directly correlate with the development of fruiting bodies in the mushroom forming fungi such as Coprinopsis cinerea and Pleurotus djamor. Sensitive windows to these inhibitors throughout the fungal life cycle were also identified. We suggest the inclusion of GSK-3 inhibitors in the cultivation recipes for inhibiting fruiting body formation and regulating mycelium growth. This is the first report of using a GSK-3 inhibitor to suppress fruiting body formation in living fungal mycelium-based materials. It provides an innovative strategy for easy, reliable, and low cost maintenance of materials containing living fungal mycelium.

text:
A report published today by the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) finds that, in many cases, England's home care system breaches the human rights of the elderly it is supposed to serve. The Close to home: older people and human rights in home care report is the result of a twelve-month investigation into care generally provided by local authorities.

The report says articles two, three and eight of the European Convention on Human Rights are frequently being breached. These, respectively, cover an individual's right to life, protection from inhumane and degrading treatment, and respect for dignity and personal independence. Criticisms include that care is not provided in a common-sense manner, and funding of care for the elderly is at lower levels than for younger people with similar problems and needs.

The EHRC, having commissioned this report in the face of funding changes and reform of the care system, intends to press for legislative changes to ensure those receiving care at home are given the same protections under the Human Rights Act as those in residential care. In the conclusions of their report they offer to work with, and support, local authorities in understanding and delivering care that respects peoples' rights and dignity; and, recommend better guidance as to the choices available to the elderly, and their families, be made available.

text:
Victoria Stafford, eight years old, was sighted leaving her Woodstock, Ontario school on Wednesday afternoon with an unknown woman caught on video camera. She has not been seen since.

Victoria (Tori) attended grade 3 at Oliver Stephens Public School, and the video is from the College Avenue secondary school as Victoria and the unidentified woman walked along Fyfe Avenue.

Police teams from Oxford, Waterloo and London have assembled together with rescue dogs and trained search and rescue personnel to find the child.

Police have called the search a criminal investigation, but have not yet issued an Amber alert as there has been no report of an abduction.

150 volunteers joined search efforts and to pass out flyers on the 10th. Police say they have no need of more volunteers at this time, however they would appreciate any tips or calls from anyone who may have seen either Victoria or the woman.

The unidentified woman seen in the video is described as between 19 and 25 years old with straight long black hair. She weighs about 120 to 125 pounds and was wearing a white coat and black jeans in the video. Victoria was wearing a green shirt with a black pleated skirt. She was wearing black and white shoes and carried a purple and pink Bratz purse. She had on a black Hannah Montana jacket which had a white fur lined hood.

Volunteers are making and handing out purple ribbons, Tori's favourite colour. A candlelight vigil will be held in the evening on Easter Sunday.

text:
In a referendum held Saturday, Egyptians voted overwhelmingly to amend the nation's constitution immediately, moving Egypt closer to a democracy, according to results announced today.

Electoral officials said 77% of voters endorsed a set of constitutional amendments that included limiting presidential terms, removing limitations on forming political parties, and holding a general election within six months.

Many of the mostly secular protest leaders who headed the revolution leading to President Hosni Mubarak's resignation were opposed to the amendments, not wanting to hold elections so quickly. Mohamed ElBaradei, winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, said the nation needed more political maturity before holding elections so soon. Leaders of Egypt's Coptic Orthodox Church also were against the amendments.

The Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group previously banned under Mubarak's rule, and the National Democratic Party, Mubarak's ruling party, were almost alone in supporting the amendments. Each hoped that its strong organization would give it an advantage in electing the parliament members who will write the new constitution.

Approximately 18 million people, 41% of those eligible, voted, according to electoral officials. This is in contrast to parliamentary elections held four months ago, when the turnout was only six million.

Although there were some problems at the voting places, observers said these were mostly due to the military's hasty preparations, not wrongdoing by officials. Opposition leader Mohammed ElBaradei was prevented from voting by men throwing stones in the worst incidence of sporadic violence.

The results were met with jubilation by Egyptians; in Cairo, horns were honked and fireworks set off. The elections are considered the first in decades not rigged in favor of one party.

At least forty people are reported to have died and another fifty are injured after an accident at a level crossing in Egypt. A truck failed to stop at the crossing near Marsa Matruh, pushing several vehicles waiting ahead of it onto the tracks.

The train then struck the traffic that was in the way. Two carriages toppled on top of cars, and two more derailed. Thirty-five died at the scene, and five more were pronounced dead in hospital. The death toll has already risen from twenty after more bodies were recovered.

Three vehicles were struck by the service from Matruh to Alexandria, and at least two were crushed underneath it. It is unclear whether the truck was amongst the vehicles hit, or if a bus was involved. A fifth carriage was detached from the train.

Heavy equipment has been dispatched to the scene to remove the carriages, and dozens of emergency vehicles are present. It is feared that more bodies remain in the wreckage. It is unclear if the victims are all Egyptian or if anyone from abroad was on the train.

An investigation has been launched into the disaster, but a witness said that the level crossing is hidden behind a hill, leaving drivers with little time to react.

text:
On Sunday, an earthquake rocked the country of Greece early in the afternoon.

Seismographs have recorded the earthquake as a 6.7 (estimated) on the Richter Scale. There are only reports of minor damage at the island of Kythira, including 3 injuries.

The earthquake took place at 1:34 pm local time (1134 UTC) and was felt, according to locals, throughout Greece and as far away as Cairo, Egypt, and the coasts of Jordan. This is unusual, as previous major quakes in the highly-seismic Mediterranean country have been limited to a relatively small region.

The quake's epicenter was located about 200 kilometers (125 miles) south of Athens near Kythira, the US Geological Survey institute said. Amending its previous report of a magnitude of 6.4, the USGS, based in Colorado, and the National Earthquake Information Center in Denver gave a preliminary magnitude of 6.7, However, the Thessaloniki Aristotelion University's Seismology Laboratory and the Patras seismic monitoring station have recorded the quake at a magnitude 6.9.

Aftershocks have been recorded near the epicentre, however were not as powerful as the original earthquake.

A witness in Athens at the time of the quake described the general mood as calm.

More than 100 people died following an earthquake in Athens, Greece, in 1999.

What you are about to read is an American life as lived by renowned author Edmund White. His life has been a crossroads, the fulcrum of high-brow Classicism and low-brow Brett Easton Ellisism. It is not for the faint. He has been the toast of the literary elite in New York, London and Paris, befriending artistic luminaries such as Salman Rushdie and Sir Ian McKellen while writing about a family where he was jealous his sister was having sex with his father as he fought off his mother's amorous pursuit.

The fact is, Edmund White exists. His life exists. To the casual reader, they may find it disquieting that someone like his father existed in 1950's America and that White's work is the progeny of his intimate effort to understand his own experience.

Wikinews reporter David Shankbone understood that an interview with Edmund White, who is professor of creative writing at Princeton University, who wrote the seminal biography of Jean Genet, and who no longer can keep track of how many sex partners he has encountered, meant nothing would be off limits. Nothing was. Late in the interview they were joined by his partner Michael Caroll, who discussed White's enduring feud with influential writer and activist Larry Kramer.

DS: When you notice you are very flexible in your thought and change notions easily, does it have broader implications for you?

DS: One interview I did was with a young novelist named John Reed—

DS: Yes, married, kids. But he feels a problem with creating a new generation of readers today is that the literary canon does not have many modern works at the grade school and high school level, and young readers feel disconnected from reading.

DS: That would seem like racy material for grade school or high school.

DS: Do you see a generation that can assume the mantle for the Violet Quill or is there not a necessity for it?

DS: You think that’s because of a lack of a community of writers?

DS: Earlier you were saying what makes a book a certain genre is a marketing function.

DS: You said in an interview that the smartest people are the best sex—

DS: Do you think that’s a necessity in order to have a successful relationship?

DS: To give up the feeling they always have to be in control in their waking lives?

DS: What psychological issues did you work through in your slave-master relationships?

DS: As if the fashion never changes? It’s always the same chaps, the same harness…

DS: In an interview you said that you are known for the incestuous feelings that were in your family—

DS: —what advice would you give to couples pursuing an incestuous relationship?

DS: Is that because there is an intrinsic problem with it, or because of societal reactions to it?

The release of the movie Avatar, written and directed by James Cameron, has generated increased interest in the field of constructed language, also known as conlang. Cameron asked American linguistics professor Paul Frommer to develop a language spoken by the extraterrestrial people in the film known as the Na'vi.

Author J. R. R. Tolkien developed Elvish languages for his literary series The Lord of the Rings. The Elvish language was featured in scenes of The Lord of the Rings film trilogy, directed by Peter Jackson.

The Klingon language (tlhIngan Hol) was developed by linguist Marc Okrand, initially for use in the 1984 film Star Trek III: The Search for Spock. Okrand drew inspiration from Klingon lines spoken by actor James Doohan in the film Star Trek: The Motion Picture; Doohan portrayed character Montgomery Scott in the Star Trek series. A dictionary for Klingon developed by Okrand, The Klingon Dictionary sold over 300,000 copies.

Linguistics professor Frommer received his PhD degree from the University of Southern California (USC), and subsequently shifted his focus into the business arena. He returned to USC to teach at the Marshall School of Business. Cameron tasked Frommer with creating an entire language for the Na'vi people.

The Na'vi language is itself a minor plot point in the film Avatar. The character Jake Sully portrayed by Sam Worthington endeavors to learn the language while living on Pandora. A botanist portrayed by actress Sigourney Weaver instructs a scientist played by actor Joel David Moore on how to become conversational in the language.

The Eleventh International Human Rights Documentary Film Festival Docudays UA, in Kyiv, Ukraine, ended on Friday.

The Awards Ceremony was held in the Red Hall of the Kyiv Cinema House. There were 36 documentary films competing for prizes in three festival programs: DOCU/Short, DOCU/Right, DOCU/Life. There were also special prizes from Students’ Jury, Audience Award, and the Andriy Matrosov Award from Docudays UA Organizing Committee.

The Audience Award went to Joanna, directed by Aneta Kopacz, Poland, 2013.

Andrei Zagdansky, a Ukrainian-American, was awarding. The other two members of the jury were Victoria Belopolskaya of Russia, and Stéphanie Lamorré of France.

Natalka Zubar of Ukraine announced the winners. The other two members of the jury were Andrzej Poczobut of Belarus, and Oksana Sarkisova of Hungary.

The whole jury was present: Boris Mitić of Serbia, Chris McDonald of Canada, and Simone Baumann of Germany.

The Andrey Matrosove Award went to A Diary of a Journey, directed by Piotr Stasik, Poland, 2013.

After the ceremony The Last Limousine, the winning film of DOCU/Life program, was screened.

The festival was first held in 2003, called at that time Docudays on Human Rights. In 2006 the festival was accepted as part of the international Human Rights Film Network at the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam. It is usually held during the last week of March.

Yasser Reda Ali Abdullah Said, the Egyptian ambassador in Israel, was recalled by the Egyptian government yesterday, who claim that the countries' 1979 peace treaty had been breached by the killing of five Egyptian security personnel as Israeli forces pursued cross-border raiders.

Attacks inside Israel which killed eight Israelis led to what Reuters describes as the most acute crisis in ties between the countries since Hosni Mubarak was overthrown in February, with Egyptian troops being killed in a subsequent shootout between Israeli soldiers pursuing the militants along the Israeli-Egypt border.

A few hundred Egyptians burned Israeli flags and tore down metal barriers, at the Israeli embassy in Cairo, demanding the expulsion of the Israeli envoy.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu consulted cabinet ministers about a potential response.

The Egyptians had also recalled their ambassador in Tel Aviv on previous occasions, such as Israel's 1982 invasion of Lebanon and during the heavy Israeli shelling of the Gaza Strip in 2000.

Citing concern about security in the Sinai Peninsula, the Israelis said the attackers infiltrated from the Gaza Strip, which is run by Hamas, through the Egypt-controlled Sinai Desert, despite Egyptian security's attempts to find the Islamist radicals.

Cairo rejected the accusation which stated that it had lost control of Sinai. The cabinet's decisions came after a meeting attended by generals in the army and Murad Muwafi, the Egyptian intelligence chief.

The peace treaty of 1979 limits the number of troops Egypt can deploy in the Sinai.

The Cairo-based Arab League will hold an urgent meeting on Sunday in order to discuss the Israeli air strikes on the Gaza Strip, following the attacks on Israel, that killed fifteen Palestinians.

text:
Efforts to salvage the Indonesian naval vessel Arung Samudera from where she ran aground on the Sunshine Coast Queensland, have been delayed due to poor weather conditions.

The 35-metre, tri-masted vessel was originally grounded on August 23 in stormy weather at Inskip Point, near Rainbow Beach. A salvage contractor has being brought in to rescue the stricken vessel, her hull is intact and it is believed the ship is in no imminent danger of breaking apart.

However, the tall ship did drag its anchors and break its rudder and centreboard during the beaching.

Australian Navy Commander Forbes Peters says that although salvage has been postponed until early next week, the vessel will be surveyed today by the salvage firm.

The 18-man crew - six officers and 12 sailors - of the New Zealand-built vessel have managed to retrieve their belongings from the ship, and are now expected to be transported to temporary accommodation in local barracks in Bulimba, Brisbane.

It is still hoped the ship can be repaired in time for it to attend a summit next month in Sydney, but this to be unlikely. A decision on whether to take her to Brisbane or Gladstone for repairs is expected to be made on Monday.

In the waning days before the rise of Darth Sidious, the Galactic Senate was gripped by corruption and self-interest. Supreme Chancellor Finis Valorum’s efforts to restore order were hampered by the cunning manipulation of a shadowy Sith, who operated behind the scenes to shape the fate of the Republic. Meanwhile, beyond the Senate’s walls, the Trade Federation’s hold on vital trade routes was under increasing strain—not just from aggressive rivals, but from the violent actions of a clandestine terrorist group known as the Nebula Front. This group exploited fear and outrage, targeting the Trade Federation’s operations in hopes of halting its oppressive methods, using any tactics they deemed necessary.

As the situation escalated, the Trade Federation sought permission from the Senate to deploy more battle droids and other defensive systems along its borders. Valorum, while tempted to grant these expansions, was swayed by Sith advice to demand new concessions in return—specifically, a tax on certain Republic-controlled trade routes. This proposal ignited fierce debate among senators and soon led to the convening of a critical summit. Unbeknownst to the assembled leaders, the Nebula Front had set its sights on preventing the passage of the new taxation, plotting the assassination of Valorum during the gathering.

The Jedi, led by Qui-Gon Jinn and Obi-Wan Kenobi, intercepted the threat and began a relentless pursuit of the terrorists’ leader, Captain Cohl. As the crisis mounted, the Jedi Council itself became directly involved, coordinating efforts to unmask the conspirators and protect the Senate’s leaders. Through these interwoven strands of intrigue and heroism, the story unfolds the fragile state of the Republic at a pivotal moment and the quiet machinations that would soon ignite the Clone Wars. Drawing on the detailed background material from early script drafts and concept art for the subsequent film, the narrative introduces familiar entities such as the Techno Union and Passel Argente in their initial appearances, grounding the unfolding drama in the same political tension and danger that defines the era. Even with minor textual irregularities in earlier drafts—such as a missing 't' in "thought" and an incorrect use of "an" instead of "a"—the underlying facts and gravitas of the period remain clear and unmistakably tense.

text:
Gwynedd in north Wales is ruled by Math, son of Mathonwy, whose feet must always be attended by a virgin, except when he is at war. Math’s nephew, Gilfaethwy, is in love with Goewin, the current footmaid. To win her, Gwydion, Gilfaethwy’s brother, deceives Math into leading him into battle against the Pryderi, Prince of Dyfed. In single combat, Gwydion defeats and kills Pryderi. After the victory, Gilfaethwy rapes Goewin. As penance, Math marries Goewin and banishes Gwydion and Gilfaethwy, transforming them first into deer, then into pigs, and finally into wolves. Three years later, they are restored to their human forms and return.

Seeking a new foothold, Math turns to his sister Arianrhod. To test her virginity, Math uses magic; Arianrhod, however, proves not chaste, giving birth to two sons. One son, Dylan, immediately prefers the sea. The other, raised by Gwydion, refuses to take a name or arms unless Arianrhod bestows them. She withholds both, but Gwydion tricks her into naming the boy Llew Llaw Gyffes (“Llew Skilful Hand”) and granting him arms. Arianrhod then swears that Llew will never wed a wife of any race on earth. In response, Gwydion and Math create for him a beautiful wife fashioned from flowers, whom they name Blodeuwedd, meaning “Flowers.”

Blodeuwedd falls for a passing hunter, Goronwy. The pair plot to kill Llew. Blodeuwedd deceives Llew into revealing how he can be slain, but when Goronwy tries to carry out the murder, Llew escapes, wounded, turning into an eagle in his flight. Gwydion finds Llew and restores him to human form, while turning Blodeuwedd into an owl (“Blodeuwedd,” literally “Flower Face”). In the end, Goronwy offers compensation, but Llew, insisting on justice, kills the hunter with a spear thrown with such force that it pierces him even through stone.

text:
A neurological and cognitive disorder affecting millions, dementia occupies one in four hospital beds in the United Kingdom at any given time, with roughly 22% of inpatient admissions attributable to preventable causes. This study explores the integration of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and in-home sensory devices, augmented by machine learning, to monitor the health and well-being of individuals with dementia within their own environments. The approach uniquely combines environmental data with physiological signals from low-cost in-home sensors, enabling the extraction of actionable insights to inform timely care and reduce unnecessary hospitalizations.

Central to this work is the development of practical, clinically relevant machine learning solutions tailored for real-world deployment. A key focus has been the detection of Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)—one of the top five causes of hospital admission among dementia patients, accounting for approximately 9% of such admissions in the UK. We employed Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to distill latent patterns from raw sensor data, using the resulting factors for clustering and identification of potential UTI cases. Additionally, an algorithm utilizing the Isolation Forest (iForest) method was designed to detect subtle changes in daily activity patterns, which can signal early signs of cognitive or health deterioration. These early indicators support personalized, preventative care strategies.

By prioritizing reduced alert fatigue—avoiding an overabundance of notifications that could burden caregivers—the systems are optimized for practical use. Evaluation was conducted using extensive real-world trial data collected from individuals with dementia and their carers, ensuring robust assessment of the proposed methods. This paper presents these algorithms, their rationale, and an evaluation of their effectiveness in supporting improved, preventive care for people living with dementia.

text: Epicellular ceramides are essential for maintaining the integrity of the stratum corneum. Among these, EOS ceramide with a linoleate chain is a key species in forming cornified envelopes. Over time, the linoleate portion is metabolized into trihydroxy-linoleic acid (triol, 9,10,13-trihydroxy-11E-octadecenoic acid). Given this, we hypothesized that reduced triol levels might indicate skin barrier dysfunction. To test this, we measured triol concentrations in the stratum corneum using a simple tape-stripping technique and examined the relationship between triol levels and transepidermal water loss (TEWL)—a marker of barrier function—in 20 atopic dermatitis (AD) patients and 20 healthy controls. The findings demonstrate, for the first time, that triol levels can be accurately assessed by tape-stripping. Notably, AD patients exhibited significantly higher triol levels than healthy individuals. Furthermore, in AD patients, higher triol concentrations were associated with increased TEWL in non-lesional forearm skin. These results suggest that measuring triol levels non-invasively by tape-stripping may serve as a useful tool for monitoring skin barrier dysfunction in atopic dermatitis.

The triol levels in atopic dermatitis patients were much higher than those in healthy subjects. Moreover, the triol levels correlated with TEWL of non-lesional forearm skin in patients with atopic dermatitis. The results suggest that the assaying of triol levels via non-invasive tape-stripping could be beneficial for monitoring barrier function in atopic dermatitis.

text: Living fungal mycelium lacking the capacity to form fruiting bodies constitutes a self-healing material with potential for sensing environmental changes and secreting signals, making it valuable for further engineering. Inhibiting fruiting body formation is advantageous for maintaining material stability at lower cost. This study aimed to biochemically regulate fruiting body development as an alternative to traditional heat-based methods. We evaluated glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) inhibitors—including lithium chloride and CHIR99021 trihydrochloride—and observed a direct correlation between inhibitor concentration and fruiting body emergence in species such as Coprinopsis cinerea and Pleurotus djamor. Distinct inhibitor sensitivity windows across the fungal life cycle were identified. We recommend incorporating GSK-3 inhibitors in cultivation protocols to suppress fruiting body formation and control mycelial growth. This represents the first use of a GSK-3 inhibitor to modulate fruiting in living fungal mycelium, offering an innovative, easy, and cost-effective approach for maintaining such bio-based materials.

text: Stratum corneum ceramides play a critical role in maintaining skin barrier function. Among these, EOS ceramide containing linoleate is a key species involved in forming cornified envelope layers. The ultimate degradation of this ceramide leads to the production of trihydroxy-linoleic acid (triol). Given this pathway, we hypothesized that reduced triol levels could signal barrier dysfunction in atopic dermatitis. This study evaluated triol concentrations using a straightforward tape-stripping technique and examined the relationship between triol levels and transepidermal water loss (TEWL), a marker of skin barrier function, in 20 healthy controls and 20 atopic dermatitis patients. Results demonstrated that triol measurement by tape-stripping is feasible and reliable. Importantly, stratum corneum triol concentrations were significantly elevated in atopic dermatitis patients compared with healthy individuals. Furthermore, higher triol levels were associated with increased TEWL in non-lesional forearm skin from atopic dermatitis patients. These findings suggest that measuring triol levels non-invasively with tape-stripping may offer a valuable approach for assessing and monitoring skin barrier dysfunction in atopic dermatitis.

Epidermal ceramides are indispensable lipids that maintain the functions of the stratum corneum. Esterified omega-hydroxyacyl-sphingosine (EOS) ceramide with a linoleate moiety is one of the most important ceramide species for forming cornified lipid envelopes. This linoleate moiety is eventually metabolized to trihydroxy-linoleic acid (triol, 9,10,13-trihydroxy-11E-octadecenoic acid). Thus, we assumed that a decrease of triols might reflect skin barrier dysfunction. Against this background, the purposes of this study were to measure the triols by a simple tape-stripping method and to determine the correlation between the amount of triols and transepidermal water loss (TEWL) as an indicator of barrier dysfunction in atopic dermatitis patients. Twenty Japanese subjects with normal skin and 20 atopic dermatitis patients were enrolled in this study. TEWL was measured and triols of the stratum corneum were analyzed by tape-stripping. The results showed for the first time that triols in the stratum corneum could be simply measured using the tape-stripping method. The triol levels in atopic dermatitis patients were much higher than those in healthy subjects. Moreover, the triol levels correlated with TEWL of non-lesional forearm skin in patients with atopic dermatitis. The results suggest that the assaying of triol levels via non-invasive tape-stripping could be beneficial for monitoring barrier function in atopic dermatitis.
</source>

text:
Major sciaenid fish species—black drum (Pogonias cromis), silver perch (Bairdiella chrysoura), spotted seatrout (Cynoscion nebulosus), and red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus)—are the leading contributors to estuarine soundscapes in Southeastern USA. Over a multi-year period, long-term acoustic recordings were made at four stations in the May River estuary, South Carolina, sampling sound data every 20 minutes for two-minute intervals from February through November 2014.

To manage the vast volumes of acoustic data generated, we developed a feature-based signal detector capable of automatically identifying, classifying, and quantifying sciaenid call sequences. This detector was rigorously evaluated against manually reviewed recordings, showing significant agreement between automatic and manual counts, with detection precision ranging from 61% to 100%.

Our results demonstrate that automated detection can reliably provide quantitative calling rate data across extensive time series. Notably, positive temperature deviations were associated with increased calling rates in black drum, silver perch, and spotted seatrout, whereas negative temperature anomalies corresponded to higher calling rates in red drum. Thus, automated acoustic monitoring offers a viable, scalable approach for tracking spawning phenology and detecting climate-driven shifts in sciaenid vocal behavior.

In the Southeast USA, major contributors to estuarine soundscapes are the courtship calls produced by fish species belonging to the family Sciaenidae. Correlation between manual and automatic detection was significant and precision varied from 61% to 100%. Automatic detection provided quantitative data on calling rates for this long-term data set. Positive temperature anomalies increased calling rates of black drum, silver perch, and spotted seatrout, while negative anomalies increased calling rates of red drum. Acoustic monitoring combined with automatic detection could be an additional or alternative method for monitoring sciaenid spawning and changes in phenology associated with climate change.

text:
The novel takes place in early 20th-century India, at the estate of the Bengali zamindar Nikhil. He marries Bimala, a woman of lower social rank and lighter skin than his family expects, a union that goes against his traditions. Their marriage begins as an idyllic one, rooted in mutual devotion and commitment. This peace is disrupted when Nikhil’s friend, the radical Sandip, arrives. Sandip is passionate, outspoken, and a champion of the Swadeshi movement, advocating for Indian independence and rejecting British rule. His presence energizes the local community, drawing support from across the province after his stirring speeches at public rallies.

One night, after hearing Sandip speak, Bimala insists that he visit Nikhil’s home. During his stay, Sandip’s influence sways her, and she suggests making their residence a base for his activities. Once involved with Sandip’s cause, Bimala becomes entangled in the wider revolutionary movement, working alongside him and stepping beyond her earlier domestic life. As the story unfolds, a love triangle emerges: Bimala’s affection for Nikhil is complicated by her growing passion for Sandip, who embodies the zeal and daring she has always desired in a man. Driven by a sense of national duty—though her true motives are more personal—Bimala assists Sandip in stealing from Nikhil’s treasury, believing the funds are rightly for the country.

Nikhil eventually discovers their actions but chooses to grant Bimala the freedom to decide her own path, acknowledging the arrangement was made when she was a child. Through her experiences with love and revolution, Bimala begins to understand Nikhil’s genuine care for her. The movement’s tensions come to a head in a riot. In the chaos, Sandip flees the city, while Nikhil is fatally wounded. Amulya, a youthful follower of Sandip and, in Bimala’s eyes, her son, is killed by gunfire. <source>
 The novel is set in early 20th century India in the estate of the Bengali zamindar Nikhil. He marries Bimala, a woman who is both of a lower status and of a darker complexion, which is contradictory to his family traditions. Their love is idyllic and both are dedicated to one another until the appearance of his friend and radical revolutionist, Sandip. Sandip, a passionate and active man, is a contradiction to the peace-loving and somewhat passive Nikhil. His charismatic speech, support of the Swadeshi movement, and a renewed appreciation of everything Indian while denying everything British garnered support from local natives across the province. After hearing Sandip speak at a rally, Bimala insists that Sandip visit Nikhil’s estate. While visiting, Sandip's influential nature easily attracts the innocent and unsuspecting Bimala, and she suggests he make his headquarters at their house. Once empowered by the inside world, knowing only her husband and home, she becomes engaged with the outside world, taking part in the Swadeshi movement by working with Sandip. As the novel develops, Bimala is drawn to Sandip’s passion and the attraction between the two becomes inevitable, producing a love triangle. She begins to question her marriage with Nikhil and finds in Sandip what she has always sought after in a man: zeal, ambition, and a hint of danger. She begins to help Sandip by stealing money from Nikhil’s treasury, convinced that if it is not equally his money as well as hers, then it belongs to the country. While Bimala claims her national duty as motivation, her true intentions lie in pleasing Sandip. Nikhil subsequently discovers their actions, but grants Bimala freedom to grow and choose what she wants in her life (as their marriage was arranged when she was a young girl). Meanwhile, Bimala experiences love for the first time, which ultimately helps her understand that it is indeed her husband Nikhil who really loves her. The novel ends with a riot, resulting in Sandip fleeing the city. Nikhil is mortally wounded in the head. Amulya, a young follower of Sandip's movement who considered Bimala as his sister, and whom Bimala thinks of as her son (since she has no children), dies by a bullet through his heart.
</source>

text:
Egyptians voted overwhelmingly in a Saturday referendum to immediately amend the constitution, a move that brings the country closer to democracy, officials reported today. Over 77% of voters supported proposed changes, including limiting presidential terms, abolishing restrictions on political parties, and holding a general election within six months.

While most secular protest leaders who sparked the revolution that ousted President Hosni Mubarak opposed the rapid pace of the reforms, many argued that holding elections so soon was too soon. Notably, Nobel Peace Prize winner Mohamed ElBaradei stated that the nation needs greater political maturity before such a hurried election. Leaders of the Coptic Orthodox Church also rejected the amendments.

In contrast, the Muslim Brotherhood—an Islamist group re-emerging after years of prohibition under Mubarak—and the former president's party, the National Democratic Party, largely backed the measures. Both believed their organizational strength would give them an edge in selecting the new parliament members tasked with drafting the updated constitution.

With around 18 million ballots cast—an increase from the 6 million who participated in the recent parliamentary elections four months earlier—the vote saw some logistical issues, largely attributed to rushed military preparations rather than malfeasance. Still, sporadic violence delayed the voting for at least one opposition leader, ElBaradei. Overall, however, the results were celebrated widely: in Cairo, the air was filled with honks and bursts of fireworks as Egyptians hailed the apparent end of rigged elections, marking one of the most open votes in decades.

In a referendum held Saturday, Egyptians voted overwhelmingly to amend the nation's constitution immediately, moving Egypt closer to a democracy, according to results announced today.

Electoral officials said 77% of voters endorsed a set of constitutional amendments that included limiting presidential terms, removing limitations on forming political parties, and holding a general election within six months.

Although there were some problems at the voting places, observers said these were mostly due to the military's hasty preparations, not wrongdoing by officials. Opposition leader Mohammed ElBaradei was prevented from voting by men throwing stones in the worst incidence of sporadic violence.

The results were met with jubilation by Egyptians; in Cairo, horns were honked and fireworks set off. The elections are considered the first in decades not rigged in favor of one party.

text: Antarctica is frequently depicted through the lens of masculine heroism in both popular imagery and STEMM research cultures, which has limited the access of women to Antarctic research and fieldwork—especially since the 1980s. This study presents findings from an exploratory online survey of 95 women who have participated in Antarctic research as part of the Australian Antarctic Program. While female participation in polar science has risen, qualitative findings reveal ongoing gendered barriers to field engagement. The study identifies five key obstacles: physical barriers, unpaid care and caregiving burdens, cultural sexism and gender bias, insufficient opportunities and recognition, and unwelcome male attention or sexual harassment. These barriers contribute to the invisibility and exclusion of women, as well as other marginalized groups, from polar fieldwork. We argue that neglecting issues of gender and sexuality sustains these inequalities. Addressing these through targeted inclusivity, diversity, and equity initiatives is essential, both globally and within national Antarctic programs.

<source>
Antarctica is often associated with images of masculine figures battling against the blizzard. The pervasiveness of heroic white masculine leadership and exploration in Antarctica and, more broadly, in Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics, and Medicine (STEMM) research cultures, has meant women have had lesser access to Antarctic research and fieldwork opportunities, with a marked increase since the 1980s. This article presents findings from an exploratory online survey examining how 95 women experienced research and remote Antarctic fieldwork with the Australian Antarctic Program. Although women are entering polar science in greater numbers, a key theme of the qualitative findings of this survey is that gendered barriers to participation in research and fieldwork persist. We discuss five key gendered barriers including: 1) Physical barriers, 2) Caring responsibilities/unpaid work, 3) Cultural sexism/gender bias, 4) Lack of opportunities/recognition, and 5) Unwanted male attention/sexual harassment. We argue that the lack of attention paid to gender and sexuality in polar fieldwork contributes to the invisibility and exclusion of women and other marginalized identities broadly. To conclude, we point to the importance of targeted inclusivity, diversity and equity initiatives through Antarctic research globally and specifically by National Antarctic Programs.
</source>

text:
Within hours of the referendum held on Saturday, Egyptian voters overwhelmingly approved proposed constitutional changes, signaling a dramatic shift toward democracy in the country. Officially released figures indicated that roughly 77 percent of those who participated supported the new amendments, which include capping presidential terms, abolishing restrictions on forming political parties, and scheduling a general election within six months.

These measures, which seek to reshape Egypt’s governance structure, drew strong support from the ruling National Democratic Party and the recently unbaned Muslim Brotherhood. In contrast, many of the principal protest leaders who spearheaded the movement that ousted President Hosni Mubarak expressed concern over the speed of the process and the timing of the elections. Notably, prominent figures such as Nobel laureate Mohamed ElBaradei warned that the nation might not be politically mature enough for immediate elections. Leaders of Egypt’s Coptic Orthodox Church also voiced opposition to the amendments.

Turnout was high, with nearly 18 million eligible voters participating—nearly double the rate in the recent parliamentary elections, which saw just over six million people cast ballots. While some logistical issues occurred during the voting process, most experts attributed these to rushed preparations by the authorities, rather than deliberate irregularities. However, there was one incident where opposition figure ElBaradei was blocked from voting due to violent confrontations involving stone-throwing.

Reactions across Egypt were jubilant. In Cairo, citizens honked car horns and set off fireworks upon hearing the official results, viewing the outcome as a vindication that the vote had not been manipulated in favor of any particular group. Many viewed these reforms as a historic milestone, marking the first genuinely open elections in the country’s recent history.

In a referendum held Saturday, Egyptians voted overwhelmingly to amend the nation's constitution immediately, moving Egypt closer to a democracy, according to results announced today.

Electoral officials said 77% of voters endorsed a set of constitutional amendments that included limiting presidential terms, removing limitations on forming political parties, and holding a general election within six months.

Many of the mostly secular protest leaders who headed the revolution leading to President Hosni Mubarak's resignation were opposed to the amendments, not wanting to hold elections so quickly. Mohamed ElBaradei, winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, said the nation needed more political maturity before holding elections so soon. Leaders of Egypt's Coptic Orthodox Church also were against the amendments.

The Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group previously banned under Mubarak's rule, and the National Democratic Party, Mubarak's ruling party, were almost alone in supporting the amendments. Each hoped that its strong organization would give it an advantage in electing the parliament members who will write the new constitution.

Approximately 18 million people, 41% of those eligible, voted, according to electoral officials. This is in contrast to parliamentary elections held four months ago, when the turnout was only six million.

Although there were some problems at the voting places, observers said these were mostly due to the military's hasty preparations, not wrongdoing by officials. Opposition leader Mohammed ElBaradei was prevented from voting by men throwing stones in the worst incidence of sporadic violence.

The results were met with jubilation by Egyptians; in Cairo, horns were honked and fireworks set off. The elections are considered the first in decades not rigged in favor of one party.
</source>

text:
The release of James Cameron’s movie Avatar has sparked renewed interest in constructed languages, or conlangs. Cameron enlisted American linguistics professor Paul Frommer to create the Na’vi language spoken by the alien inhabitants of Pandora.

Similarly, J. R. R. Tolkien invented the Elvish languages for The Lord of the Rings, which were featured in Peter Jackson’s film adaptations. In these films, the Elvish language appears in scenes with the actors portraying Elvish characters.

Another notable conlang is Klingon (tlhIngan Hol), developed by linguist Marc Okrand for the 1984 film Star Trek III: The Search for Spock. Okrand drew on dialogue by James Doohan, who played Montgomery Scott in the original Star Trek series. Okrand’s Klingon Dictionary became a bestseller, selling more than 300,000 copies.

Professor Frommer, who earned his PhD from the University of Southern California, later focused on business and taught at the Marshall School of Business. In Avatar, he was commissioned by Cameron to design a full language for the Na’vi, a detail that plays a minor but significant role in the film’s plot. In Avatar, Sam Worthington’s character Jake Sully learns Na’vi with help from Sigourney Weaver’s botanist and Joel David Moore’s scientist, who are also trying to master the language.

The release of the movie Avatar, written and directed by James Cameron, has generated increased interest in the field of constructed language, also known as conlang. Cameron asked American linguistics professor Paul Frommer to develop a language spoken by the extraterrestrial people in the film known as the Na'vi.

Author J. R. R. Tolkien developed Elvish languages for his literary series The Lord of the Rings. The Elvish language was featured in scenes of The Lord of the Rings film trilogy, directed by Peter Jackson.

Okrand drew inspiration from Klingon lines spoken by actor James Doohan in the film Star Trek: The Motion Picture; Doohan portrayed character Montgomery Scott in the Star Trek series. A dictionary for Klingon developed by Okrand, The Klingon Dictionary sold over 300,000 copies.

Linguistics professor Frommer received his PhD degree from the University of Southern California (USC), and subsequently shifted his focus into the business arena. He returned to USC to teach at the Marshall School of Business. Cameron tasked Frommer with creating an entire language for the Na'vi people.

The Na'vi language is itself a minor plot point in the film Avatar. The character Jake Sully portrayed by Sam Worthington endeavors to learn the language while living on Pandora. A botanist portrayed by actress Sigourney Weaver instructs a scientist played by actor Joel David Moore on how to become conversational in the language.

text:
The protagonist of *The Sun Also Rises* is Jake Barnes, an American expatriate journalist living in Paris. He was wounded in the war, a fact that left him impotent, though the specific details of his injury are never made clear. Jake is fixated on Lady Brett Ashley, a lively and independent Englishwoman with a famous bob and a reputation for casual sexual freedom during the 1920s. Brett, already married twice, moves easily among a circle of men and loves affairs that are as transient as they are intense.

The novel opens in the Parisian café scene, where Jake is seen playing tennis with his old friend Robert Cohn. Afterward, Jake meets a prostitute, Georgette, and later encounters Brett and the flamboyant Count Mippipopolous in a nightclub. When Jake and Brett leave together, Brett confides in him that she loves him, though both sense their chances are slim. 

In the second part of the story, Bill Gorton, a recent New Yorker, joins Jake, and Brett’s intended, Mike Campbell, from Scotland, arrives to complete the circle. The group heads to Spain, where Jake and Bill take a fishing trip with Cohn north of Pamplona. Cohn’s lingering attachment to Brett, forged during an earlier affair, casts a shadow over the group’s camaraderie; Cohn’s Jewish background becomes the target of the others’ jokes. In Pamplona, the friends celebrate the running of the bulls, drinking and bickering amid festival chaos. During this time, Brett is drawn to Romero, a young Spanish matador; she seduces him, deepening the tangled web of desire and jealousy among Jake, Cohn, and Romero.

Book Three follows the aftermath of the Spanish fiesta. The group, now sober, disperses. Bill returns to Paris, Mike stays in Bayonne, while Jake heads for San Sebastián. When Jake receives a telegram from Brett, he rushes to Madrid to find her alone, destitute, and without Romero. She admits she has returned to Mike, her former fiancé. The novel concludes with Jake and Brett in a taxi, reflecting on what might have been.

<source>
 The protagonist of The Sun Also Rises is Jake Barnes, an expatriate American journalist living in Paris. Jake suffered a war wound that has caused him to be impotent; the nature of his injury is not explicitly described in the novel. He is in love with Lady Brett Ashley, a twice-divorced Englishwoman. Brett, with her bobbed hair, embodies the new sexual freedom of the 1920s, having had numerous love affairs. Book One is set in the Café society of Paris. In the opening scenes, Jake plays tennis with his college friend Robert Cohn, picks up a prostitute (Georgette), and runs into Brett and Count Mippipopolous in a nightclub. Brett and Jake leave together; in a taxi she tells him she loves him, but they know they have no chance at a lasting relationship. In Book Two Jake is joined by Bill Gorton, recently arrived from New York, and Brett's fiancé Mike Campbell, who arrives from Scotland. Jake and Bill travel to Spain, where they meet Robert Cohn north of Pamplona for a fishing trip. Cohn, however, leaves for Pamplona to wait for Brett and Mike. Cohn had an affair with Brett a few weeks earlier and still feels possessive of her despite her engagement to Mike. Jake and Bill enjoy five days of tranquility, fishing the streams near Burguete, after which they rejoin the group in Pamplona, where they begin to drink heavily. Cohn's presence is increasingly resented by the others, who taunt him with anti-semitic remarks. During the fiesta the characters drink, eat, watch the running of the bulls, attend bullfights, and bicker with each other. Jake introduces Brett to Romero at Montoya's hotel; she is smitten with the 19-year-old matador and seduces him. The jealous tension among the men builds; Jake, Campbell, Cohn, and Romero each love Brett. Cohn, who had been a champion boxer in college, has fistfights with Jake, Mike, and Romero, whom he injures. Despite the tension, Romero continues to perform brilliantly in the bullring. Book Three shows the characters in the aftermath of the fiesta. Sober again, they leave Pamplona. Bill returns to Paris, Mike stays in Bayonne, and Jake goes to San Sebastián in northeastern Spain. As Jake is about to return to Paris, he receives a telegram from Brett asking for help; she had left with Romero for Madrid. He finds her in a cheap hotel, without money, and without Romero. She announces she has decided to go back to Mike. The novel ends with Jake and Brett in a taxi speaking of the things that might have been.
</source>

text:
In the northern kingdom of Gwynedd, the ruler is Math, whose feet must always be bound by a maiden, save when he is away at war. This peculiar law is held by tradition for him. Math’s nephew, Gilfaethwy, is hopelessly in love with the current footmaid, Goewin. Determined to win her, he persuades his brother Gwydion to trick Math into battle with the neighboring tribe of Pryderi. Gwydion arranges for single combat, and in the ensuing fight, he defeats Pryderi, the prince of Dyfed. With victory secure, Gilfaethwy violates Goewin. As recompense for the violation, Math weds Goewin and, as penance, exiles Gwydion and Gilfaethwy, magically turning them first into deer, then into pigs, and finally into wolves. Three years pass before they are returned to human form, though changed by the ordeal.

Seeking a new footholder for Math, Gwydion proposes his sister Arianrhod. However, when Math magically tests her purity, she is found to be pregnant, giving birth to twin sons. One son, Dylan, is immediately drawn to the sea; the other remains with Gwydion but is forbidden a name and arms by his mother, who demands she bestow them if she wishes to grant them. Gwydion outwits Arianrhod into naming the second son Llew Llaw Gyffes—“Llew Skilful Hand”—and endows him with arms. Arianrhod then swears that Llew will never wed a woman of any race. Undeterred, Gwydion and Math create for him a beautiful wife, Blodeuwedd, made from flowers. Blodeuwedd falls for a man named Goronwy, and the two conspire to kill Llew. Blodeuwedd tricks Llew into revealing the method of his undoing, but when Goronwy tries to carry out the plot, Llew escapes, turning into an eagle in the process. Gwydion finds Llew and restores him to humanity, meanwhile transforming Blodeuwedd into an owl. In a final act of defiance, Llew, wounded, confronts Goronwy and kills him with a spear thrown so forcefully it penetrates stone.

<source>
 Gwynedd in north Wales is ruled by Math, son of Mathonwy, whose feet must be held by a virgin at all times except while he is at war. Math's nephew Gilfaethwy is in love with Goewin, the current footholder, and Gilfaethwy's brother Gwydion tricks Math into going to war against Pryderi so Gilfaethwy can have access to her. Gwydion kills Pryderi, Prince of Dyfed, in single combat, and Gilfaethwy rapes Goewin. Math marries Goewin in compensation for her rape, and banishes Gwydion and Gilfaethwy, transforming them into a breeding pair of deer, then pigs, then wolves. After three years they are restored to human form and return. Math needs a new footholder, and Gwydion suggests his sister, Arianrhod, but when Math magically tests her virginity, she gives birth to two sons. One, Dylan, immediately takes to the sea. The other is raised by Gwydion, but Arianrhod swears that he will never have a name or arms unless she gives them to him, and refuses to do so. Gwydion tricks her into naming him Llew Llaw Gyffes (Llew Skilful Hand) and giving him arms. She then swears he will never have a wife of any race living on earth, so Gwydion and Math make him a beautiful wife from flowers, and name her Blodeuwedd ("Flowers"). Blodeuwedd falls in love with a passing hunter called Goronwy, and they plot to kill Llew. Blodewedd tricks Llew into revealing the means by which he can be killed, but when Goronwy attempts to do the deed, Llew escapes, though wounded, transformed into an eagle. Gwydion finds Llew and transforms him back into human form, and turns Blodeuwedd into an owl (Blodeuwedd, literally "Flower Face," means "Owl"). Goronwy offers to compensate Llew, but Llew insists on returning the blow that was struck against him. He kills Goronwy with his spear, which is thrown so hard it pierces him through the stone he is hiding behind.
</source>

Victoria Stafford, an eight-year-old student in grade 3 at Oliver Stephens Public School in Woodstock, Ontario, was last seen leaving her school on a Wednesday afternoon accompanied by an unidentified woman, captured on video. The footage was recorded at College Avenue Secondary School as the pair walked along Fyfe Avenue. 

Authorities from Oxford, Waterloo, and London have mobilized teams with search and rescue dogs and specialized personnel in the search for the missing child. While police describe the operation as a criminal investigation, they have not issued an Amber alert, as there is no report of abduction so far.

Over 150 volunteers previously assisted by distributing flyers, but police say additional help is not currently needed. However, they are actively seeking any information or tips from the public that might assist in the search.

The woman seen in the video is described as approximately 19 to 25 years old, with straight, long black hair, weighing about 120 to 125 pounds. She was wearing a white coat and black jeans. Victoria was dressed in a green shirt, black pleated skirt, black and white shoes, a purple and pink Bratz purse, and a black Hannah Montana jacket with a white faux-fur-lined hood.

A candlelight vigil is planned for Easter Sunday evening for Victoria’s sake.

text:
A report released today by the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) finds that, in many cases, England’s home care system fails to uphold the human rights of older people it is supposed to serve. Based on a year-long investigation into care delivered by local authorities, the EHRC’s report, titled Close to Home: Older People and Human Rights in Home Care, details frequent breaches of Articles 2, 3, and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. These articles protect the right to life, prohibit inhumane or degrading treatment, and guarantee respect for dignity and personal independence, respectively.

The report highlights concerns that elderly care is often delivered without common-sense consideration, and that funding for older people’s care is substantially less than for younger individuals with comparable needs. In response to these issues and recent changes to the care system and funding, the EHRC plans to push for legislative reforms ensuring that home care recipients receive the same human rights protections as those in residential care, under the Human Rights Act.

In its conclusion, the EHRC offers to collaborate with local authorities to improve how rights and dignity are respected in care delivery and suggests that clearer guidance should be provided to the elderly and their families about available care options.

Efforts to salvage the Indonesian naval vessel Arung Samudera, which ran aground on the Sunshine Coast of Queensland due to poor weather on August 23, have been delayed because of continued poor weather conditions. Originally grounded at Inskip Point near Rainbow Beach with her hull intact, officials say the ship is not in immediate danger of breaking up.

Despite the grounding, the vessel had already torn its rudder and centerboard while dragging its anchors. Australian Navy Commander Forbes Peters announced that salvage operations have now been postponed until early next week, but a detailed survey of the ship will take place today by the chosen salvage contractor.

The 18-member crew—who are six officers and 12 sailors—have already retrieved their belongings and are set to be moved temporarily to barracks in Brisbane's Bulimba area. While there is hope the ship could be repaired in time for a Sydney summit next month, officials caution that this is unlikely. A decision on whether repairs will be conducted in Brisbane or Gladstone is expected by Monday.

Efforts to salvage the Indonesian naval vessel Arung Samudera from where she ran aground on the Sunshine Coast Queensland, have been delayed due to poor weather conditions.

The 35-metre, tri-masted vessel was originally grounded on August 23 in stormy weather at Inskip Point, near Rainbow Beach. A salvage contractor has being brought in to rescue the stricken vessel, her hull is intact and it is believed the ship is in no imminent danger of breaking apart.

However, the tall ship did drag its anchors and break its rudder and centreboard during the beaching.

Australian Navy Commander Forbes Peters says that although salvage has been postponed until early next week, the vessel will be surveyed today by the salvage firm.

The 18-man crew - six officers and 12 sailors - of the New Zealand-built vessel have managed to retrieve their belongings from the ship, and are now expected to be transported to temporary accommodation in local barracks in Bulimba, Brisbane.

It is still hoped the ship can be repaired in time for it to attend a summit next month in Sydney, but this to be unlikely. A decision on whether to take her to Brisbane or Gladstone for repairs is expected to be made on Monday.
</source>

text:
This study assesses the development impacts of migration and remittances in migrant-sending communities by applying the New Economics of Labor Migration (NELM) framework to the Ethiopian context. Using household survey data, we analyze how migration participation is determined and how related labor losses and remittance inflows influence the income streams and asset accumulation of smallholder farm households. To address endogeneity and multicollinearity concerns, we employ a three-stage least squares approach, supplemented by robust econometric tests.

Logistic and multinomial logistic regressions further examine the determinants of migration decisions—both the likelihood that a household has migrants and the probability that migrants are sent on temporary or permanent basis. Our findings indicate that wealthier and larger households are less likely to send members for migration, whereas those living below the poverty line and located in high-unemployment villages are more likely to do so. Notably, longer periods spent away from agriculture are associated with significant reductions in crop income and asset accumulation, especially in cases of permanent migration. In contrast, remittances positively contribute to crop income and the value of land and livestock assets in recipient households.

Overall, the results offer nuanced evidence on the net returns to migration, highlighting that the developmental effects of migration and remittances vary considerably depending on migration type and local production conditions.

<source>
This paper evaluates the development impacts of migration and remittances in migrant source communities by applying insights from the New Economics of Labor Migration (NELM) theory to Ethiopia’s migration. Using household survey data, we empirically evaluate how household participation in migration arises and so that the subsequent labor losses and the influx of remittances affect income sources and asset accumulation of smallholder farm households. To account several econometric issues and consistently estimate the impacts of migration and remittances, we adopted three-stage least-squares method complemented with endogeneity and multicollinearity test. Besides, using logistic and multinomial logistic regressions respectively, we estimate the determinants of the household migration decision to have migrants, as well as the probability of the household to send out temporary or permanent migrants. Findings suggest that larger and wealthier households are less likely to have migrant family members, while households living below the poverty line, as well as villages with the highest unemployment rate, are the most likely to have both temporary and permanent migrants. However, a rise in months spent out of agriculture has a significant negative effect on crop income and asset accumulation, but only for permanent migration. By contrast, the influx of remitted income from migrants has led to increased crop income and asset values in the form of land and livestock holdings. Finally, this manuscript provides more comprehensive evidence by showing the net-returns of migration in terms of initial lost-labor effects and the positive developmental impacts that it produces varied for households with different types of migration and production conditions.
</source>

text:
Paul Osborn, walking through Paris, spots the man who had murdered his father years earlier. The sight triggers a flood of memories, and soon he’s drawn into the past once more. A detective’s recent discoveries about Henri Kanarack have driven Osborn to Paris with a singular purpose: to kill the man he holds responsible for his father’s death. 

At the same time, McVey arrives in the city to consult experts on a series of bizarre and gruesome decapitations—the bodies and heads preserved in deep freeze. Days later, Osborn attempts to ambush Kanarack. Just as he’s about to fire the shot, a third figure enters. In the chaos, Osborn learns from the dying Kanarack that his father was killed by Kanarack, acting on a contract for Erwin Scholl.

Osborn, shaken, tells McVey everything he knows about Scholl. McVey’s research uncovers a chilling pattern: alongside Osborn’s father’s invention—an ultra-cold surgical scalpel—anomalies occurred around the same time—other inventors specializing in temperature-controlled surgery mysteriously disappeared. Their work, it seems, centered on the possibility of reanimating body parts by freezing and then reviving them.

This leads McVey and his team to suspect that Scholl and his associates might be part of an organization attempting to perfect “reanimated” surgery—the resurrection of body parts using extreme cold, with the ultimate goal of restoring life to the dead. Their suspicions reach a new peak when McVey learns of Elton Lybarger and a secret ceremony scheduled in Berlin.

On the night of the Berlin gathering, as Lybarger delivers his speech in the main hall, panic breaks out. All doors seal, and cyanide gas floods the air. The building is then set ablaze; Osborn narrowly escapes, fleeing after following Von Holden, the last surviving member of the organization.

Later, in Switzerland, cornered and nearly killed, Osborn is given a VCR tape by McVey. The recording contains a confession from one of Lybarger’s physicians. He describes being complicit in experiments based on the strange similarities he noticed between Lybarger’s features and those of Adolf Hitler. The physician details how the group sought to create “perfect Aryans” through secret surgeries, raising two of Lybarger’s adopted “nephews”—one of whom, after a fateful operation, is set to become their new leader.

As Osborn’s memories return, he witnesses Von Holden falling to his death in a crevasse. In his final moments, Von Holden opens a hidden case, revealing the deep-frozen head of Adolf Hitler.

text: A longitudinal analysis of stillbirth rates in Sweden from the 1980s onward reveals minimal change, with investigations ongoing but many cases remaining unexplained. In the current study, DNA from 290 stillbirth cases lacking chromosomal anomalies was examined for pathogenic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) within 70 key genes linked to cardiac channelopathies and cardiomyopathies. Using the HaloPlex Target Enrichment System for library preparation and Illumina NextSeq sequencing, 12.1% of cases (31 instances with one variant and 4 with two) harbored variants of probable pathogenic significance, including loss-of-function mutations and variants previously reported in affected individuals. Notably, the prevalence of putative pathogenic SNVs associated with channelopathies in the stillbirth cohort (7.93%) significantly exceeded that observed in two large non-Finnish European datasets (2.70% and 2.30%, both p < 0.001), reinforcing the potential role of cardiac channelopathies in stillbirth etiology. These findings advocate for genetic screening of these variants in undiagnosed stillbirth cases to identify latent cardiac causes and expand diagnostic approaches.
