The incidence of stillbirth in Sweden has essentially remained constant since the 1980’s, and despite thorough investigation, many cases remain unexplained. It has been suggested that a proportion of stillbirth cases is caused by heart disease, mainly channelopathies. The aim of this study was to analyze DNA from 290 stillbirth cases without chromosomal abnormalities for pathogenic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in 70 genes associated with cardiac channelopathies and cardiomyopathies. The HaloPlex Target Enrichment System (Agilent Technologies) was utilized to prepare sequencing libraries which were sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq platform. We found that 12.1% of the 290 investigated stillbirth cases had one (n = 31) or two (n = 4) variants with evidence supporting pathogenicity, i.e. loss-of-function variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice site substitutions), evidence from functional studies, or previous identification of the variants in affected individuals. Regarding identified putative pathogenic variants in genes associated with channelopathies, the prevalence was significantly higher in the stillbirth cohort (n = 23, 7.93%) than the corresponding prevalence of the same variants in the non-Finnish European population of the Exome Aggregation Consortium (2.70%, p<0.001) and SweGen, (2.30%, p<0.001). Our results give further support to the hypothesis that cardiac channelopathies might contribute to stillbirth. Screening for pathogenic SNVs in genes associated with heart disease might be a valuable complement for stillbirth cases where today’s conventional investigation does not reveal the underlying cause of fetal demise.
</source>

text: Research demonstrates that dementia constitutes a significant neurological and cognitive disorder affecting a substantial population globally, with UK healthcare statistics indicating that one in four occupied hospital beds at any given time is occupied by individuals with dementia. Notably, nearly one-fifth of such hospital admissions result from conditions that could be prevented through earlier intervention. This study investigates the application of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies alongside low-cost in-home sensory devices, integrated with machine learning approaches, for continuous monitoring of individuals living with dementia. The aim is to enhance the effectiveness of care and reduce unnecessary hospitalizations, largely by leveraging a combination of environmental and physiological data collected within the home setting. A central contribution of this work is the development of algorithms that avoid excessive alarms, mitigating the burden on caregivers while maintaining reliable monitoring. One focused algorithm utilizes Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to identify latent patterns from sensory data, enabling the detection of Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)—a leading cause of hospital admission in this demographic, accounting for roughly nine percent of such cases in the UK. Additionally, another algorithm employs the Isolation Forest (iForest) method to detect deviations in daily activity patterns, facilitating the early recognition of potential cognitive or health deterioration. These systems were co-designed with clinical professionals to ensure practicality and applicability in real-world environments. Evaluations were conducted using extensive real-world trial data from people with dementia and their caregivers, further validating the algorithms’ effectiveness and suitability for routine home care scenarios.

<source>
Dementia is a neurological and cognitive condition that affects millions of people around the world. At any given time in the United Kingdom, 1 in 4 hospital beds are occupied by a person with dementia, while about 22% of these hospital admissions are due to preventable causes. In this paper we discuss using Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and in-home sensory devices in combination with machine learning techniques to monitor health and well-being of people with dementia. This will allow us to provide more effective and preventative care and reduce preventable hospital admissions. One of the unique aspects of this work is combining environmental data with physiological data collected via low cost in-home sensory devices to extract actionable information regarding the health and well-being of people with dementia in their own home environment. We have worked with clinicians to design our machine learning algorithms where we focused on developing solutions for real-world settings. In our solutions, we avoid generating too many alerts/alarms to prevent increasing the monitoring and support workload. We have designed an algorithm to detect Urinary Tract Infections (UTI) which is one of the top five reasons of hospital admissions for people with dementia (around 9% of hospital admissions for people with dementia in the UK). To develop the UTI detection algorithm, we have used a Non-negative Matrix Factorisation (NMF) technique to extract latent factors from raw observation and use them for clustering and identifying the possible UTI cases. In addition, we have designed an algorithm for detecting changes in activity patterns to identify early symptoms of cognitive decline or health decline in order to provide personalised and preventative care services. For this purpose, we have used an Isolation Forest (iForest) technique to create a holistic view of the daily activity patterns. This paper describes the algorithms and discusses the evaluation of the work using a large set of real-world data collected from a trial with people with dementia and their caregivers.
</source>

text: On Fire Island, during the Fourth of July weekend, two straight couples gather at a house belong to Sally, inherited from her brother, who died of AIDS. While they fill the summer day with feasts, alcoholic drinks, crosswords, and playful fireworks, their conversations drift in quiet introspection. Each, in turns unseen by the others, lets slip thoughts of loneliness and the pressing weight of mortality. These feelings deepen as they notice only the distant sounds of celebration from neighboring houses—where gay men party unseen. For the couples, the holiday brings little real joy, their laughter masking a growing sense of separation from both each other and from the world around them.

text:
Benjamin was born looking like he was already in his seventies, though he could already talk. His father, Roger, wanted him to blend in with the neighborhood kids, so he forced Benjamin to play with toys meant for children. Benjamin only complied to avoid upsetting his father.

At age five, he was sent to kindergarten. But he fell asleep through most of the activities and was sent home early, considered a poor fit among the other children.

By the time he reached twelve, the Button family noticed something strange: Benjamin was aging backward. When he turned eighteen, he enrolled at Yale College. On the day of registration, they discovered he had no hair—the officials, mistaking him for a fifty-year-old man, sent him home, convinced he was delusional.

In 1880, Benjamin was actually twenty, but by then the family had recognized his unusual aging. That year, Roger made him a partner, giving Benjamin control of Roger Button & Co. Hardware. At a societal gathering, he met Hildegarde Moncrief—the daughter of General Moncrief. He was instantly smitten, mistaking her for the younger sister he never knew existed. Unaware of Benjamin’s true age or appearance, they married six months later.

Over the years, Benjamin’s business thrived, but his home life became tedious. Hildegarde, now no longer as vibrant as she once was, nagged relentlessly, which left Benjamin restless and bored. The monotony drove him to join the Spanish-American War in 1898. He distinguished himself in the military, rising to lieutenant colonel and earning a medal before resigning when his business called for his attention.

In 1910, Benjamin turned over the company to his son, Roscoe, and enrolled at Harvard, now looking like a twenty-year-old. His first year at Harvard was exceptional—he dominated college sports, especially American football, and even got his revenge on Yale after an earlier embarrassment.

But by his final two years at Harvard, Benjamin had regressed mentally and physically to a frail sixteen-year-old, unable to play football or handle his academic work. After graduation, Benjamin returned home only to find his wife had moved to Italy. Roscoe, now stern and distant, treated Benjamin with formal distance, even making him address him as “Uncle” to visitors.

As the years went on, Benjamin’s mood and maturity fluctuated, eventually slipping back to the level of a young child. Eventually, Roscoe had a child who went to kindergarten with Benjamin. After that, Benjamin’s memories faded. Gradually, everything slipped away until he could only recall his nurse, and then nothing at all—only darkness remained.

text:
Ozaena lemoulti larvae belong to the myrmecophilous subfamily Paussinae, sharing obligate associations with ants at some life stage. Previous studies have reported myrmecophily in Paussini tribe members and several Ozaenini genera, such as Physea and Eustra. In this study, we report the first detailed description of the first instar larva of O. lemoulti, which exhibits the most extreme morphological modifications among all examined ozaenine larvae.

Unlike all other ozaenine larvae—which inhabit and seal burrows with their terminal disk—the O. lemoulti larva displays a radically different body plan, indicating it does not reside in a burrow and instead relies on direct association with ants. Its anatomy suggests a lifestyle based on mobility within an ant nest, supported by elongated legs likely used for movement. The larval mouthparts also appear adapted for consuming soft, lightly sclerotized prey such as ant brood.

Comparisons with the non-myrmecophilous relative, Goniotropis kuntzeni, highlight evolutionary adaptations specific to Ozaena that support a shift toward myrmecophily. Molecular and morphological analyses of gut contents confirm that adult O. lemoulti feed exclusively on Camponotus ants. These findings provide independent evidence that Ozaena has independently evolved a myrmecophytic lifestyle within the Paussinae subfamily. Taken together, the observed morphological changes across life stages in Ozaena lemoulti document a clear transition to nest-dwelling dependence in this beetle group.

The carabid subfamily Paussinae contains many species known to be obligately associated with ants during at least one stage of their life history. Myrmecophilous larvae have been documented for members of the tribe Paussini as well as several genera in the tribes Ozaenini, including Physea and Eustra. Here we describe the first instar larva of Ozaena lemoulti, and find it to be the most highly modified ozaenine larva that we have examined to date. Many structures of the larva suggest that it is a myrmecophile. Unlike all other described ozaenine larvae, which live in burrows that they construct and seal with their terminal disk, the completely unique larval morphology suggests Ozaena has adapted to living without the protection of a burrow and therefore must have a completely different feeding strategy than the typical ambush strategy of burrow dwelling larvae. We hypothesize that Ozaena larvae live in association with ants and use their long legs for running within the nest, and modifications of the mouthparts suggest the larva feeds on soft lightly sclerotized prey, such as ant brood. Our findings support an earlier hypothesis that Ozaena is mymecophilous during the adult stage. Comparisons of the functional anatomy of the eggs, larvae and adult between Ozaena lemoulti and the closely related, non-myrmecophilous general arthropod predator, Goniotropis kuntzeni, provide complementary, yet independent, evidence suggestive of this shift in lifestyle. We also examine and molecularly identify gut contents, providing direct evidence that adult Ozaena exclusively eat Camponotus ants. We conclude that Ozaena represents an independent shift to adopting a life of myrmecophily among beetles classified within the carabid subfamily Paussinae and document the morphological changes at each life history stage associated with the shift to a nest parasite lifestyle.
</source>

text:
Edmund White’s life is one of crossroads—Classicism meeting the edges of pop notoriety. He has been celebrated in New York, London, and Paris, his circle including literary figures like Salman Rushdie and Ian McKellen. His memoirs and biographies delve deeply into a family marked by complicated, often tangled, emotional dynamics—notably his jealousy over his sister’s intimacy with their father and his own entanglements with his mother. His writing, rooted in personal experience, has explored these themes with directness and insight.

White, now a professor at Princeton University, is known for his work on Jean Genet as well as for novels that often probe the boundaries of desire, identity, and taboo. He has acknowledged the discomfort his life and work can inspire, especially when discussing the intersection of family, sexuality, and artistry. In conversations, he has spoken candidly about the HYPOCRISY OF FAMILY MEMBERS, the challenges of writing about inherited pain, and the way literary reputation can blur personal reality—especially in circles where reputation is built on both brilliance and controversy.

A Wikinews reporter once interviewed him, and the resulting piece made no distinction between the private and the public. When his partner, Michael Carroll, joined the discussion, the subject turned to enduring feuds, such as the long-running rivalry with Larry Kramer. White’s perspectives on creativity and the transmission of literary canon were equally unflinching: he suggested that the lack of modern works taught in schools leaves young readers adrift, and that the market draws lines—genres, taboos—more by accident of promotion than by organic necessity. He has also mused on the allure and dangers of seeking control in love, and on how society’s strictures shape the way desire is written about and read.

When pressed on whether certain subjects—such as incestuous relationships—should remain off-limits in literature, White offered no easy answers. He suggested that both societal stigma and the intrinsic complexity of such themes inform the way these stories are told, but did not take a position one way or the other.

In sum, Edmund White’s life and work persist as an unflinching mirror to the tensions between art and life, personal trauma and public acclaim. His voice, once described as oscillating between high culture and low-brow edge, remains unmistakably his own—brutally honest, unflinching in the discomfort it exposes.

text: A 6.7-magnitude earthquake struck Greece in the early afternoon on Sunday. The quake was detected around 1:34 p.m. local time (1134 UTC), with its epicenter approximately 200 kilometers south of Athens near the island of Kythira. While the initial US Geological Survey estimate was 6.4, later analyses raised the magnitude to 6.7. text: Sciaenid fish courtship calls were the dominant acoustic source in the Southeastern U.S. estuarine environment, identified through two years of continuous monitoring at four coastal stations in the May River, South Carolina. Over 2-minute intervals, collected every 20 minutes from February through November 2014, researchers manually identified four sciaenid species as principal sound producers: black drum (Pogonias cromis), silver perch (Bairdiella chrysoura), spotted seatrout (Cynoscion nebulosus), and red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus). To manage the large volume of recordings, a feature-based signal detector was developed and evaluated against manually labeled data. The detector automatically detected, classified, and tallied sciaenid calls in each audio file, achieving detection accuracies ranging from 61% to 100% precision, with correlation to manual counts being statistically significant. Temperature anomalies also influenced calling behavior: negative temperature changes were associated with increased calling rates for red drum, while positive temperature shifts enhanced the calling activity of black drum, silver perch, and spotted seatrout. Integrating automated detection into long-term acoustic monitoring presents a scalable alternative for tracking reproductive phenology and potential climate-driven shifts in spawning behavior among sciaenid fish.

In the Southeast USA, major contributors to estuarine soundscapes are the courtship calls produced by fish species belonging to the family Sciaenidae. Long-term monitoring of sciaenid courtship sounds may be valuable in understanding reproductive phenology, but this approach produces massive acoustic datasets. With this in mind, we designed a feature-based, signal detector for sciaenid fish calls and tested the efficacy of this detector against manually reviewed data. Acoustic recorders were deployed to collect sound samples for 2 min every 20 min at four stations in the May River estuary, South Carolina, USA from February to November, 2014. Manual analysis of acoustic files revealed that four fish species, belonging to the family Sciaenidae, were the major sound producers in this estuarine soundscape, and included black drum (Pogonias cromis), silver perch (Bairdiella chrysoura), spotted seatrout (Cynoscion nebulosus), and red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus). Recorded calls served as an acoustic library of signature features that were used to create a signal detector to automatically detect, classify, and quantify the number of calls in each acoustic file. Correlation between manual and automatic detection was significant and precision varied from 61% to 100%. Automatic detection provided quantitative data on calling rates for this long-term data set. Positive temperature anomalies increased calling rates of black drum, silver perch, and spotted seatrout, while negative anomalies increased calling rates of red drum. Acoustic monitoring combined with automatic detection could be an additional or alternative method for monitoring sciaenid spawning and changes in phenology associated with climate change.
</source>

text:
Mycoplasma hyorhinis and M. hyosynoviae are known to be associated with arthritis in pigs. This study examined how these bacteria were detected in the tonsils of pigs with a history of lameness. Researchers assessed whether both M. hyorhinis and M. hyosynoviae could be detected by dual PCR in sows at one and three weeks after giving birth, as well as in their young pigs at the same times. The researchers also evaluated whether the presence of these bacteria in piglets was related to an increased risk of developing lameness during the wean-to-finish phase by correlating lameness scores with PCR results from tonsil samples.

Nearly 40% of sows tested positive for both M. hyorhinis and M. hyosynoviae at both one and three weeks post-partum. First-time sows were more likely to have M. hyorhinis detected at both sampling times (about 57% and 74%) than multiparous sows. In contrast, the proportion of first-time sows with M. hyosynoviae detection was lower at one week (about 38%) but rose to 50% at three weeks. Among piglets, only 8.3% tested positive for M. hyorhinis at one week, rising to 50% by the third week (p < 0.05), while M. hyosynoviae was detected in almost none at either time point. Lameness was assessed in pigs from 5 to 22 weeks of age, with the highest scores seen at five weeks. Tonsil PCR results showed that piglets positive for M. hyorhinis at three weeks had a significantly higher relative risk of developing lameness later (r = 0.44; p < 0.05), indicating an association. However, the bacteria’s presence in sows did not predict its presence in their piglets. These findings suggest that detecting M. hyorhinis in piglets around three weeks post-weaning may help predict an increased risk of lameness in later production stages.

text:
The stillbirth incidence in Sweden has remained largely unchanged since the 1980s, with many cases remaining unexplained. Several studies have proposed that a fraction of stillbirth cases may be attributed to heart disease, particularly channelopathies. In this study, DNA from 290 stillbirth cases lacking chromosomal issues was analyzed for pathogenic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in 70 cardiac channelopathy and cardiomyopathy-associated genes. Using the HaloPlex Target Enrichment System (Agilent Technologies), sequencing libraries were prepared and sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq platform.

We detected pathogenic variants in 12.1% of the cases—31 with one such variant and 4 with two. These included loss-of-function variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site) and variants supported by functional data or prior patient reports. Notably, the prevalence of pathogenic variants linked to channelopathies in the stillbirth group (23 cases, 7.93%) was significantly higher than in two large non-Finnish European cohorts (2.70% and 2.30% in Exome Aggregation Consortium and SweGen, respectively; p < 0.001), supporting the hypothesis that cardiac channelopathies may contribute to stillbirth.

Our findings suggest that genetic screening for pathogenic SNVs in relevant cardiac genes could offer valuable additional diagnostic insight for unresolved stillbirth cases.

text:
A recent report by the Equality and Human Rights Commission reveals that England’s home care system often fails to uphold the human rights of older people intended to receive it. Based on a year-long review of care provided by local authorities, the study identified repeated breaches of articles two, three, and eight of the European Convention on Human Rights. These articles protect the right to life, prohibit inhumane or degrading treatment, and guarantee respect for dignity and personal independence.

The investigation highlighted several issues: care arrangements are often not delivered with basic common sense, and older adults and their families frequently receive less funding than younger people with comparable needs. As a result, many are at risk of being denied adequate dignity, choice, and protection from neglect or abuse in their own homes.

In response, the EHRC, who commissioned the report amid recent changes to the care system and funding, is calling for legislative updates that would extend stronger human rights protections to elderly care recipients living at home. The commission pledges to assist local authorities in improving care practices and ensuring that respect and choice are genuinely considered when decisions are made for older people and their families. Improved guidance for both elderly individuals and their loved ones is also recommended to help ensure better access to information and support.

Egypt’s foreign ministry announced yesterday that Ambassador Yasser Reda Ali Abdullah Said was recalled to Cairo, citing what Egyptian officials described as a violation of the 1979 peace treaty after five Egyptian security officers were killed by Israeli forces during cross-border operations targeting militant infiltrators.

Egyptian officials pointed to intelligence reports that the attackers originated from Gaza—under Hamas control—and crossed the Sinai Peninsula, an area under Egypt’s sovereignty, despite Egyptian efforts to secure the border. Cairo denied losing control over Sinai, a territory covered by the terms of the 1979 treaty, which restricts the size of Egyptian military deployments on the territory.

The situation intensified further, as the Arab League prepared to convene an emergency session Sunday to address recent Israeli airstrikes in Gaza, which had left fifteen Palestinians dead.

text:
Ozaena lemoulti belongs to the Carabid subfamily Paussine, a group largely known for species with obligate associations with ants. Larval stages in Paussini and certain Ozaenini genera, including Ozaena, are frequently myrmecophilous; larvae often depend on ants for protection or access to food. In this study, the first instar larva of O. lemoulti is described as exhibiting the most extensive larval modifications observed among Ozaenini. These structural adaptations strongly indicate that Ozaena lemoulti larvae are adapted to living in close association with ants, differing from other ozaenine larvae that reside in self-built, sealed burrows and employ ambush feeding strategies.

In contrast to the typical ozaenine larval lifestyle, the O. lemoulti larva displays a morphology suggesting it does not use a burrow, implying a distinct feeding and survival strategy. The larva’s long legs and specialized mouthparts likely facilitate locomotion within an ant nest and consumption of soft, lightly sclerotized prey such as ant brood. Comparative analyses between Ozaena lemoulti and the non-myrmecophilous relative, Goniotropis kuntzeni, across developmental stages suggest evolutionary adaptations specific to nest parasitism in Ozaena. Molecular gut content analysis further confirms that adult Ozaena lemoulti exclusively consume Camponotus ants.

Collectively, these findings support the hypothesis that Ozaena lemoulti represents an independent evolutionary shift toward myrmecophily within Paussine beetles, accompanied by specific morphological, anatomical, and behavioral adaptations across its life stages.

<source>
The carabid subfamily Paussinae contains many species known to be obligately associated with ants during at least one stage of their life history. Myrmecophilous larvae have been documented for members of the tribe Paussini as well as several genera in the tribes Ozaenini, including Physea and Eustra. Here we describe the first instar larva of Ozaena lemoulti, and find it to be the most highly modified ozaenine larva that we have examined to date. Many structures of the larva suggest that it is a myrmecophile. Unlike all other described ozaenine larvae, which live in burrows that they construct and seal with their terminal disk, the completely unique larval morphology suggests Ozaena has adapted to living without the protection of a burrow and therefore must have a completely different feeding strategy than the typical ambush strategy of burrow dwelling larvae. We hypothesize that Ozaena larvae live in association with ants and use their long legs for running within the nest, and modifications of the mouthparts suggest the larva feeds on soft lightly sclerotized prey, such as ant brood. Our findings support an earlier hypothesis that Ozaena is mymecophilous during the adult stage. Comparisons of the functional anatomy of the eggs, larvae and adult between Ozaena lemoulti and the closely related, non-myrmecophilous general arthropod predator, Goniotropis kuntzeni, provide complementary, yet independent, evidence suggestive of this shift in lifestyle. We also examine and molecularly identify gut contents, providing direct evidence that adult Ozaena exclusively eat Camponotus ants. We conclude that Ozaena represents an independent shift to adopting a life of myrmecophily among beetles classified within the carabid subfamily Paussinae and document the morphological changes at each life history stage associated with the shift to a nest parasite lifestyle.
</source>

text:
The Eleventh International Human Rights Documentary Film Festival Docudays UA concluded on Friday in Kyiv, Ukraine.

The Awards Ceremony took place in the Red Hall of the Kyiv Cinema House. Thirty-six documentary films competed for top prizes across three categories: DOCU/Short, DOCU/Right, and DOCU/Life. Special awards included the Students' Jury prize, the Audience Award, and the Andriy Matrosov Award, presented by the Docudays UA Organizing Committee.

The Audience Award was awarded to “Joanna,” directed by Aneta Kopacz (Poland, 2013). The Andriy Matrosov Award was given to “A Diary of a Journey,” directed by Piotr Stasik (Poland, 2013). The jury panel, comprising Andrei Zagdansky (Ukrainian-American), Victoria Belopolskaya (Russia), and Stéphanie Lamorré (France), selected the winners. Natalka Zubar of Ukraine, along with Andrzej Poczobut (Belarus) and Oksana Sarkisova (Hungary), announced the results.

Boris Mitić of Serbia, Chris McDonald of Canada, and Simone Baumann of Germany also attended the event. Following the ceremony, the winning film from the DOCU/Life program, “The Last Limousine,” was screened. The festival, originally launched in 2003 as Docudays on Human Rights, has been an international event since 2006, now recognized by the Human Rights Film Network at IDFA in Amsterdam and typically held in the final week of March.

text:
The upcoming release of the film Avatar, directed by James Cameron, has sparked renewed curiosity about constructed or invented languages, or conlangs. In the movie, Cameron enlisted Paul Frommer, a former linguistics professor at the University of Southern California, to invent the Na'vi language for the alien inhabitants of Pandora. Frommer, who earlier earned his PhD in linguistics at USC before transitioning to business, was responsible for designing the Na'vi’s grammar and vocabulary for the film.

Another well-known example comes from J.R.R. Tolkien’s fantasy works. The Elvish languages he created for The Lord of the Rings found their way into Peter Jackson’s film adaptations. Additionally, the Klingon language (tlhIngan Hol) was crafted by linguist Marc Okrand for the 1984 Star Trek film Star Trek III: The Search for Spock. Okrand drew on recordings of the original series’ actor, James Doohan, who portrayed Scotty, when developing the language, and later published The Klingon Dictionary, which sold more than 300,000 copies.

In real-world film and franchise settings, linguists have translated their expertise from academia to pop culture—such as Frommer, whose teaching now focuses on business rather than pure linguistics. Meanwhile, languages like Na’vi and Klingon have become culturally significant, even if they exist only on screen or in fictional worlds.

text:
Nikhil, a Bengali zamindar in early 20th-century India, lives on his estate where he is married to Bimala. Bimala, of inferior social standing and darker skin, is less favored by Nikhil’s family. Their marriage, arranged when Bimala was young, is otherwise loving but shaped by the constraints of tradition and social expectation. This harmony is disrupted when Nikhil’s friend, Sandip—a passionate advocate for Indian independence and the Swadeshi movement—arrives. Sandip’s strong beliefs and magnetic presence stand in sharp contrast to the more reserved Nikhil and the cautious routines of the estate.

At a local rally, Sandip’s powerful oratory inspires the local community. Bimala, moved by his words and by the youthful fervor he brings, invites Sandip to stay at their home. There, Sandip’s influence gradually draws Bimala away from her quiet life and into the world of activism. She begins to participate in Swadeshi activities alongside Sandip, feeling both pulled by duty and by her growing attraction to him.

This involvement creates a complicated relationship among the three. Bimala finds in Sandip the zeal, ambition, and excitement she never found in Nikhil. Yet as she steals from Nikhil’s treasury, her motives blend nationalism with personal desire, with her actions ultimately guided as much by love for Sandip as by a sense of national duty. Nikhil discovers the theft but, respecting their marriage’s arrangement and recognizing Bimala’s lack of choices at that time, allows her space to decide her path.

The tension escalates when a riot breaks out. In the chaos, Sandip leaves the region. Nikhil is fatally injured. Amulya, Sandip’s young follower who regarded Bimala as a sister and whom Bimala almost sees as a son—since she herself has no offspring—dies from a gunshot. Through these events, Bimala is forced to confront the realities of love, loss, and loyalty. In the aftermath, she finds clarity: Nikhil’s enduring love for her is what she truly values, even as the world around her has changed dramatically.

Meanwhile, Bimala experiences love for the first time, which ultimately helps her understand that it is indeed her husband Nikhil who really loves her. text:
Before the events of *The Phantom Menace*, Supreme Chancellor Finis Valorum finds himself subtly but skillfully manipulated by Palpatine, who operates in the shadows as the Sith Lord, Darth Sidious. Working behind the scenes, Sidious subtly influences key figures in the Galactic Senate, aligning allies such as the Neimoidians and the Trade Federation to pave the way for a blockade of the planet Naboo. Simultaneously, a terrorist group known as the Nebula Front begins to threaten the Trade Federation’s operations, staging protests and employing violence aimed at halting the Federation’s exploitative tactics. Their leader, Captain Cohl, is determined to provoke violent disruption wherever the Trade Federation’s reach extends.

As the situation escalates, the Trade Federation seeks permission from the Senate to deploy more battle droids and other advanced defenses. Sensing the Federation’s ambitions, Chancellor Valorum agrees to a compromise—he will allow the expansion of droid forces only if the Republic secures a say through taxation of key trade routes. Palpatine’s advice is pivotal here, as he encourages Valorum’s move to preserve his own political standing while further empowering the Sith’s agenda. This proposal sparks intense debate within the Senate, ultimately leading to the scheduling of a crucial summit to decide the future of taxation and planetary rights.

Amid these escalating tensions, the Nebula Front, desperate to halt Senate intervention and prevent the new taxation, plots to assassinate Valorum at the upcoming summit. Sensing the threat, the Jedi Knights—specifically Qui-Gon Jinn and Obi-Wan Kenobi—take up the cause of protecting Senate officials. Together with the Jedi Council, they set out to track down Captain Cohl and the would-be assassins, racing against time to avert disaster.

In crafting this narrative, James Luceno drew on insights from early drafts of *Attack of the Clones*, incorporating new characters and organizations such as the Techno Union and Passel Argente for the first real-time on-page appearances. The prose retains the tense, analytical tone of a general-audience exposition, and the facts, qualifications, and argumentative undertones are preserved, with only minor adjustments for clarity and flow.

text:
Tattooing is particularly frequent among adults—spanning diverse socioeconomic backgrounds—and is often associated with risk-taking behavior. When done under unsanitary conditions, the procedure can pose health hazards. In Myanmar, evidence on the prevalence of tattoos and understanding of potential blood-borne infection transmission is limited. This study, conducted among adults aged 18–35 in four locations of the Mandalay district, aimed to estimate self-reported tattooing prevalence and assess knowledge of transmission risks and their determinants.

Among 401 surveyed adults, 19.5% (95% confidence interval: 16–24) reported having a tattoo. Over 78% of participants recognized at least one blood-borne viral infection transmissible via tattooing. Higher formal education, manual work, and living with family members were linked with greater awareness of these risks. The ability to remove a tattoo independently was significantly associated with continued practice (aOR 1.91; 95% CI 1.06–3.45; p=0.03). Tattooing was notably more common among men (aOR 13.07; 95% CI 6.25–27.33; p<0.001), an association that remained independent.

This study finds that roughly one in five adults in central Myanmar, predominantly males, have tattoos, amid a lack of regulatory oversight for tattoo parlors and limited public health guidelines. These results highlight key target groups and risk factors for future health education efforts. Additional research should examine tattooists’ perspectives to promote safer practices and reduce the risk of blood-borne infection transmission.

<source>
Tattooing especially gains popularity among both men and women in adulthood from the wide range of socioeconomic groups and is noted as a risk taking behaviour in adults. Especially when tattooing does not perform to the highest standards, it can potentially be the hazardous practice. Myanmar has a paucity of evidence-based information on the estimated prevalence of tattoos and awareness of potential disease transmission from tattooing under insanitary conditions as well as the infection risk. The present research was undertaken to help identify the self-reported prevalence of tattooing among adults (18–35 years) and their knowledge of transmission risk of blood-borne infections and its determinants.

A community-based cross-sectional study focused on residents aged 18–35 years was carried out in two urban and two rural areas in Mandalay district, Mandalay Region during 2015. Trained interviewers used a pre-tested structured questionnaire for face-to-face interviews with one eligible participant per selected household (n = 401). Bivariate analysis and multivariable analysis using binary logistic regression were done to ascertain the relevant explanatory variables.

The overall self-reported prevalence of tattooing was 19.5% (78/401) (95% CI = 16–24). Nearly 80% of participants (318/401) knew at least one blood-borne viral infection that could be transmitted from tattooing. The persons who had high formal education, manual laborers and those who lived with their families were significantly more likely to cite at least one blood-borne viral infection. Their perceived possibility to remove tattoo independently influenced the practice of tattooing (aOR = 1.91, 95% CI = 1.06–3.45; p = 0.03) compared with participants who reported no perceived possibility. Tattooing was more common in male (aOR = 13.07, 95% CI = 6.25–27.33; p<0.001) compared to female which was independently significant.

This study ascertained the tattoo prevalence as two in ten adults of working age especially among male in central part of Myanmar in the context of lack of registration system for tattoo parlours and the issuance of safety guidelines. Findings have suggested the target groups and risk factors to be included in future health promotion programs. Future research directions should focus on perspectives of tattooists to create and sustain the sanitary practices to reduce the chance of transmission of blood-borne viral infections.
</source>

On Sunday, an earthquake rocked the country of Greece early in the afternoon.

Seismographs have recorded the earthquake as a 6.7 (estimated) on the Richter Scale. There are only reports of minor damage at the island of Kythira, including 3 injuries.

The earthquake took place at 1:34 pm local time (1134 UTC) and was felt, according to locals, throughout Greece and as far away as Cairo, Egypt, and the coasts of Jordan. This is unusual, as previous major quakes in the highly-seismic Mediterranean country have been limited to a relatively small region.

The quake's epicenter was located about 200 kilometers (125 miles) south of Athens near Kythira, the US Geological Survey institute said. Amending its previous report of a magnitude of 6.4, the USGS, based in Colorado, and the National Earthquake Information Center in Denver gave a preliminary magnitude of 6.7, However, the Thessaloniki Aristotelion University's Seismology Laboratory and the Patras seismic monitoring station have recorded the quake at a magnitude 6.9.

Aftershocks have been recorded near the epicentre, however were not as powerful as the original earthquake.

A witness in Athens at the time of the quake described the general mood as calm.

More than 100 people died following an earthquake in Athens, Greece, in 1999.
</source>

text: Mr. and Mrs. Edward Brookenham host a rather superficial and corrupt social circle. They are the parents of the aimless Harold and the intelligent, though young, Nanda, now eighteen. At one of their soirees, Mr. Longdon is struck by how much Nanda resembles his long-lost beloved—his former lover, now married to another man. Meanwhile, the underpaid civil servant, Vanderbank, looks up to both Mrs. Brookenham—affectionately called "Mrs. Brook"—and Nanda herself. Mr. Longdon quietly hints to Vanderbank that he could provide a substantial dowry should he marry Nanda. Elsewhere, Mrs. Brook is scheming to match Nanda with the wealthy but unsophisticated Mitchy from their circle. Nanda, however, counsels Mitchy to consider Aggie, the rather naive step-niece of a friend of the Duchess. Mitchy follows her advice, only to find himself abandoned by Aggie, who quickly loses interest. Meanwhile, Vanderbank remains indecisive about proposing to Nanda. When confronted, Nanda asks him—and Mitchy—to remember his mother, then prepares to stay at Mr. Longdon's country estate as if she were his daughter.

text:
At least forty people have died and fifty more been injured following a level crossing accident in Egypt. A truck failed to halt at the crossing near Marsa Matruh, barreling into several vehicles already stopped ahead. This caused a train to collide with the pile-up, with two carriages falling onto cars and two others derailing.

Thirty-five were killed at the scene, and five more died in hospital, raising the death toll to at least forty-five. The total number of casualties may rise as authorities continue to search the wreckage. Three vehicles were hit by the Matruh to Alexandria service; at least two were crushed beneath the train, and a fifth carriage was derailed from the rail line.

Emergency crews have arrived with heavy equipment to safely remove the damaged carriages, while dozens of ambulances respond to the scene. Authorities suspect additional bodies may still be trapped inside the wreckage, and it remains unclear whether all victims are Egyptian or if any are foreign nationals. An investigation has begun, but witnesses note that the level crossing is concealed by a hill, leaving drivers with little time to react.

text:
The Eleventh International Human Rights Documentary Film Festival, Docudays UA, concluded its proceedings in Kyiv on Friday. Across three main programs—DOCU/Short, DOCU/Right, and DOCU/Life—thirty-six documentary films were presented for top honors. Additional special awards were awarded by the Students’ Jury, the Audience, and the Andriy Matrosov Committee of Docudays UA Organizing Committee.

At the Awards Ceremony in the Kyiv Cinema House’s Red Hall, the prizes were handed out by a diverse international jury composed of Andrei Zagdansky from Ukraine–America, Victoria Belopolskaya from Russia, and Stéphanie Lamorré from France. Natalka Zubar of Ukraine, alongside Andrzej Poczobut from Belarus and Oksana Sarkisova from Hungary, completed the judging panel. Notably, Boris Mitić from Serbia, Chris McDonald from Canada, and Simone Baumann from Germany were also in attendance.

Among the winners, the Audience Choice was granted to the documentary "Joanna," directed by Aneta Kopacz of Poland (2013). Additionally, the Andriy Matrosov Award went to "A Diary of a Journey," directed by Piotr Stasik, Poland (2013). The documentary that earned the DOCU/Life top prize, "The Last Limousine," had its screening immediately following the ceremony. The festival, which began in 2003 under the name Docudays on Human Rights, has since been recognized as part of the international Human Rights Film Network at the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam and is typically held in the final week of March.

text:
Lila, a young girl with a dream, wants to become a firework-maker, much like her father, Lalchand. However, Lalchand believes that such a vocation is unsuitable for women. Lila is determined to prove him wrong and embarks on a quest to obtain Royal Sulphur from Razvani the Fire-Fiend atop Mount Merapi—an essential step for any would-be firework-maker. Her journey nearly fails, since she lacks both protection against the Fire-Fiend’s fiery challenges and the required Three Gifts to offer Razvani.

 luck turns when her friends, Hamlet, a wise talking white elephant, and Chulak, Hamlet’s steadfast companion, help by bringing her the water of the Goddess of the Emerald Lake. Surprisingly, despite Lila’s uncertainty about the Three Gifts, Razvani acknowledges her as a true firework-maker upon receiving them.

Returning home, Lila discovers that Lalchand has been imprisoned for Hamlet’s disappearance. To rescue him, Lila and her father must compete in the Firework Festival, facing fierce rivals. Their victory allows Lalchand to reveal the truth: the Three Gifts are not objects, but qualities—talent (honed through years working with her father), courage (shown on her perilous journey), and luck (granted by her loyal companions, Chulak and Hamlet).

text: This study assesses how migration and associated remittances influence development in migrant origin communities in Ethiopia, building on the conceptual framework of the New Economics of Labor Migration (NELM). Empirical analysis, based on household survey data and employing a three-stage least squares approach alongside endogeneity and multicollinearity diagnostics, examines the effects of household migration participation on income diversification and asset accumulation among smallholder farmers. The determinants of migration (both temporary and permanent) were analyzed using logistic and multinomial logistic regressions, revealing that households below the poverty line and those in villages with higher unemployment rates are notably more likely to send both types of migrants. The results indicate that longer spells outside agriculture are associated with negative effects on agricultural income and asset accumulation, though this holds primarily for permanent migrants. In contrast, receipt of remittances consistently correlates with increased agricultural incomes and greater ownership of land and livestock. These findings offer nuanced evidence on the net returns from migration, demonstrating that the developmental impacts of migration and remittances differ across household contexts and migration types.

This paper evaluates the development impacts of migration and remittances in migrant source communities by applying insights from the New Economics of Labor Migration (NELM) theory to Ethiopia’s migration. Using household survey data, we empirically evaluate how household participation in migration arises and so that the subsequent labor losses and the influx of remittances affect income sources and asset accumulation of smallholder farm households. To account several econometric issues and consistently estimate the impacts of migration and remittances, we adopted three-stage least-squares method complemented with endogeneity and multicollinearity test. Besides, using logistic and multinomial logistic regressions respectively, we estimate the determinants of the household migration decision to have migrants, as well as the probability of the household to send out temporary or permanent migrants. Findings suggest that larger and wealthier households are less likely to have migrant family members, while households living below the poverty line, as well as villages with the highest unemployment rate, are the most likely to have both temporary and permanent migrants. However, a rise in months spent out of agriculture has a significant negative effect on crop income and asset accumulation, but only for permanent migration. By contrast, the influx of remitted income from migrants has led to increased crop income and asset values in the form of land and livestock holdings. Finally, this manuscript provides more comprehensive evidence by showing the net-returns of migration in terms of initial lost-labor effects and the positive developmental impacts that it produces varied for households with different types of migration and production conditions.
</source>

text:
Jake Barnes, a wounded American journalist living in Paris, serves as the novel’s central figure. His war injury, which left him impotent, shapes both his identity and his yearning for intimacy, though the exact nature of his physical harm remains withheld. His principal desire is to be with Brett Ashley, an independent and fiercely modern Englishwoman with a penchant for brief, passionate connections and a penchant for bobbed hair reflecting the liberation of the 1920s. Early in the story, Jake is depicted in the vibrant Parisian café scene, engaging first in tennis with his old college friend Robert Cohn. That evening, Jake encounters Brett and the flamboyant Count Mippipopolous in a Parisian nightclub, eventually joining her for a tense ride through the city. In the taxi, Brett confesses her love, but both sense their chances are slim.

The narrative shifts as Jake’s circle expands: Bill Gorton, a steady New Yorker, arrives from America, and Brett’s intended, Mike Campbell, a reserved Scottish man, comes from across the sea. The group heads to Spain, where Jake and Bill share a tranquil fishing trip with Cohn near Burguete—a respite complicated by Cohn’s lingering obsession and jealousy over Brett. Despite the initial camaraderie, Cohn’s presence unsettles the group, who make fun of his Jewish heritage, underscoring the brittle social bonds among them. In Pamplona, the characters immerse themselves in the exuberant Spanish fiesta. They witness the running of the bulls, enjoy feasts, and are repeatedly embroiled in heated arguments—especially over Brett, whose attention is now shared with the young matador, Romero. Brett’s attraction to Romero ignites further rivalry, especially between Cohn, who fights Jake and Mike after being provoked, and the others.

After the revelry, the mood shifts as the group disperses: Bill returns to Paris, Mike stays behind in Bayonne, while Jake heads north to San Sebastián. However, a crisis interrupts this separation—Brett has fled to Madrid with Romero, leaving her without funds and seemingly alone. Jake rushes to her aid, finding her in a modest hotel and emphasizing the sense of lost opportunities throughout their encounters. When Brett announces her decision to return to Mike, the novel closes on a note of resignation and regret, with Jake and Brett in a taxi, reflecting on what might have been. Throughout, the novel explores the emptiness beneath the era’s exuberance and the enduring pain of unfulfilled desires.

<source>
 The protagonist of The Sun Also Rises is Jake Barnes, an expatriate American journalist living in Paris. Jake suffered a war wound that has caused him to be impotent; the nature of his injury is not explicitly described in the novel. He is in love with Lady Brett Ashley, a twice-divorced Englishwoman. Brett, with her bobbed hair, embodies the new sexual freedom of the 1920s, having had numerous love affairs. Book One is set in the Café society of Paris. In the opening scenes, Jake plays tennis with his college friend Robert Cohn, picks up a prostitute (Georgette), and runs into Brett and Count Mippipopolous in a nightclub. Brett and Jake leave together; in a taxi she tells him she loves him, but they know they have no chance at a lasting relationship. In Book Two Jake is joined by Bill Gorton, recently arrived from New York, and Brett's fiancé Mike Campbell, who arrives from Scotland. Jake and Bill travel to Spain, where they meet Robert Cohn north of Pamplona for a fishing trip. Cohn, however, leaves for Pamplona to wait for Brett and Mike. Cohn had an affair with Brett a few weeks earlier and still feels possessive of her despite her engagement to Mike. Jake and Bill enjoy five days of tranquility, fishing the streams near Burguete, after which they rejoin the group in Pamplona, where they begin to drink heavily. Cohn's presence is increasingly resented by the others, who taunt him with anti-semitic remarks. During the fiesta the characters drink, eat, watch the running of the bulls, attend bullfights, and bicker with each other. Jake introduces Brett to Romero at Montoya's hotel; she is smitten with the 19-year-old matador and seduces him. The jealous tension among the men builds; Jake, Campbell, Cohn, and Romero each love Brett. Cohn, who had been a champion boxer in college, has fistfights with Jake, Mike, and Romero, whom he injures. Despite the tension, Romero continues to perform brilliantly in the bullring. Book Three shows the characters in the aftermath of the fiesta. Sober again, they leave Pamplona. Bill returns to Paris, Mike stays in Bayonne, and Jake goes to San Sebastián in northeastern Spain. As Jake is about to return to Paris, he receives a telegram from Brett asking for help; she had left with Romero for Madrid. He finds her in a cheap hotel, without money, and without Romero. She announces she has decided to go back to Mike. The novel ends with Jake and Brett in a taxi speaking of the things that might have been.
</source>

text:
Edmund White’s life has been marked by complexity and contradiction. He has built his reputation at the intersection of high culture and popular fiction. As a professor of creative writing at Princeton University and the author of the acclaimed biography of Jean Genet, White occupies a position recognized in New York, London, and Paris. His relationships and personal history—including family dynamics involving jealousy and complicated parental figures—have informed his writing. White has maintained close ties with notable figures such as Salman Rushdie, Sir Ian McKellen, and others in the arts. 

White’s work often explores themes of desire, taboo, and the complexities of familial bonds. He has expressed difficulty keeping track of the number of romantic encounters he has had, suggesting an openness to discussing the messy realities of sexuality and identity. This candor has been part of his reputation among peers and critics. In interviews, he has acknowledged the influence of his personal background on his craft, particularly the emotional turbulence within his own family. 

In conversations about literature’s role in shaping new generations, White has noted a gap between classic texts taught in schools and the current needs of young readers. He has observed that many influential works remain unfamiliar to younger audiences, which can leave them without relatable connections to literature. He has also commented on genre classification, suggesting that what is labeled as a particular genre often depends more on marketing than on intrinsic qualities of the work. 

White’s writing has at times drawn attention to themes that are considered provocative or transgressive, including those related to sexuality and power dynamics. He has discussed how these themes reflect real psychological challenges and societal taboos, rather than merely sensationalism. In his own experiences, he has addressed the tensions between control and vulnerability, particularly in the context of intense personal relationships. 

When asked about the psychological dimensions of his past relationships, White has not shied from reflecting on the emotional cost and negotiation involved in such dynamics. He has also questioned whether the persistence of certain motifs—such as those associated with incest in his work—stems from intrinsic truths about human experience or from the reaction of society and readers. For him, the exploration of difficult subjects often serves as a means to understand broader questions about desire, forbiddenness, and the limits of narrative. 

White’s approach to writing, influenced by both literary tradition and his own lived experience, continues to provoke debate and discussion. His work remains a testament to the power of literature to grapple with uncomfortable truths, shaping both his own identity and the cultural conversation around representation and taboo.

What you are about to read is an American life as lived by renowned author Edmund White. His life has been a crossroads, the fulcrum of high-brow Classicism and low-brow Brett Easton Ellisism. It is not for the faint. He has been the toast of the literary elite in New York, London and Paris, befriending artistic luminaries such as Salman Rushdie and Sir Ian McKellen while writing about a family where he was jealous his sister was having sex with his father as he fought off his mother's amorous pursuit.

The fact is, Edmund White exists. His life exists. To the casual reader, they may find it disquieting that someone like his father existed in 1950's America and that White's work is the progeny of his intimate effort to understand his own experience.

Wikinews reporter David Shankbone understood that an interview with Edmund White, who is professor of creative writing at Princeton University, who wrote the seminal biography of Jean Genet, and who no longer can keep track of how many sex partners he has encountered, meant nothing would be off limits. Nothing was. Late in the interview they were joined by his partner Michael Caroll, who discussed White's enduring feud with influential writer and activist Larry Kramer.

DS: When you notice you are very flexible in your thought and change notions easily, does it have broader implications for you?

DS: One interview I did was with a young novelist named John Reed—

DS: Yes, married, kids. But he feels a problem with creating a new generation of readers today is that the literary canon does not have many modern works at the grade school and high school level, and young readers feel disconnected from reading.

DS: That would seem like racy material for grade school or high school.

DS: Do you see a generation that can assume the mantle for the Violet Quill or is there not a necessity for it?

DS: You think that’s because of a lack of a community of writers?

DS: Earlier you were saying what makes a book a certain genre is a marketing function.

DS: You said in an interview that the smartest people are the best sex—

DS: Do you think that’s a necessity in order to have a successful relationship?

DS: To give up the feeling they always have to be in control in their waking lives?

DS: What psychological issues did you work through in your slave-master relationships?

DS: As if the fashion never changes? It’s always the same chaps, the same harness…

DS: In an interview you said that you are known for the incestuous feelings that were in your family—

DS: —what advice would you give to couples pursuing an incestuous relationship?

DS: Is that because there is an intrinsic problem with it, or because of societal reactions to it?

T'Pol must reckon with whether this desperate choice truly violates the Vulcan code—or if she has, in fact, betrayed it most deeply.

text:
Benjamin was born looking like an elderly man, though he could already speak and seemed remarkably articulate for his age. His father, Roger, noticed his oddness and, trying to help, encouraged him to play with the neighborhood children and their toys. But Benjamin complied only because he wanted to please his father, never really feeling at home in those settings. By age five, he was enrolled in kindergarten, but he quickly fell asleep through almost every activity, leading to his eventual removal from the class.

By the time Benjamin reached twelve, the Button family noticed he wasn’t aging as he should. When he turned eighteen, he tried to join Yale College, but the school’s registration staff, startled by his youthful appearance and the fact that his hair was faded, sent him home, convinced he was a deluded 50-year-old man. Years earlier, in 1880, at the age of twenty, Benjamin had inherited Roger Button & Co. Wholesale Hardware. During this period, he met Hildegarde Moncrief, the daughter of a general, and was immediately smitten with her. Hildegarde, believing Benjamin to be a much younger brother, welcomed him into her family life without realizing his true age or condition.

Their marriage, arranged quickly out of mutual affection, brought little joy to Benjamin. Over time, he grew weary of Hildegarde’s relentless nagging and the loss of the beauty and vibrancy he once enjoyed. Family life became monotonous and unsatisfying for him. Seeking escape, Benjamin enlisted in the Spanish-American War in 1898. He distinguished himself in the military, rising to lieutenant colonel and earning a medal before eventually leaving the service due to the demands of his business.

By 1910, after years of success running the family hardware company, Benjamin transferred management to his son, Roscoe, and decided to return to education. He enrolled at Harvard as a young man, his appearance now that of a twenty-year-old. His first year at Harvard was marked by remarkable academic and athletic achievement, especially in American football, where he sought and won revenge against his old rival, Yale. However, as his time at Harvard wore on, Benjamin began to weaken. By his final two years, he was barely able to keep up with the coursework or play football, his physical and mental state that of a much younger boy.

After graduating, Benjamin returned home, only to discover that his wife had moved to Italy. He was forced to live with his son Roscoe, who treated him with strict formality, insisting that Benjamin call him “Uncle” in front of visitors. As the years passed, Benjamin regressed from a thoughtful young man into a moody teenager, and then, gradually, into the mindset of a young child. Eventually, Roscoe’s own child attended kindergarten with Benjamin. After kindergarten, Benjamin’s grasp on his past faded, his memories diminishing until all that remained was the comfort of his nurse. And then it was all darkness.

<source>
 Benjamin is born with the physical appearance of a 70-year-old man, already able to speak. His father Roger invites neighborhood boys to play with him and orders him to play with children's toys, but Benjamin only obeys to please his father. At five, Benjamin is sent to kindergarten but is quickly withdrawn after he repeatedly falls asleep during child activities. When Benjamin turns 12, the Button family realizes that he is aging backward. At the age of 18, Benjamin enrolls in Yale College but having run out of hair dye on the day of registration, is sent home by officials, who think he is a 50-year-old lunatic. In 1880, Benjamin is 20, his father gives him a control of Roger Button & Co. Wholesale Hardware. He meets Hildegarde Moncrief, a daughter of General Moncrief, and falls in love with her at the first sight. Hildegarde mistakes Benjamin for a 50-year old younger brother of Roger Button, and without realizing the fact of Benjamin's abnormality, the two get married six months later. Years later, Benjamin's business has been a great success, but his family life hasn't been well for him. Benjamin starts to get tired of Hildegarde because she's a nagging woman that is no longer beautiful as before. His family life is so boring that he joins the Spanish-American War in 1898. He had a great success in the military, ranked up to lieutenant colonel, and rewarded with a medal. He then quits the military because his company requires his care. In 1910, Benjamin turns over control of his company to his son, Roscoe, and enrolls at Harvard University, having the appearance of a twenty-year-old. His first year at Harvard is a great success, and he is dominant in American football, notably obtaining revenge against Yale for his earlier unpleasant experience. However, by the time Benjamin reaches his last 2 years, he is a weak sixteen-year-old, unable to play football and barely able to cope with the academic load. After graduation, Benjamin returns home, only to learn his wife has moved to Italy. He lives with Roscoe, who treats him very sternly, making Benjamin call him "Uncle" in front of his house guests. As the years progress, Benjamin turns from a moody teenager into a young child. Eventually Roscoe has a child that later attends kindergarten with Benjamin. After kindergarten, Benjamin slowly begins to lose memory of his earlier life. His memory fades away to the point where he cannot remember anything except his nurse. Then everything fades to darkness.
</source>

text: A couple, a husband and wife locked in their home near Brockwell Park in South London, are found in a near-fatal state—severely dehydrated, bound, and one of them severely injured, with the husband on the brink of death. Their 8-year-old son, Rory Peach, has vanished. Detective Inspector Jack Caffery leads the investigation, haunted by the parallel to his brother Ewan, who went missing at nearly the same age in a similar abduction years before. As Caffery races to locate Rory, he supports his close friend as she recovers from a recent sexual assault, while also seeking evidence that might shed light on Ewan’s fate. The investigation uncovers disturbing patterns of child sexual abuse within the park’s history. Caffery identifies a man from his youth, involved in the abuse of another child in the same park long ago. When the missing boy’s body is eventually found and DNA evidence points to the husband, Alek, as a contributor through sexual assault, the case takes a startling turn. However, the presence of mismatched bite marks on the child’s shoulder suggests a different scenario—one where the boy, Rory, was forced to abuse his own sibling. Caffery’s efforts intensify as he follows new leads, which ultimately reveal another family of young boys has been trapped. Through careful evidence review and persistent analysis, Caffery gradually reconstructs the identity of the captors and comes to believe his own brother might still be alive, held captive by a notorious child molester operating within a local paedophile ring.

text:
Tattooing is more common among adults in Myanmar, particularly within 18–35-year-old men and women across various socioeconomic groups. Studies indicate this practice is associated with risk-taking behaviors, especially when performed under unsanitary conditions. Evidence suggests a concerning potential for blood-borne infection transmission during such procedures. However, data on the prevalence and the associated awareness of infection risks in Myanmar remains limited.

A cross-sectional survey of 401 adults aged 18–35 in four urban and rural locations within the Mandalay district collected self-reports on tattooing. The estimated self-reported prevalence of tattoos in this population was 19.5% (95% confidence interval: 16–24). Most participants (approximately 80%) reported awareness of at least one blood-borne viral infection that can be transmitted via tattooing. Factors linked with higher knowledge about infection transmission included higher levels of formal education, manual labor, and living with family members. The ability to remove a tattoo independently was also associated with a greater likelihood of getting tattooed (adjusted odds ratio 1.91; 95% CI 1.06–3.45, p = 0.03).

Gender was a strong predictor: men were over 13 times more likely to have a tattoo than women (adjusted odds ratio 13.07; 95% CI 6.25–27.33; p < 0.001), and this association was statistically independent. The findings highlight that, in the absence of regulated tattooing practices and safety guidelines, a notable proportion of young adults, especially men, are getting tattoos, increasing the risk of blood-borne pathogen exposure. These results identify key target populations and risk factors that should be central to future public health interventions. Further research is needed to examine the perspectives and practices of tattoo artists to promote safer standards in the industry.

<source>
Tattooing especially gains popularity among both men and women in adulthood from the wide range of socioeconomic groups and is noted as a risk taking behaviour in adults. Especially when tattooing does not perform to the highest standards, it can potentially be the hazardous practice. Myanmar has a paucity of evidence-based information on the estimated prevalence of tattoos and awareness of potential disease transmission from tattooing under insanitary conditions as well as the infection risk. The present research was undertaken to help identify the self-reported prevalence of tattooing among adults (18–35 years) and their knowledge of transmission risk of blood-borne infections and its determinants.

A community-based cross-sectional study focused on residents aged 18–35 years was carried out in two urban and two rural areas in Mandalay district, Mandalay Region during 2015. Trained interviewers used a pre-tested structured questionnaire for face-to-face interviews with one eligible participant per selected household (n = 401). Bivariate analysis and multivariable analysis using binary logistic regression were done to ascertain the relevant explanatory variables.

The overall self-reported prevalence of tattooing was 19.5% (78/401) (95% CI = 16–24). Nearly 80% of participants (318/401) knew at least one blood-borne viral infection that could be transmitted from tattooing. The persons who had high formal education, manual laborers and those who lived with their families were significantly more likely to cite at least one blood-borne viral infection. Their perceived possibility to remove tattoo independently influenced the practice of tattooing (aOR = 1.91, 95% CI = 1.06–3.45; p = 0.03) compared with participants who reported no perceived possibility. Tattooing was more common in male (aOR = 13.07, 95% CI = 6.25–27.33; p<0.001) compared to female which was independently significant.

This study ascertained the tattoo prevalence as two in ten adults of working age especially among male in central part of Myanmar in the context of lack of registration system for tattoo parlours and the issuance of safety guidelines. Findings have suggested the target groups and risk factors to be included in future health promotion programs. Future research directions should focus on perspectives of tattooists to create and sustain the sanitary practices to reduce the chance of transmission of blood-borne viral infections.
</source>

text: Buffy runs into two demons while shopping, and she notices a shy, gangly blonde girl watching from a distance. After the confrontation, Buffy tries to speak with the girl, but she bolts away before Buffy can catch up. Meanwhile, at school, Dawn befriends a young girl named Arianna, who is isolated due to her abusive mother and a lifelong longing to become a hero. When Buffy realizes Arianna possesses the same extraordinary strength she encountered at the store, the group begins investigating the source of Arianna’s powers. At the same time, a demon named Aurek is searching desperately for his daughter, knowing she is destined to become the Reaver—a being capable of destroying entire dimensions. After brief moments of connection with Buffy, Arianna starts pulling away, fearful that Buffy might one day destroy her in the end. Now, Arianna must decide if she will retain her humanity in the face of her family's darkness and her own growing strength.

text:
Over forty individuals have perished and at least fifty have been injured following a rail accident at a level crossing near Marsa Matruh, Egypt. A truck failed to halt at the crossing, forcing several vehicles stopped there to move forward into the railway tracks. The oncoming train then collided with the trapped traffic, causing two carriages to overturn onto the stationary cars, while two more carriages derailed.

As a result of the crash, thirty-five people lost their lives at the scene, with an additional five fatalities confirmed in hospital, bringing the total number of deaths to at least thirty-nine. The toll may rise as authorities continue searching for additional casualties among the wreckage. Three vehicles were involved in the incident, at least two of which were crushed beneath the train. One carriage was completely separated from the rest of the train.

Emergency teams have been mobilized to the site to safely remove the damaged rail carriages, and numerous emergency vehicles are on the scene. Authorities have launched an investigation into the accident. Witnesses have noted that the level crossing is concealed by a hill, which reportedly limited drivers' visibility and reaction time. It remains unclear whether all the victims were Egyptian, or if any foreign nationals were among those onboard.

text: At the Brookenham home, an outdated and somewhat decadent social circle thrives, centered around the well-to-do Mr. and Mrs. Edward Brookenham. Their children, Harold—considered lacking ambition—and the intelligent, eighteen-year-old Nanda, are the focus of local gossip and ambition. One evening, Mr. Longdon, a man seemingly outside the inner circle, unexpectedly attends a Brookenham gathering and is astonished to notice Nanda's striking resemblance to his old love, whom he once lost to another man. Meanwhile, the underpaid civil servant, Vanderbank, finds himself drawn to both Mrs. Brookenham and Nanda, though his affections seem split. Mrs. Brookenham, known affectionately as "Mrs. Brook," appears desperate to be entangled with Vanderbank, even as he seems more drawn to Nanda. Unbeknownst to Nanda, her mother is scheming to match her with the wealthy but inexperienced Mitchy from their own circle. However, Nanda advises Mitchy instead to wed Aggie, her supposed step-niece and a girl thought sheltered. When Mitchy obeys, Aggie quickly abandons him. In the midst of these tangled relationships, Nanda, perceptive and resolute, prepares to leave for Mr. Longdon’s country estate, apparently seeking refuge as a substitute for the family she feels has failed to protect her.

text:
On a gray Paris afternoon, Paul Osborn strolls through the city when he spots a man who once killed his father—years gone, but haunting memory returns with a single glance. The past surges as Osborn’s mind spirals back. He becomes fixated on finding the man, Henri Kanarack, the supposed murderer now living quietly among them. Meanwhile, Detective McVey arrives in Paris, drawn by the string of bizarre decapitations where victims’ heads and bodies are found frozen deep below ground. A few days after his arrival, Osborn’s obsession boils over—he tries to kill Kanarack in a fit of madness. But before he can finish the deed, another figure bursts into the scene. In the chaos, Osborn learns from Kanarack’s dying words that his father was killed for money by someone working for Erwin Scholl.

McVey reviews Osborn’s background and the case files, uncovering a strange thread: Osborn’s father had invented a revolutionary scalpel capable of surgical work at temperatures of absolute zero. Around the same year his father died, other brilliant minds—all involved in cryogenic surgery—suddenly vanished, their inventions lost. This pattern raises McVey’s suspicions. There might be a secret society obsessed with reviving and reassembling human body parts using extreme cold, perhaps aiming to resurrect or recreate famous individuals.

As the investigation deepens, McVey learns of Elton Lybarger and an upcoming event in Berlin—a ceremony that, on the scheduled day, turns sinister. During Lybarger’s speech in the main hall, all doors lock and cyanide gas fills the air. The building soon catches fire, and Osborn narrowly escapes, his survival tied to the actions of one of the organization’s remaining members, Von Holden. Fleeing to Switzerland, Osborn is nearly killed, but McVey saves him by giving him a VCR tape. On it, a physician’s confession emerges: he participated in experiments on Elton Lybarger, part of a plot to create descendants with features matching Adolf Hitler. The aim was to raise “perfect Aryans” who could lead a new Third Reich, using Lybarger as a figurehead—his “nephews” being raised from childhood in secret.

Memory fragments return sharply for Osborn. He sees Von Holden fall into a deep crevasse and notices the package he carried—a deep-frozen head, unmistakably that of Adolf Hitler. The truth becomes clear: the society sought to use advanced cryogenic surgery not only for resurrection but to build a new, evil regime. Osborn, once a man haunted by personal loss, is now caught in the middle of a battle for the soul of science—and humanity itself.

text:
On Wednesday afternoon, an eight-year-old girl named Victoria Stafford, a third-grader at Oliver Stephens Public School in Woodstock, was last seen leaving her school with an unknown woman. Surveillance footage captured the scene near Fyfe Avenue, close to College Avenue Secondary School. Since then, Victoria has not been located.

Authorities from Oxford, Waterloo, and London have coordinated a search involving police, specialized rescue teams, and trained dogs. The operation is being treated as a criminal investigation. So far, no abduction report has prompted the issuance of an Amber alert.

Over 150 community members had previously joined the search effort, distributing flyers across the area. Police say they no longer need additional volunteer searchers at this stage, though they are actively asking for anyone with information or sightings of Victoria or the woman seen with her—described by Police as a woman between 19 and 25 years old, with straight, long black hair, weighing around 120 to 125 pounds. She was dressed in a white coat, black jeans, a black Hannah Montana jacket with a white fur-lined hood, and was carrying a purple and pink Bratz purse. Victoria wore a green shirt, black pleated skirt, black and white shoes, and the same-sized Bratz purse.

As an Easter Sunday candlelight vigil is planned for Victoria’s honour, authorities urge anyone with information to come forward.

text: Glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) inhibitors, such as lithium chloride and CHIR99021 trihydrochloride, were shown to directly influence fruiting body development in the fungi Coprinopsis cinerea and Pleurotus djamor. These compounds allow for precise regulation of fruiting initiation without the need for heat treatment, which is often required to suppress fruiting in mycelial materials. By modulating GSK-3 activity, it is possible to establish specific inhibitor concentration ranges that effectively prevent fruiting body formation throughout various stages of the fungal life cycle. These sensitive windows offer a biochemical approach for controlling mycelial growth and stability at lower costs. This study represents the first application of GSK-3 inhibitors to inhibit fruiting in living fungal mycelium-based substrates, opening new avenues for the engineered maintenance and functional use of mycelium-derived materials.
