<source>
Living fungal mycelium with abolished ability to form fruiting bodies is a self-healing substance, which is particularly valuable for further engineering and development as materials sensing environmental changes and secreting signals. Suppression of fruiting body formation is also a useful tool for maintaining the stability of a mycelium-based material with ease and lower cost. The objective of this study was to provide a biochemical solution to regulate the fruiting body formation, which may replace heat killing of mycelium in practice. The concentrations of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) inhibitors, such as lithium chloride or CHIR99021 trihydrochloride, were found to directly correlate with the development of fruiting bodies in the mushroom forming fungi such as Coprinopsis cinerea and Pleurotus djamor. Sensitive windows to these inhibitors throughout the fungal life cycle were also identified. We suggest the inclusion of GSK-3 inhibitors in the cultivation recipes for inhibiting fruiting body formation and regulating mycelium growth. This is the first report of using a GSK-3 inhibitor to suppress fruiting body formation in living fungal mycelium-based materials. It provides an innovative strategy for easy, reliable, and low cost maintenance of materials containing living fungal mycelium.
</source>

text: Antarctic research environments have historically favored masculine stereotypes, limiting women’s participation in fieldwork. A recent survey of 95 women in the Australian Antarctic Program reveals ongoing obstacles to engagement in Antarctic research and remote fieldwork. Five persistent gendered challenges were identified. First, physical barriers continue to impede women’s access to remote sites. Second, caregiving and unpaid labor duties frequently preclude women from leading or joining field expeditions. Third, cultural sexism and gender bias remain prevalent, shaping workplace dynamics and opportunities. Fourth, women often face insufficient recognition or advancement despite their contributions. Fifth, women encounter unwanted attention and harassment, further deterring participation. These findings highlight the need for systemic change, as current inclusivity initiatives in polar science have not adequately addressed gender or sexual orientation. Targeted diversity and equity programs are essential to ensure all researchers, regardless of gender or identity, can participate equitably in Antarctic science.

<source>
Antarctica is often associated with images of masculine figures battling against the blizzard. The pervasiveness of heroic white masculine leadership and exploration in Antarctica and, more broadly, in Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics, and Medicine (STEMM) research cultures, has meant women have had lesser access to Antarctic research and fieldwork opportunities, with a marked increase since the 1980s. This article presents findings from an exploratory online survey examining how 95 women experienced research and remote Antarctic fieldwork with the Australian Antarctic Program. Although women are entering polar science in greater numbers, a key theme of the qualitative findings of this survey is that gendered barriers to participation in research and fieldwork persist. We discuss five key gendered barriers including: 1) Physical barriers, 2) Caring responsibilities/unpaid work, 3) Cultural sexism/gender bias, 4) Lack of opportunities/recognition, and 5) Unwanted male attention/sexual harassment. We argue that the lack of attention paid to gender and sexuality in polar fieldwork contributes to the invisibility and exclusion of women and other marginalized identities broadly. To conclude, we point to the importance of targeted inclusivity, diversity and equity initiatives through Antarctic research globally and specifically by National Antarctic Programs.
</source>

text:
Forty families were evacuated from the Guardia Civil barracks in Calahorra, La Rioja, after a car bomb detonated around 2 p.m. The explosion damaged the building’s structure, forcing an immediate emergency response. One Civil Guard officer was injured when he ducked to the ground to escape the blast; he suffered a neck injury and received treatment for minor trauma. National Radio reported that eight people were seen at the local hospital, all released after medical evaluation. No one died.

The bomb was planted in a blue Honda Civic, which was thrown across the street by the force of the blast. The vehicle had been stolen at gunpoint earlier that day; its two owners were discovered later in the afternoon, bound and unconscious in a remote mountain region roughly 100 kilometers away. Authorities confirmed the vehicle’s theft and the details surrounding it.

The attack was claimed by ETA, the Basque separatist group. Thirty minutes before the explosion, a call was made to the DYA road assistance service in Vizcaya, identifying itself as ETA. The bombing occurred in a high-traffic zone, just after one of Spain’s major Holy Week processions ended. The barracks had been targeted once before, in 1983, when ETA carried out an attack that caused no casualties.

Security forces maintained heightened vigilance due to the possibility of a secondary device. The regional government of La Rioja, under President Pedro Sanz, denounced the attack. Sanz planned to visit the site and attend a 8 p.m. demonstration at Calahorra Town Hall. He said that a major loss of life would have occurred had the evacuation not happened so quickly. This event follows the killing of Isaías Carrasco, a former Socialist councillor, in Mondragón two weeks earlier—an incident also linked to ETA.

text:
Nearly twenty years after the last chapter of the original *Tales of the City* concluded, Armistead Maupin returns to the city and its people with *Michael Tolliver Lives*. The narrative opens not in a grand scene, but with Michael Tolliver colliding in a San Francisco café with someone from his past—brief, awkward, and charged with everything unsaid. That moment pulls him back into a history he’s spent years carrying: the loss of friends to AIDS, the city’s slow shift from the raw energy of the 1980s to the sterile glow of the dot-com era.

This time, the story unfolds through Michael’s own voice—no longer an observer, but the center of the frame. The third-person distance of the earlier books is gone. Now, when he speaks of Anna Madrigal, the old woman whose apartment on Barbary Lane once held the heart of a scattered community, it’s not with nostalgia, but with the weight of having outlived most of them.

He’s still close to Brian Hawkins and his daughter Shawna, who’s grown into a pansexual writer with a restless edge. Mary Ann Singleton still circles through, her old questions now filtered through the years. The new people are different: Ben, his younger partner, whose energy feels both welcome and unsettling; Jake Greenleaf, a trans man at work, quiet but present, carrying a history that only a few in the room recognize.

The plot tightens when Michael learns his mother, long estranged over his sexuality, is dying in Florida. She had once called him a “disgrace.” Now, the guilt of that rejection isn’t just memory—it’s a choice. He’s torn between flying to her bedside and staying in San Francisco to support Anna, who’s been through more than anyone, and now needs him most. The city has changed. The people have changed. He hasn’t. Not really.

The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) has suspended Niger after the country held a legislative election on Tuesday, defying regional appeals to postpone it. The vote followed a disputed August referendum that altered the constitution to extend President Mamadou Tandja’s term. ECOWAS had warned that proceeding without a political consensus would trigger suspension, and now enforces that consequence.

Tandja rejected calls from ECOWAS leaders to delay the election, citing that preparations were too far advanced to halt. The regional body had requested an indefinite postponement to allow for dialogue aimed at resolving the crisis stemming from the contested referendum. The opposition has boycotted the vote for 113 parliamentary seats, arguing the process is illegitimate. This boycott continues a pattern of resistance, including a prior strike against the referendum, and reflects persistent skepticism toward Tandja’s authority—especially after he dismissed the constitutional court for ruling the referendum unconstitutional.

Alat Mogaskiya, co-founder of Niger’s Party for Democracy and Socialism, said that while Tandja may have had the legal power to dissolve parliament, he failed to meet the 90-day constitutional deadline for calling new elections. Mogaskiya maintains the new government is both illegal and without legitimacy due to the unconstitutional extension of the president’s term.

Issoufou Tamboura, the ruling party’s communications secretary, responded that the opposition’s absence would not compromise the election’s credibility. He pointed to the ruling party’s size as a measure of support, and noted participation from several smaller parties. Tamboura insisted the election would proceed as scheduled, that the government remains committed to forming a new assembly, and that it will continue its work. He emphasized that participation is voluntary and that the process, as it stands, is expected to be credible.

text: Ceramides in the stratum corneum are essential for skin barrier integrity. One form, EOS ceramide with linoleate, contributes directly to the formation of the cornified envelope. As this ceramide breaks down, it yields trihydroxy-linoleic acid—triol. Because triol is a degradation product, we proposed that diminished levels might reflect barrier failure in atopic dermatitis. To test this, we measured triol in the stratum corneum using tape-stripping, a minimal-invasive method, in 20 healthy individuals and 20 people with atopic dermatitis. The technique proved practical and yielded consistent results. Surprisingly, triol concentrations were higher in atopic dermatitis patients than in controls. Within atopic dermatitis patients, elevated triol levels in non-lesional forearm skin correlated with increased transepidermal water loss. This suggests that triol is not simply a byproduct but may reflect altered lipid turnover or oxidative stress. The data indicate that tape-stripping to measure triol could provide a viable, non-invasive way to assess barrier status in atopic dermatitis.

text:
Alaric walked alone for eight months after the farmers who raised him turned him away. Found as a baby, wrapped in bloodied cloth, his ankle clutched in a severed hand, he had always been different. The power to vanish and reappear—no word for it, no name they could give—made him unwelcome. Now he carries just a knapsack, a change of clothes, and his lute, moving through roads that lead nowhere. He didn’t seek the castle, but the gate opened. The towers rose like the end of a song, and he was given a place at court.

Medron, the king’s magician, watched him too closely. Princess Solinde spoke in riddles, her eyes never quite resting on his face. He didn’t mean to get caught, but he was drawn into the quiet war behind the walls. When he left, he didn’t look back.

The Inn of the Black Swan stood at the edge of a nameless moor, its sign hanging crooked, its hearth cold. Stories followed him there—how the dead walked in the courtyard, how silence lasted for three days after a man died. He stayed two nights, then moved on.

A village nestled in the folds of old hills, where the trees leaned too far and the wind never spoke without meaning. There, an old woman traced the mark on his palm. She said his blood remembered what he’d forgotten. He was not a freak, not a curse. His people had shaped time, moved through space without effort. His gift was not a flaw. It was inheritance. The Lords of All Power had not died. They had returned, in him.

text:
A retrospective analysis of 152 patients with stage II–IV bladder cancer who received curative-intent radiotherapy between 2000 and 2010 found varied outcomes across disease stages: 72 had stage II, 49 stage III, and 31 stage IV. Treatment was either concurrent chemoradiotherapy (n = 97) or radiotherapy alone (n = 55). Pelvic radiation averaged 63 Gy, mostly delivered with cisplatin-based regimens. Median follow-up was 35.5 months.

Sixty-nine patients achieved a complete response to radiotherapy, representing 45.4% of the cohort. Five-year overall survival stood at 45.8%, cause-specific survival at 48.9%, and disease-free survival at 20.8%. Univariate analysis linked survival to age, initial hemoglobin, clinical T and N stages, clinical stage group, tumor response, presence of hydronephrosis, and chemotherapy use. Multivariate modeling confirmed age as a significant predictor of both overall (p = 0.003) and cause-specific (p < 0.017) survival. Tumor response remained strongly associated with improved overall (p = 0.002) and cause-specific (p < 0.001) survival. Concurrent chemotherapy independently predicted better disease-free survival (p = 0.046). These survival rates align with published data from comparable groups. Tumor response and concurrent chemoradiotherapy emerged as key determinants of outcome. The findings underscore the need for randomized trials to clarify radiotherapy’s role in muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

Morales, who had long pushed for a constitutional assembly, now appears poised to reconsider that stance. Rodríguez Veltzé has committed to holding early elections, possibly as soon as December. One notable disruption occurred when ElBaradei was prevented from voting after a group of demonstrators threw stones near his polling station. Security forces responded with batons, and the area briefly descended into chaos.

In Cairo, crowds gathered outside government buildings, blowing car horns and setting off firecrackers as the results were announced. Many saw the outcome as proof that the vote had not been rigged in favor of any faction. The reforms, they argued, marked a turning point—the first time Egypt had moved toward open, competitive elections since the early 2000s.

text:
Dementia affects millions worldwide, and in the UK, it’s common for one in four hospital beds to hold someone with the condition. Nearly 20% of these hospitalizations stem from issues that might have been avoided with earlier action. This study explores how low-cost, in-home sensory devices—linked via the Internet of Things—can support continuous monitoring of people with dementia. By combining environmental signals and physiological measurements collected in the home, the system aims to improve care coordination and reduce emergency admissions.

A key challenge is preventing alert fatigue. The system uses machine learning to filter out noise, reducing false alarms while maintaining accuracy. One algorithm uses Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to detect recurring patterns in sensor data. When anomalies emerge—such as changes in movement, sleep, or bathroom use—it flags potential urinary tract infections (UTIs), which account for about 9% of dementia-related hospitalizations in the UK.

Another algorithm applies Isolation Forest (iForest) to track daily routines. It identifies subtle shifts in behavior that may precede cognitive decline or physical health issues, allowing for earlier intervention.

All components were built in collaboration with clinical staff to ensure they reflect real care settings. Testing used long-term, real-world data gathered from individuals with dementia and their caregivers, including traces from actual home environments. Results confirm that these approaches work under practical conditions, offering a viable path to more responsive, less disruptive care.

Lila wants to make fireworks, not because it’s easy, but because she’s watched her father, Lalchand, shape the bright bursts from ash and powder since she was small. He’s never said no to her touch, but he hasn’t said yes, either. When the law requires a proof of fire-spirit to begin, he turns away. The Royal Sulphur lies at the base of Mount Merapi, a place where the air burns and stone cracks under heat. No girl has ever brought it back. Lila goes anyway.

She climbs through blackened rock, her hands blistered and cracked, her breath sharp with smoke. The Fire-Fiend’s roar girds the mountain, and her body shudders with heat. No charm protects her—she carries none. The Three Gifts are not something she can name, only sense when they arrive. At a turning point, Hamlet, the white elephant with eyes like pale ice, and Chulak, his keeper, appear from a blind ravine. They carry a flask of water from the Emerald Lake, not for healing, but for truth. Lila drinks.

Razvani sees her—not the girl, but the fire she brings. He calls her maker. She doesn’t know what the Three Gifts are. She only knows she walked through the furnace and came out still breathing.

When she returns, Lalchand is in chains. The village elders say he left Hamlet behind during the last festival. To free him, they must win the Firework Festival. Lila and Lalchand face five teams, each with older hands and sharper edges. They win. Afterward, Lalchand tells her: the Three Gifts were never gifts. Talent—years of watching. Courage—the climb. Luck—Hamlet and Chulak, who never let go. Lila had them all. She had them before she even knew their name.

Near Alexandria, just beyond the Temple of Taposiris Magna, Egyptian archaeologists have found fragments that might lead to the burial site of Cleopatra and Marc Antony. The discovery comes from a region where noble mummies—some wrapped in vivid linens—were recently unearthed. The temple, built around 300 BC by Ptolemy II and dedicated to Isis, sits atop a rocky hill overlooking the Mediterranean. Its location, not far from the summer residence once occupied by Egypt’s former president Hosni Mubarak, adds to the site’s historical weight.

Dr. Roger Vickers’ team used ground-penetrating radar to detect three chambers buried 40 feet (12 meters) beneath the surface. These chambers lie within the hill that forms the temple’s foundation. The Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA) expedition, led by Zahi Hawass, has not yet entered them. They plan to return on April 22 with additional radar scans. Among their aims: to identify a royal crown or hieroglyphic cartouches that could confirm the presence of a monarch.

Hawass, who serves as Secretary General of the SCA, works alongside Martinez, an expert on Cleopatra’s life. Plutarch’s account notes that Caesar permitted Antony and Cleopatra to be buried side by side, a detail that informs the current search. The team’s research remains constrained by seasonal delays. Due to ongoing security issues, they may defer excavation until cooler months. No further action is expected before summer.

A year after Archbishop Iakovos of America died, a memorial service was held in Boston on April 9, 2006. Professor Athanasios Angelopoulos, affiliated with the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, and Nicolas Mottas, a politics graduate from Westminster University in London, attended the first annual commemoration. They came as representatives of the Ecumenical Hellenism program and the Institute for National and Religious Studies in Thessalonika.

At the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America, they met Nikie Calles, who had served as the archbishop’s personal secretary and director of his archives for years. Later, they spoke with Paulette Poulos, director of development for Leadership 100 and formerly an aide to Iakovos at the Onassis Cultural Centre in New York. Their discussions centered on previously unpublished letters and documents relating to human rights and national matters, an effort now nearing completion. The collection will be released in both Greek and English later in the year.

They also met with Demetrios, the current Archbishop of America. The Ecumenical Hellenism program, established in 1996, was initially supported by Hellenic Republic President Constantinos Stephanopoulos. It now operates under the patronage of the Ecumenical Patriarchate and the Church of Greece.

text:
In the winter of 1864, a small village in the Netherlands huddled near its network of canals, where frost had gripped the water for weeks. Fifteen-year-old Hans Brinker and his younger sister Gretel watched the ice thicken, not just as a season’s turn, but as a threshold. The annual ice-skating race was the only thing that made the village pause. The prize—Silver Skates—had not been won by a local in ten years. Hans’s skates were made of wood and nailed together by his own hands; they cracked at the first sharp turn. Gretel’s were worse, barely more than splinters wrapped in leather.

Their father, Raff Brinker, had not worked since a fall from the dike five years earlier. He wandered the house muttering, sometimes striking at shadows, his eyes wide and unfocused. Their mother worked three shifts a week at the laundry, earning enough to keep bread on the table and a sliver of firewood in the hearth. The neighbors spoke to them only when necessary, not out of malice, but because poverty made them invisible.

Hans found Dr. Boekman at the edge of the village, near the old schoolhouse. The doctor had not spoken to anyone since his wife and child died in the typhus epidemic. He wore a coat too fine for the cold, his hands stiff and pale. Hans approached him with the last of his savings—six coppers and a rusted button he’d traded for a single penny. He did not ask for medicine. He offered the coins for a chance to speak with the surgeon about his father.

Boekman looked at the boy, then at the coins, and did not laugh. He sat with Raff that night, listened to his fragmented speech, and ordered a trephining. The operation was not a promise, but a risk: a hole drilled through bone to relieve pressure on the brain. He did it for free. No statement, no gesture—just a final nod.

The operation worked. Raff woke the next morning, knew his wife’s name, remembered Gretel’s birthday. He sat up, drank water from a tin cup, and asked for bread. The family did not weep. They sat in silence, one by one, as if the air had changed.

Later, Hans stood on the ice in steel skates, not his own. He won the boys’ race, but gave the Silver Skates to his friend, who had no shoes to wear to the event. Gretel won the girls’ race, her face pressed into the wind, not because she was fast, but because she had not stopped.

A trunk was found under the stairs. Inside, untouched by damp or time, were ten silver ducats and a folded letter from 1854. The money had been there all along.

Dr. Boekman returned to the village. He had not known the boy was his son—Raff had remembered him only from a flash of a face, years later, in a dream. He began visiting the house not as a doctor, but as a man who had forgotten how to look at another’s face without fear. He sent Hans to school. The boy studied until his hands shook, then wrote prescriptions.

Gretel married a fisherman. They lived by the canal, close to where the ice once held its breath. The Brinkers were not rich. They were not famous. But they were not afraid anymore.

text: A longitudinal review of stillbirth rates in Sweden since the 1980s shows little overall change, despite ongoing investigations, with many cases still without clear cause. In this study, DNA from 290 stillbirths—those without chromosomal abnormalities—was analyzed for pathogenic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in 70 genes tied to cardiac channelopathies and cardiomyopathies. Library prep used the HaloPlex Target Enrichment System, and sequencing was performed on the Illumina NextSeq platform. Among these cases, 12.1% (31 with one variant, 4 with two) carried variants of likely pathogenic significance, including loss-of-function mutations and previously documented variants in affected individuals. The rate of putative pathogenic SNVs linked to channelopathies in this stillbirth cohort—7.93%—was substantially higher than in two large non-Finnish European control groups (2.70% and 2.30%, both p < 0.001). This disparity strengthens the argument that cardiac channelopathies may underlie a meaningful proportion of stillbirths. The results support including screening for these variants in undiagnosed stillbirth cases to detect hidden cardiac etiologies and improve diagnostic yield.

text: This study examined the yellow seed trait in Brassica oilseed crops, centering on the specific genetic basis of seed coat pigmentation in *B. rapa* var. Yellow Sarson. The goal was to breed yellow-seeded varieties in both *B. rapa* and *B. napus*. To isolate the major quantitative trait locus (QTL) for seed coat color, SCA9-2 on chromosome A9, researchers generated near-isogenic lines (NILs) using Yellow Sarson as the donor. These NILs enabled high-resolution mapping of the QTL region, narrowing it to 18.4 to 22.79 Mb on chromosome A9. Within this interval, six simple sequence repeat (SSR) markers were identified, with recombination rates between 0.63% and 5.65%. Transcriptome profiling of developing seeds uncovered 55 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the SCA9-2 region. Among these, three transcription factors stood out: Bra028039 (NAC family), Bra023223 (C2H2-type zinc finger), and Bra032362 (TIFY). Several other DEGs encoded proteins of unknown function or nucleic acid binding domains, suggesting possible roles in pigment regulation. Functional enrichment analysis revealed strong associations with biosynthetic pathways, particularly flavonoid, phenylpropanoid, and suberin metabolism. This work marks the first detailed analysis integrating linkage mapping and transcriptome data to investigate the genetic control of yellow seed color in Yellow Sarson.

text:
Bobby, fifteen and raised in the South Bronx, lived with his parents and younger sister in a cramped apartment near the elevated train tracks. He’d been seeing Maria for nearly a year—quiet, steady, the kind of girl who remembered his favorite sandwich and always wore the same faded blue scarf. They walked to school together every morning, sometimes talking, sometimes not, just moving through the city’s rhythm.  

One early June morning, they were set upon near the 149th Street station. Two men in black hoodies, no faces, no warning—just shoves, kicks, and a knife to Maria’s neck. She didn’t scream. She just went still. They were found by a janitor, lying in a puddle near a fire hydrant. Maria was airlifted to Montefiore; Bobby was in surgery for seven hours.  

She died three days later. Her face was unrecognizable—skin pulled, bone exposed. The doctors said she’d have survived if not for the nerve damage.  

Afterward, Bobby was taken in by Moishe, a man who lived on the same block, behind a rusted gate with a Star of David painted in faded red. Moishe didn’t talk much at first. He served tea with sugar, always too much. But he knew about loss. He’d been in Auschwitz. He told Bobby about the train ride, the smell of oil and burning hair, the way they counted dead people by the number of shoes left behind.  

Bobby didn’t cry. He sat in silence, staring at the wall where a photo of Maria used to hang. He didn’t ask for revenge. He just remembered the way her scarf had fluttered in the wind that morning, before the hoodies came.

text: Basal autophagy maintains cellular health by dismantling damaged components and recycling their parts into usable material. Its regulation under steady-state conditions remains unclear. In this study, loss of the Drosophila gene vap—previously classified as a putative enzyme—leads to elevated basal autophagy. This hyperactivity consumes excess energy, indicating a breakdown in normal metabolic balance. Surprisingly, under starvation, this overactivation does not occur. Instead, the starvation-induced pathway fails: autolysosomes do not form, and the cells cannot complete autophagic flux. We suspect this failure stems from an imbalance in membrane trafficking, specifically an overabundance of certain membranes required for autophagosome formation. This disruption correlates with neurodegeneration previously observed in adult vap mutant brains. The protein Spri, a known Vap partner, counteracts this effect by limiting membrane accumulation. Spri is essential not only for baseline autophagy but also for the sensitivity to starvation seen in vap mutants. Rab5 activity, which governs early endosomal dynamics and the assembly of pre-autophagosomal structures, plays a critical role in this process. Together, Vap and Spri appear to modulate vesicle traffic originating at the plasma membrane, a pathway that directly influences the initiation and progression of basal autophagy. The imbalance caused by vap loss disrupts this delicate trafficking, leading to pathological autophagic flux.

text:
A gray afternoon in Paris. Paul Osborn walks through the city, half-remembering, half-seeing—then he sees Henri Kanarack. Not a face from a photograph, not a name in a file. The man who killed his father, years after the act, still walks the world. Osborn freezes. Not from cold, not from shock—but from the weight of a memory that had buried itself deep, only to rise again with the force of a physical blow.

He starts looking for Kanarack. Not because he expects answers, but because the act of looking is the only thing keeping him from vanishing into the past. A few days later, in a café near the Seine, Osborn makes a move. He corners Kanarack, not with a weapon, but with a kind of desperate clarity. Before he can finish it, a man bursts through the door—McVey, the detective, already on the trail of a pattern.

McVey came to Paris because of the bodies. Five of them. Heads severed, found frozen beneath rubble in the old subway tunnels. No signs of struggle. No witnesses. Just cold and silence. He finds Osborn’s file, learns his father died under suspicious circumstances—on the same year Osborn’s father’s cryosurgical scalpel was patented, a device that worked at temperatures near absolute zero.

Then he finds the pattern: five other researchers linked to cryogenic surgery. All brilliant. All vanished. Their work erased. The files show no records of death, no funerals. Just absence.

McVey begins to wonder if the murders aren’t random. If they’re not just about killing, but about something worse—reclamation.

A lead emerges. Elton Lybarger. An academic. A man with a speech scheduled for Berlin. McVey tracks him. The event begins normally—lectures, applause—then the doors lock. Cyanide floods the air. The fire starts fast. Osborn survives, not by luck, but because Von Holden, a man he’d seen in the crowd, throws him through a side hatch. The man never speaks. He falls into a crevasse on the way out, clutching a package wrapped in steel foil.

Later, in Switzerland, Osborn is nearly dead when McVey finds him. He hands over a VCR tape. The recording is from a doctor, voice cracked, confessing to experiments on Lybarger. Not just experiments—breeding. The goal: to produce a new generation of men with Hitler’s facial structure, raised in secret, molded from infancy to carry his legacy. Lybarger was not a leader. He was a prototype—a father figure for a new regime.

Osborn sees it now. Not just resurrection. Not just science. Control. The scalpel wasn't meant to save lives. It was meant to preserve the tools of a new order.

He remembers Von Holden’s fall. The package. He opens it. The head is frozen solid. The jaw, the nose—familiar. The face is not just preserved. It is waiting.

The society wasn’t just rebuilding the dead. It was building a world that never died. And Osborn, once a man shaped by grief, is now standing in the middle of it.

The morning began without warning. The Dalmatians stirred to silence—no voices, no footsteps. All across the city, humans and animals lay still, deep in sleep. Then came Cadpig’s bark, sharp and faraway, pulling from London’s center. She was the Prime Minister’s dog now, and she’d called them. Scattered reports confirmed the same stillness everywhere.

Pongo and Missus left for Cruella de Vil’s house. They brought a handful of dogs, Tommy, and a white Persian cat who’d long been treated as one of their own. The front door opened on its own. Inside, she was asleep, just like the rest.

They moved next to Trafalgar Square. Atop Nelson’s Column stood Sirius—no longer a myth, but a being from beyond, claiming dominion over all dogs. To every dog, he appeared as their own kind. He offered sanctuary, a place beyond Earth’s dangers: war, neglect, the violence of human hands. The dogs weighed the choice. Pongo, who had seen more than most, was asked to decide.

Three thin strays arrived then, three dogs whose names nobody remembered. Pongo expected them to want to leave, but they didn’t. They wanted to stay. They hoped, quietly, to find owners. Pongo told Sirius the dogs would not abandon their people. Sirius nodded. He gave them one gift: the chance to reach his home before the sleep broke. The strays accepted. They ran toward Battersea, not knowing if they’d find home, but certain they’d try.

On the second day of the European Union summit in Brussels, leaders finalized a framework of binding targets to lower greenhouse gas emissions and increase the use of biological fuels. The 27 member states accepted three main goals, aligned with the international aim of limiting global warming to under 2°C above pre-industrial levels. Each country will design its own emission reduction strategy based on its current energy systems and capacity for transformation, though no enforceable mechanism has been put in place. The E.U. signaled it might strengthen its commitments if major industrialized nations follow suit, and called on non-member countries to submit climate action plans before the Kyoto Protocol ends in 2012. German Chancellor Angela Merkel intends to share the E.U.’s approach with the Group of Eight in June.

The agreement allows each nation to determine its energy path, including decisions about nuclear power. This compromise reflects real differences: Germany is closing its nuclear plants, while France relies on nuclear reactors for 70% of its electricity—roughly 13% of its total energy supply. Nuclear safety remains a central concern in any discussion of its future role.

The summit also instructed the European Commission to draft measures by 2008 and 2009 to cut energy use in lighting and office equipment. A key goal is replacing traditional incandescent bulbs with more efficient models. The E.U. reaffirmed its focus on energy security, particularly for eastern members, through expanded market coordination, cross-border energy networks, and mutual support during supply disruptions, including those potentially triggered by Russia.

The two-day gathering also covered growth, employment, regulatory changes, and foreign policy.

text:
Benjamin arrived in the world with the face of a man past sixty, skin slack, eyes deep-set and weary. His voice, when he first spoke, was precise, almost unnervingly so—a child’s tongue, but shaped by years of unspoken thought. Roger, his father, saw the discord in him and tried to ease it, urging him to play with other boys, to hold their wooden soldiers and ride their tricycles. Benjamin did as he was told, not from desire but from dutiful obligation. He never fit in. At five, he was sent to kindergarten, but the classroom’s hum, the bright crayons, the childish laughter—none of it held him. He nodded off during circle time, then again at story hour. The teachers wrote him off as distracted. He was removed.

By twelve, the family noticed he hadn’t changed. His hands were still the same, his voice the same, his posture unchanged. At eighteen, he applied to Yale. The registration clerk, startled by his boyish face and the faint gray in his hair, dismissed him as a deluded man in his fifties. Benjamin returned home without protest. He had inherited Roger Button & Co. in 1880, when he was twenty. The business thrived under his steady hand. That year, he met Hildegarde Moncrief, daughter of a general. She thought him a younger brother, a boy on the cusp of manhood. He let her believe it.

They married quickly, drawn by a mutual sense of ease. But over time, Hildegarde’s patience wore thin. Her questions grew sharper, her tone more insistent. He had once seen the world clearly—the grain of wood, the curve of a hinge, the way light caught on brass—but now, that vision dulled. He could not keep up with her expectations. The house felt smaller, the silence heavier.

In 1898, he enlisted in the Spanish-American War. He served with distinction, rose to lieutenant colonel, earned a medal. He left not because he was tired of war, but because the company needed him. He returned to the office, to the ledger, to the daily rhythm of decisions.

By 1910, he had passed management of the business to Roscoe, his son. He enrolled at Harvard under the name Benjamin Button, appearing as a man of twenty. His first year was extraordinary—straight A’s, a starting role on the football team, a victory over Yale that felt personal. But by his second year, he began to falter. He missed lectures. He forgot the name of a professor. His body felt brittle, his thoughts scattered.

He graduated. Returned home to find Hildegarde had moved to Italy, her letters ceased. He lived with Roscoe, who now treated him with a cold politeness. Roscoe insisted he call him “Uncle” in front of guests. Benjamin obeyed.

Then the shifts came faster. The boyishness returned—not as a memory, but as a presence. He stopped thinking in full sentences. He began to cry over small things. He would sit for hours watching children at play, not understanding the point, only the sound.

One day, Roscoe’s child went to kindergarten. Benjamin followed. He sat on the floor, tried to hold a crayon. He didn’t know the name of the teacher. He didn’t know his own name anymore.

His memories dissolved like ink in water. The last thing he remembered was a woman’s hand on his forehead. Then nothing.

text:
Von Willebrand factor (VWF) is essential to primary hemostasis, acting through its multimeric form to mediate platelet adhesion at sites of vascular injury. Arginine vasopressin (AVP) release triggers the secretion of VWF, especially the high molecular weight forms, into the bloodstream. In a prior observation, children who experienced febrile seizures (FS) had significantly higher serum copeptin levels—markers of AVP release—than children with fever alone. Whether this neuroendocrine surge translates into a measurable physiological effect remains uncertain. We examined whether AVP release during FS correlates with increased VWF functional activity, testing the possibility that stress signaling directly engages hemostatic pathways.

We conducted a prospective, cross-sectional study of children aged 6 months to 5 years presenting to the emergency department with fever or within four hours of a febrile seizure. Serum samples were analyzed for copeptin, VWF:antigen (VWF:Ag), VWF:collagen binding activity (VWF:CB), and multimer composition across three groups: 30 with FS, 10 with febrile infection but no seizure, and 14 without fever. Median copeptin was markedly higher in the FS group (24.73 pmol/L, IQR 13.65–68.65) than in febrile controls (5.66 pmol/L, IQR 4.15–8.07; p = 0.002) or non-febrile controls (4.78 pmol/L, IQR 3.33–5.30; p < 0.001). VWF:CB was significantly elevated in FS patients (2.29 U/mL, IQR 1.88–2.97) compared to febrile (1.41 U/mL, IQR 1.27–1.93; p = 0.048) and non-febrile (1.15 U/mL, IQR 0.98–1.21; p < 0.001) controls. VWF:Ag showed a trend toward higher values in FS but did not reach statistical significance. Multivariate regression confirmed FS status and copeptin as independent predictors of VWF:CB. These results demonstrate that neuroendocrine activation during febrile seizures coincides with measurable increases in VWF functional capacity, particularly collagen binding. This links AVP release to hemostatic modulation in FS and positions VWF:CB as a candidate biomarker for physiological changes during these events.

text:
Edmund White’s life unfolds in the margins between public acclaim and private reckoning. His name appears in academic circles at Princeton, among the citadels of letters in New York, London, and Paris, not as an outsider but as someone whose presence has long been accepted, even expected. His biography of Jean Genet stands as a measured, sustained act of literary devotion—structured, attentive, deeply considered. Yet this same figure, who composes with precision, has written with a different kind of urgency about his own experience: the uneven weight of family, the friction between siblings, the way a father’s silence could shape a son’s hunger for language.

He has known Salman Rushdie in the flesh, not just as a name, and spoken with Sir Ian McKellen not in passing but in quiet rooms, over long meals. These are not casual affiliations. They are connections formed in continuity, across years, in the absence of spectacle. His writing, like these relationships, carries a quiet authority—unforced, but not unearned.

What emerges from his work is not a single theme, but a persistent set of questions: how desire operates beneath the surface of everyday life, how familial intimacy can become a form of violence, how power slips between lovers, parents, friends. He once said he lost count of the people he has been close to—romantically, emotionally, physically—because the tally never felt fixed. Not because he counted, but because the boundaries kept shifting, as they do when intimacy becomes a subject, not just a state.

He has remarked on how the books taught in schools—those deemed essential—often feel remote to today’s students. Not because they lack value, but because they do not speak to the way young people now sense themselves, their bodies, their histories. The gap isn’t just generational. It’s existential. Literature, he suggests, has been sold as a monument, not a tool.

Genre labels don’t interest him as much as the way they are applied—how a book becomes “gay” not because of its content but because of who wrote it, who published it, who chose to read it. He has noted, dryly, that a novel might be called a “memoir” not because it claims to record truth, but because it’s been marketed that way.

His work has drawn attention not for shock, but for its refusal to look away. The recurring motifs—those charged with tension, with danger, with the unspeakable—do not appear by accident. text:
At the Brookenham house, where the air smells of old wood and unspoken obligations, the family’s social orbit holds tight. Mr. and Mrs. Brookenham maintain their standing through polite gestures and inherited ease. Their son Harold drifts through life with little direction, while their daughter Nanda, eighteen and sharp-eyed, draws quiet attention. She listens more than speaks, observes more than acts. One evening, Mr. Longdon arrives—an outsider, not of their circle—and halts mid-conversation when he sees Nanda. Her face, he thinks, is a ghost of someone he once loved, lost to another man’s design.

Vanderbank, a civil servant paid just enough to survive, finds himself caught between Mrs. Brookenham’s eager glances and Nanda’s quiet reserve. She watches him, not with longing, but with something like assessment. Mrs. Brookenham, who calls herself "Mrs. Brook" to strangers and intimates alike, seems to want him, though he hardly notices her. He’s drawn to Nanda, not because she offers anything, but because she doesn’t.  

Unaware, Nanda’s mother arranges for her to marry Mitchy, a wealthy youth with no sense of consequence. Nanda, instead, steers Mitchy toward Aggie—her supposed step-niece, raised in isolation, given to quiet tears. Mitchy follows. Aggie leaves him within weeks.  

Now, Nanda prepares to go. Not to marry. Not to stay. She is leaving for Mr. Longdon’s estate, a place she’s never visited, not because she wants to escape him, but because she knows he, too, has not protected anyone. She does not expect salvation. She only expects to be elsewhere.

In 1840, in the village of Tskhvareli, Iago, a peasant boy, fell for Nunu, whose mother had died in childbirth. Her father, a soldier who had fought in Shamil’s rebellion, was now absent, likely dead or captured, leaving her with her uncle’s family. They resented her connection to Iago, whom they dismissed as a lowborn boy with no future. Instead, they favored Grigola, the Russian-appointed village administrator, a man already married but fixated on Nunu. Grigola told her his brother wanted to marry her, though he had no intention of marrying her—only to keep her as his secret mistress. When Iago protested, Grigola had him arrested on false charges of stealing state grain. Iago was locked in the Ananuri fortress, a ruin used as a prison.

Grigola then took Nunu by force. Koba, Iago’s closest friend, saw the abduction but arrived too late. He found her in the woods, bleeding and unconscious, and carried her to a hidden stream. He did not sleep that night. The next morning, he broke into the fortress, cut the chains on Iago’s wrists, and they fled. With help from a third man, they made for the Northern Caucasus, hoping to reach Chechnya. Russian police and Cossack patrols were searching every village along the way. Though many Georgians had served in Russian regiments, Shamil’s forces accepted them. In Chechnya, they were given shelter—not out of kindness, but because resistance was still possible.

The story draws a line between those who fight for their own land and those who live under foreign rule. The Chechens were not idealized—many were armed and violent—but they were free to gather, to speak, to decide their own fate. The Georgians, under men like Grigola, could not hold meetings without permission. The old tradition of open town councils had vanished.

Meanwhile, Nunu escaped from Grigola’s house. Koba found her, told her to meet them in Vladikavkaz, and to bring her father. They planned to reunite in North Ossetia. The night before, their host, a man who had sheltered them for weeks, betrayed them. He wanted their horses. He told Grigola where they were.

After midnight, Grigola arrived with armed men. He killed Iago, the host, and Nunu’s father. He meant to accuse her of murder, to have her sent to Siberia. Koba fled through the trees, but not before hearing her scream. He did not stop.

When he learned she had died from shock and loss, not from a wound, he understood what had happened. He did not weep. He waited in a hollow near a dark forest. Grigola and his superior passed through on horseback. Koba shot both from behind a tree. He did not hide the body. He left the scene as it was.

In the end, Koba was not a hero by nature. He was not proud, nor did he speak of honor. He acted because he could not not act. He had no choice. The story does not ask who was right. It only shows what happened when power, pride, and silence met in a single moment.

Along the way, they meet Bonnie, a woman with a voice like scraped metal, whose mother is wanted for forging checks and vanishing with thousands. They cross paths with two men who carry guns and seem to be hunting for a trunk they think holds cash. The road stretches ahead, and the silence between them isn’t empty—something is on the way.

Carnelian, heir to Lord Suth, and Prince Osidian were taken from Osrakum during a raid on a sealed burial mound. They had been concealed in funeral urns, drugged and bound, their identities hidden beneath layers of dust and silence. The grave robber who discovered them had no clear path: report the princes and die, kill them and risk the wrath of the empire, or flee with them and hope to sell them to slavers. He chose flight.

Osidian’s absence from the coronation meant the throne passed to his brother, Molochite. Osidian, as the emperor’s mortal sibling, was meant to die in ritual sacrifice—his fate sealed before he ever left the capital. The journey out of the city was brutal. Osidian lay near collapse, his breath shallow, his skin pale. Carnelian carried more than his own weight; he carried the burden of keeping them both alive.

They were given to a band of nomads during a raid on the southern road. Carnelian used the chaos to switch captors. The tribesmen, wary of the pale princes, hesitated—but Osidian did not. He fought a starving wolf bare-handed, then led them through a sandstorm using the stars and a memory of maps drawn in the dust. He spoke of the plains as if he had walked them for years. The tribesmen began to listen.

As they reached the ochre tribe’s territory, Osidian’s strength returned. He stood taller, spoke with authority. The elders, who had been taught to fear the ruling blood, now watched him with something like awe. He knew the old ways, the hidden water sources, the routes where ambushes could be set. He began to speak to the elders not as a prisoner, but as someone who had seen the future.

Carnelian settled into the rhythm of life—sleeping on the ground, eating raw roots, learning the tongue. He did not fight. Osidian, though, had not come to survive. He began to speak of his brother’s rule as a betrayal. He arranged meetings between rival villages, used old grudges like flint to strike fire. He let them believe he was a prophet, a war chief, a man who could summon the wind.

By the time they stood at the edge of the high plains, Osidian had a band of men who would follow him. Not because they loved him. Because they believed he could break the empire. He would not return as a prince. He would return as a conqueror.

text: Forty-seven patients with primary hand osteoarthritis and at least one clinically inflamed joint underwent evaluation using optical spectral transmission (OST) and ultrasound (US), which served as the reference standard. The study examined the relationship between standardized OST scores and US-confirmed synovitis across all hand and wrist joints collectively, as well as separately for the wrist, proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. Linear mixed effects models accounted for previously identified US synovitis correlates: osteophytes and dorsal vascularity. Synovitis was identified in 6.7% of joints by ultrasound. A significant association between OST scores and US-confirmed synovitis emerged for all joints combined (Δ0.37SD, p<0.001) and for PIP joints alone (Δ0.81SD, p<0.001). No significant link was found for DIP joints (Δ0.14SD, p=0.484) or wrist joints (Δ0.37SD, p=0.178). These associations persisted after adjusting for osteophytes and dorsal vascularity, suggesting independence from structural OA features. Diagnostic accuracy was assessed via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. The area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC) reached 0.74 for all joints (p<0.001), 0.69 for PIP joints (p<0.001), 0.54 for DIP joints (p=0.486), and 0.61 for wrist joints (p=0.234). The results confirm a meaningful, independent relationship between OST and ultrasound-verified synovitis, with OST showing fair diagnostic value specifically in PIP joints of patients with hand osteoarthritis.

text:
The Heart of Midlothian opens in the Old Tolbooth, Edinburgh’s old prison, during the aftermath of the Porteous Riots in 1736. Two smugglers were hanged, and Captain John Porteous, in command of the city’s military, ordered his men to fire into the crowd. Four people died. The public outrage was immediate. A mob broke into the jail and dragged Porteous from his cell. He was killed there, in that same room where Jeanie Deans would later stand in prayer.

Jeanie Deans is the novel’s central figure. Her story is rooted in the life of Helen Walker, a real woman who, in 1711, traveled on foot from Scotland to London to plead for her sister’s pardon after she was falsely accused of infanticide. Walter Scott took that journey and shaped it into a narrative of moral resolve. Jeanie is raised in a strict Presbyterian household, bound by a faith that demands rigid adherence to principle. She sets out for London not just to seek the Queen’s mercy but to carry a letter from the Duke of Argyll, a man who represents political pragmatism over religious extremism.

The novel marks Scott’s first extended portrayal of a female protagonist from the lower classes. Her journey is both physical and spiritual—she walks through the Scottish countryside, through storm and hardship, guided by duty more than certainty. Scott does not dismiss her beliefs, but he presents their extremity with a quiet, steady irony. The undercurrent of Jacobitism runs through the background: the conflict between Highland loyalty and Hanoverian authority. Argyll’s position—more moderate, more politically grounded—reflects Scott’s own leaning. The book has been adapted into a film, two operas, and a television series, but none of them alter the core: a woman, a journey, and a world shaped by religious fervor and political violence.

A report from the Equality and Human Rights Commission finds that England’s home care system routinely undermines the rights of older adults it is meant to serve. After a 12-month review of services delivered by local authorities, the commission documented repeated violations of Articles 2, 3, and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights—specifically, the right to life, the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment, and the right to dignity and personal autonomy.

The review uncovered that care plans are frequently implemented without regard for practical realities, leaving older people without consistent support. This shortfall has led to situations where basic needs go unmet, increasing the risk of neglect, isolation, and physical or psychological harm within private homes.

The EHRC, which commissioned the report in response to shifting care policies and stagnant funding, is now urging Parliament to pass new legislation that would embed stronger human rights standards into home care provision. The commission will work directly with local authorities to strengthen oversight and ensure that decisions affecting older people and their families are made with genuine attention to dignity and autonomy. It also recommends clearer, accessible guidance for older adults and their caregivers, aimed at improving understanding of rights and available support.

This study examined latent and active tuberculosis in a Colombian prison, focusing on inmates with respiratory symptoms, which affected 15% of the population (301 out of 2,020). Among them, 8% had active TB—equivalent to 1,026 cases per 100,000 inmates, a rate far higher than in the general population. Mycobacterium tuberculosis was cultured from 79% of these cases, and 94.7% of the isolates remained sensitive to first-line antibiotics. One strain showed resistance to isoniazid alone.

Genetic profiling using 24-Locus MIRU-VNTR, supported by spoligotyping, identified three clusters, each with two isolates. The Haarlem lineage was most common (68.4%), followed by LAM (26.3%) and T superfamily (5.3%). One cluster included inmates housed in separate prison blocks, suggesting transmission across different units. Another pair occupied adjacent cells in the same block, while the third linked inmates in close physical proximity.

Tuberculin skin testing was performed on 95.6% of inmates, and 67.6% tested positive. The high rates of both latent and active disease point to ongoing transmission within the facility, likely driven by newly arrived inmates or reactivation of dormant infections. The presence of transmission clusters, especially those spanning blocks, indicates that TB moves between housing units despite structural separation. These findings highlight the need for immediate, focused interventions to interrupt transmission in closed environments like prisons.

text:
Epidural catheters are now standard for postoperative pain control in abdominal surgery. But they carry a risk: they may cause neurolysis, which can impair bladder function and result in postoperative urinary retention. When that happens, patients often need a bladder catheter left in longer, increasing the chance of a urinary tract infection.

The study had two goals: to map out how hospitals currently manage urinary catheters after abdominal surgery, and to find the best moment to remove the suprapubic catheter in relation to the epidural one.

A questionnaire went out to 102 German hospitals. Eighty-three responses were used to see how bladder drainage and epidural catheters are handled. Then, the team looked back at 501 patients treated at University Hospital Würzburg who had both an epidural and a suprapubic catheter after surgery. Patients were split into three groups based on when the suprapubic catheter came out: before, at the same time as, or after the epidural catheter was removed. The team then checked how many developed a catheter-associated UTI.

The survey showed that 98.8% of hospitals used both catheters after abdominal surgery. The timing of removal was split nearly evenly across the three groups—about 28% to 29% in each. The overall UTI rate was 6.7%. Women had far higher rates than men: 10.7% versus 2.5%, and the difference was statistically significant (p<0.001). There was a small rise in UTI rates when the suprapubic catheter was removed after the epidural one—8.4%—compared to 5.7% when removed beforehand, though this difference did not reach statistical significance.

The data suggest that removing the suprapubic catheter before, at the same time, or after the epidural catheter does not clearly affect UTI rates. But practices vary widely across Germany. These differences point to a need for more research to shape consistent clinical guidelines.

text:
We examined how experimentally induced pain influences body representation and spatial awareness during and after tool use. Chronic pain is known to alter these perceptions, but it remains unclear whether acute pain, as manipulated in controlled settings, produces similar effects. The body’s sense of itself and its surrounding space is continuously recalibrated through action—especially when using tools. We asked whether pain disrupts this dynamic updating.

Participants experienced three conditions: experimental pain (via thermal stimulation), a placebo (identical setup without heat), and a neutral baseline. Two tasks assessed changes: one measuring shifts in peripersonal space (how far the body extends into surrounding space) during tool use, and another tracking changes in perceived body size after tool engagement.

Tool use reliably expanded perceived space to include the tool’s endpoint, and body size perception decreased slightly after active use. These changes occurred consistently across all conditions. The presence of induced pain did not alter either effect. Despite expectations that pain would interfere with sensory integration, no disruption was observed in spatial or bodily representation recalibration.

Thus, acute experimental pain does not impair the body’s ability to update its spatial and self-representation in real time during tool use—distinguishing it from the known impacts of chronic pain.

text:
Nikhil, a Bengali zamindar, lives on his family estate in early 20th-century India. He is married to Bimala, a woman of lower social rank and darker complexion, who holds less favor with his relatives. Their marriage, arranged when she was still a child, carries a quiet affection, but it is bound by tradition and the weight of expectation. The balance shifts when Sandip arrives—Nikhil’s friend, a fervent nationalist, and an active voice in the Swadeshi movement. His energy, intensity, and unyielding convictions mark him as different from Nikhil’s measured reserve and the estate’s routine order.

At a gathering in a nearby village, Sandip speaks before a crowd. His voice cuts through the air, and his words move people. Bimala listens, not merely to the message, but to the way he carries it—like a man who believes in what he says. Afterward, she invites him to stay at their house. His presence begins to change her. She starts attending meetings, helping distribute handspun cloth, and speaking at small assemblies. The more she does, the more she feels pulled—less by doctrine, more by the sense of being seen, of being needed, of being alive in a way she hadn’t known.

Her actions grow bolder. She takes money from Nikhil’s locked chest—coins meant for repairs, for estate accounts. She justifies it to herself as necessary, as part of a larger cause. But the truth, even to her, is that she is drawn to Sandip. Not just his ideas, but him—the way he looks at her, as if she might be worth something.

Nikhil finds the gap in the ledger. He knows what she’s done. He does not confront her. He knows she had no real choice, not under the old rules of marriage, not under the pressure of a life that offered no escape. He lets her go.

When the riot erupts, Sandip vanishes. Nikhil is struck by shrapnel, dies days later. Amulya, a boy who followed Sandip and had once called Bimala *amma*, is shot. He was not close to her—no child of her own—but he had looked up to her, and she had thought of him as a kind of promise.

Afterward, Bimala stays in the house. She does not mourn Sandip. She does not regret her actions. But she understands now: the only thing that remained constant, through all the noise and change, was Nikhil’s love. Not because he was perfect, but because he never stopped believing she belonged to him.

text: In Haa province, Bhutan, where rabies does not circulate endemically, a trial evaluated inactivated rabies vaccine (Raksharab, Indian Immunologicals) administered either intramuscularly (IM) or intradermally (ID) in cattle. Antibody levels were assessed using the fluorescent antibody virus neutralisation test on day 0 and days 14, 30, 60, and 90 post-vaccination. An adequate response was defined as virus neutralising antibody (VNA) ≥0.5 IU/mL. All animals were seronegative at baseline. By day 14, 36% of ID-vaccinated cattle reached the threshold, compared to 78% in the IM group (p<0.02). At day 30, 58% of ID recipients met the criterion, while 77% of IM animals did. The cumulative proportion with adequate titres was 71% in the ID group and 89% in the IM group. Mean VNA titres remained significantly lower in the ID group across all time points (p<0.001), with a consistent mean difference greater than 0.6 IU/mL. The ID route produced a measurable immune response, but it was uniformly weaker than IM vaccination. The 0.2 mL ID dose failed to match or exceed the response generated by the 1 mL IM dose. These results show that a single 0.2 mL ID dose of Raksharab vaccine is less effective than 1 mL IM in cattle. Though intradermal administration holds promise for reducing vaccine use and cost, this study confirms that a single 0.2 mL ID dose does not yield equivalent immunogenicity. Further work is needed to define optimal dosing and regimens for intradermal rabies vaccination in cattle before it can be considered a practical alternative.

In South Africa, where HIV remains widespread, the growing burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) among educators presents a pressing challenge. The overlap of HIV and chronic conditions like hypertension or peptic ulcers affects daily work capacity, contributing to absenteeism and reduced effectiveness in classrooms. Yet little is known about how these conditions manifest within the teaching workforce, particularly among those already managing HIV.

This analysis draws on data from the 2015/16 national survey of public school educators, which used a multi-stage, stratified cluster design to select schools across all nine provinces. Schools were chosen with probability proportional to size, ensuring representation from urban and rural areas. The study focused on 2,691 HIV-positive educators who answered questions about NCDs.

Of these educators, 36.9% reported at least one NCD. Hypertension was the most common condition, reported by 17.4%. Stomach ulcers followed closely, affecting 13.5%. Women were significantly more likely than men to report an NCD (aOR = 1.5; 95% CI, 1.1–1.9; p<0.002). The risk rose sharply with age: educators aged 45–54 were 1.8 times more likely to report an NCD (95% CI, 1.4–2.2; p<0.001), and those 55 and older were 2.7 times more likely than those aged 18–24 (95% CI, 1.8–3.9; p<0.001). Conversely, educators who had not missed work due to health reasons were less likely to report an NCD (aOR = 0.7; 95% CI, 0.6–0.9; p=0.003).

These findings suggest that existing health monitoring in HIV programs must expand to include early detection and management of NCDs. Without targeted support, the dual burden of HIV and chronic illness will continue to strain the education system. The department of education must act by integrating NCD screening and preventative care into existing health initiatives for teachers. Preventive strategies should focus on early identification and sustained care, especially for mid-career and older educators.

The European Union’s competition authority fined Microsoft €899 million—about $1.35 billion—over violations of a 2004 antitrust ruling. This is the largest penalty of its kind ever issued by the EU and the first directed at non-compliance with a prior antitrust decision.

This brings the total EU penalties for this matter to €1.68 billion, distributed across three enforcement actions. The collected amount will be used to offset the EU’s annual budget.

Microsoft’s legal challenges in Brussels may not have ended. The commission is now reviewing two new complaints alleging ongoing anti-competitive behavior.

text:
Adolescents living with chronic illnesses are more common now than in the past, and their rates of alcohol and marijuana use match or surpass those of peers without health conditions. When they use these substances, they face greater chances of developing regular or problematic patterns, and their medical conditions often worsen as a result. Yet existing behavioral models for adolescent substance use don’t clearly apply to this group, leaving gaps in how to design prevention efforts that actually work for them. To explore this, researchers held in-depth interviews with 16- to 19-year-olds receiving treatment for chronic illness. The conversations were recorded, transcribed, and coded for recurring themes.  

One recurring pattern involved how illness shaped the youth’s view of health. Many described making choices based on fear of flares or treatment disruptions—some avoided substances altogether because they knew their conditions could worsen. But other impulses, rooted in typical adolescence, pushed them toward risk: a desire to feel more in control, to fit in, or to escape emotional strain. These urges sometimes overrode medical caution, leading to decisions that made long-term health harder to maintain.  

Another persistent issue was incomplete or inaccurate understanding of how substances interact with their health conditions. Some didn’t know how alcohol might interfere with their medication. Others misunderstood how cannabis could affect their neurological symptoms. This lack of clarity led them to downplay risks or base choices on guesses rather than facts.  

In response, youth took different paths: some stopped using entirely, others limited use to specific times or settings, and a few changed medication schedules without telling a provider. These varied responses show how individual experiences, personal goals, and limited information shape decisions. The findings point to a need for clinical care that includes patient-specific advice, not just general warnings—helping young people connect their daily choices to long-term health in ways that reflect their real lives.

text:
Krish and Ananya meet in the mess at IIM Ahmedabad, a place where food is often an afterthought and the air hums with competing accents. He notices her first not for how she looks—though she’s sharp-eyed and still, like a photograph caught mid-breath—but because she’s standing over a tray of lukewarm dal, arguing with the warden about whether "spicy" means "burnt." She’s already known as the fresher who speaks up, not to provoke, but to clarify. They start studying across from each other in the library, then move to a corner table with two chairs and shared notebooks. The shift isn’t sudden. It’s like the point when a river stops being a trickle and begins to carry weight.

They get jobs. She’s offered one in Mumbai, he in Delhi. They begin arranging things—dates, flights, a list of who needs to be told what. Krish goes to her parents’ home in Chennai not with a proposal, but with a folded sheet of paper: a draft of her father’s first PowerPoint, the one he’d been dreading. He helps him fix the font, adds a chart about cost efficiency. Later, he tutors her brother, Manju, who’s floundering in finance, and arranges for a lunchtime concert at Citibank, where Ananya’s mother sings with T.S. Subramanian and Hariharan. She cries during the second song. The family is soft now.

Krish’s mother, though, stays closed. Her relatives call Ananya a Madrasi, not as insult, but as geography—like saying she’s from a place that doesn’t fit. But Ananya helps with a cousin’s marriage, not with advice, but by showing up at a temple in Coimbatore, speaking to a woman over tea, and returning with a name and a date. The silence breaks.

They plan to meet in Goa, parents first. Then her parents call. They’ve heard something from Krish’s mother—something about a conversation over dinner, a look, a word that didn’t fit. The wedding is off. The silence lasts two weeks.

Then Krish’s father, who hasn’t spoken since the first winter, calls. He doesn’t say a lot. Just says, “Let them come.” The wedding happens.

Ananya gives birth to twins. They name them not for a state, but for a line in a song her mother used to hum. The story ends with two babies in a room, one on a pillow, one on a lap, and no one trying to explain why they’re not from anywhere, exactly. A man from a book called *Five Point Someone* appears in a brief scene—nothing more.

In the months leading up to Darth Sidious’s ascension, the Galactic Senate moved like a body slowing toward collapse. Its decisions were no longer shaped by principle but by calculation—by favors traded, by debts owed. Supreme Chancellor Finis Valorum tried to hold the line, but his authority eroded under the weight of systemic decay. Behind the chambers, a Sith presence worked not through open command but through quiet sabotage—feeding doubt, twisting alliances, bending officials to a hidden will.

Outside the Senate corridors, the Trade Federation strained under pressure. Its control over key supply lanes was fraying not only from rival cartels but from an underground cell called the Nebula Front. This group didn’t seek recognition. It acted in silence, striking at transport hubs, sabotaging freighters, and assassinating mid-level executives. Their weapons were fear and desperation, and they used them without hesitation.

When the Federation petitioned the Senate for additional battle droids and border defenses, Valorum hesitated. He wanted to say yes—stability demanded it. But advice from an anonymous source, later confirmed as Sith-influenced, pushed him toward a different path: extract a cost. He demanded a new tax on select Republic-controlled trade routes, calling it a "temporary measure." The proposal fractured the Senate. Delegates from the Outer Rim saw it as surrender. Those from core systems saw it as leverage.

The resulting summit drew nearly every major faction. Amid the tense negotiations, the Nebula Front made its move. Intelligence intercepted a signal from a rogue cell: Valorum was to be killed during the session. The target wasn’t the Chancellor alone—it was the idea of a functioning Republic.

Jedi Master Qui-Gon Jinn and his apprentice Obi-Wan Kenobi were already in the capital, investigating a string of explosive attacks tied to trade routes. They followed the trail to a hidden command center on a derelict freighter in the Coruscant spire zone. There, they found Captain Cohl, not a general, but a former engineer who had turned to violence after his family died in a Federation blockade.

The Jedi Council responded not with immediate force but with coordination—sending agents to monitor Senate protocol officers, rerouting security drones, and cross-referencing known affiliations. The full scope of the plot wasn’t known, but the pieces were assembling.

The Techno Union and Passel Argente appeared for the first time in official records during this period, their roles ambiguous but their presence noted in draft documents and sketchy concept art. These were not just background details; they were the first signs of a network that would soon expand into full war.

Minor errors in the original script drafts—missed letters, misplaced articles—did not obscure the core truth: the Republic was not merely failing. It was already being dismantled, one hidden hand at a time.

text: In an introductory biology course at a small liberal arts college, we replaced traditional lectures with the Integrating Biology and Inquiry Skills (IBIS) curriculum, designed to center student-driven exploration. Over three academic years, we tracked learning gains through pre- and post-tests measuring core concepts like cellular respiration and genetic inheritance. Students showed statistically significant improvement, with average gains of 22 percentage points, and their self-assessments aligned closely with these results. Early feedback noted skepticism, but by the third cohort, 76% of students described the course as “more effective than expected,” citing structured peer discussions and inquiry-based labs as pivotal. These same students reported greater confidence in applying biological reasoning, particularly during complex problem-solving tasks. The shift wasn’t immediate—initial resistance faded as successive groups experienced consistent success. When new students entered, they were more likely to engage early, referencing past cohorts’ outcomes as a benchmark for their own progress. The most consistent pattern wasn’t isolated improvement, but a cumulative effect: as each cohort demonstrated mastery, the next entered with less hesitation. This wasn’t a matter of enthusiasm alone—students identified specific elements, like lab design protocols and peer-led review sessions, as foundational. The data suggest that student-centered design, once stabilized, becomes a self-sustaining mechanism for both learning and participation.

text: From 1880 to 1889, an Ilocano family fled southern Pangasinan, pushed out by grinding poverty and the violence of Spanish colonial rule. He had served as an acolyte, not out of ambition but because it was the only path open to him. He knew the herbs used in village cures, could read the old medical texts, and understood the rhythm of healing. He wanted to become a priest, but the door closed not on his qualifications, but on his name. The execution of Mariano Gómez, José Apolonio Burgos, and Jacinto Zamora—the Gomburza—had left a scar on the archipelago. The Spanish authorities had suppressed reform, crushed dissent, and now watched every movement. The revolution was brewing, not yet united, not yet certain. Many thought the Americans might arrive, not as liberators, but as another kind of force. Istak’s life was not a narrative of conquest or resistance, but a slow negotiation with doubt. He questioned what he had been taught, what he had felt, whether faith could survive in a world that punished his people. He moved through the years with a quiet finality, shaped by absence and memory. He was chosen to carry a message to General Emilio Aguinaldo, who had begun to gather followers in the hills. On the road to him, he was shot by American soldiers. He died not in battle, not in a fight for a cause he had chosen, but in a moment of transition, caught between two histories. His life ended under fire, but he had carried his own understanding through it—unbroken, if not whole.

text: Genetic testing for coronary heart disease (CHD) prevention lacks clear evidence on its economic impact or optimal application. This study examines how genetic testing might best be combined with established risk factors to reduce CHD events, assessing cost and benefit at the population level. We evaluate multiple approaches that integrate traditional risk assessment with genetic testing, using a decision-analytic model that recalculates individual CHD risk after test results through Bayesian updating. The model draws on data from national healthcare registers, the Finnish Institute for Molecular Medicine, and published sources. The analysis takes the healthcare system’s viewpoint, tracking resource use and outcomes over ten years. Results show that the greatest net benefit occurs when genetic testing is reserved for people whose traditional risk profile offers ambiguous prognostic information. In this scenario, adding genetic testing to standard assessment lowers the expected cost per patient aged 45 or older by 2.54€ over a decade, with no reduction in expected health benefits. This outcome remains consistent across plausible variations in input assumptions, indicating stability. The findings suggest that genetic testing, when deployed selectively in this manner, supports a cost-effective strategy for CHD prevention. The evidence points not to replacing traditional risk factors, but to using genetic information as a refinement—improving precision where it matters most in population screening.

This study examined glucose tolerance one year after childbirth in a subset of the Riyadh Mother and Baby Cohort Study (RAHMA), carried out at King Khalid University Hospital. Researchers contacted women from the RAHMA database who had reached the one-year postpartum mark via telephone. Data collected during the original RAHMA enrollment—demographic, clinical, and biochemical—were merged with follow-up information. Current weight, height, and waist circumference were used to calculate BMI. Fasting blood glucose (FPG) and HbA1c levels were measured to assign participants to one of three categories: normal glucose tolerance, prediabetes, or diabetes. The proportion of women falling into each category was calculated across the cohort. Initial comparisons between groups used univariate analysis, and variables with p-values below 0.05 were entered into multivariate models. Bootstrapping was used to estimate relative risk (RR) and 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals (C.I.).

Of the 407 women who met inclusion criteria and completed the follow-up, 250 (61.4%) had normal glucose tolerance, 142 (35.0%) were in the prediabetes range, and 15 (3.6%) met diagnostic criteria for diabetes. After adjusting for multiple factors, three predictors remained significant: a history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) (RR 1.74, 95% C.I. 1.06–2.84, p = 0.01), obesity (RR 1.69, 95% C.I. 1.01–3.11, p = 0.04), and diastolic blood pressure (RR 1.04, 95% C.I. 1.01–1.09, p = 0.03). The high rate of abnormal glucose metabolism in this group confirms that GDM and obesity are strong indicators of risk, reinforcing the importance of targeted screening and early action in postpartum women in Saudi Arabia.
